features.humanInTheLoop: `wait.forToken()` is a well-designed durable gate: you create a waitpoint token, hand it to a human (or any external system), and the run suspends — "Pause runs until a token is completed via an approval workflow." Completing the token with a typed payload resumes the run with that value. Tokens have timeouts and are first-class objects in the dashboard, so pending approvals are visible and manageable. Sibling primitives `wait.for()`, `wait.until()` and `triggerAndWait()` cover delays and child-run joins. Because waits are checkpointed rather than replayed, code before the wait does not re-execute — a real advantage over LangGraph's whole-node replay.
features.parallelism: `batch.trigger()` and `batch.triggerAndWait()` fan out to many independent runs and join on results; each run is a separate container, so this is process-level isolation with elastic scaling. Concurrency is governed by named queues with per-queue concurrency limits and priorities, plus machine-size selection per task. This is the most operationally mature parallelism model in the cluster alongside Inngest's.
features.gitIsolation: None built in — but uniquely among this cluster it *could* support it: tasks run in real containers with a filesystem, so `git worktree` and arbitrary binaries (including Claude Code or Codex CLI) actually work inside a task. There is no framework-level worktree/patch/integrate model; you'd write it. Trigger.dev has publicly courted AI-coding-agent workloads on this basis.
features.multiProvider: Model-agnostic — you call whatever SDK you want inside a task. Documented integrations with OpenAI and the Vercel AI SDK, plus AI-specific helpers (streaming model output through Realtime to a frontend). No AgentProvider abstraction and no per-step model routing concept; that's application code.
features.costControl: No token or USD budgets. Cost control is infrastructure-shaped: per-queue concurrency limits, machine sizes, `maxDuration` per task, and retry limits. Model spend is unmetered by the platform.
features.observability: Strong and the closest analogue to what weft's daemon UI wants to be. "Full observability through our dashboard": a run explorer with per-run timelines, every step/wait/retry, full payload and output inspection, logs and traces per run, replay of a past run with the same payload, and a searchable run history with filters and alerts. The Realtime API "allows you to trigger tasks and get the status of runs," with React hooks (`useRealtimeRun`, `useRealtimeRunsWithTag`) so an app can render live run progress — including streaming LLM output through the run. Self-hosted deployments get the same dashboard.
features.testing: No zero-model-call replay harness. The practical loop is the dev server (`npx trigger.dev@latest dev`) which runs tasks locally against the real dashboard with hot reload, plus run replay from the dashboard. Tasks are ordinary functions so unit testing is unassisted-but-easy.
features.authoringModel: Plain TypeScript, no DSL and no directives: `export const myTask = task({ id, retry, queue, machine, maxDuration, run: async (payload, { ctx }) => {...} })`. The body is ordinary async code — loops, try/catch, awaits — with durability supplied by checkpointing rather than by constraining what you may write. Composition is `triggerAndWait()` (parent/child runs), `batch.triggerAndWait()` (fan-out/join) and `wait.*` (durable pauses). Scheduled tasks use cron declarations. Deployment is `npx trigger.dev deploy` building a container image per task set.

strengths: Container checkpoint-restore durability means no replay-determinism constraint on task bodies — you can call `Date.now()`, use randomness, hold open handles, and still survive long waits. Fundamentally different (and more permissive) trade-off from journal-replay engines.
`wait.forToken()` is a durable, typed, dashboard-visible human gate with timeouts — pending approvals are first-class objects an operator can see and manage.
Best-in-cluster run explorer: timelines, payload/output inspection, logs, traces, filters, alerts, and one-click replay of a historical run.
Realtime API + React hooks let a product surface live run progress and streamed model output with no custom infrastructure.
Real containers with a filesystem and arbitrary binaries — the only project here where running Claude Code or `git worktree` inside a step is actually viable.
Mature operational controls: named queues with concurrency limits and priorities, machine sizing, `maxDuration`, retry policies.
Apache-2.0 with a genuine self-hosting story, and 16k stars with daily commits.
weaknesses: Not an agent framework: no model abstraction, no tool loop, no memory, no structured-output validation or repair, no evals. Everything LLM-shaped is your code.
Schema validation is payload-only at trigger time; step outputs are unvalidated.
No token/USD budgets — cost controls are infra-shaped (concurrency, duration), not spend-shaped.
Checkpoint-restore durability is heavier than journaling: it needs the platform's container infrastructure, so self-hosting is real but non-trivial (Docker/K8s, object storage, Postgres, Redis).
No git/worktree/patch primitives despite being the one platform that could host them.
Locked to its own deployment model — tasks are deployed as built images to Trigger.dev cloud or a self-hosted instance, not embedded as a library in your process.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `wait.forToken()` — a durable, typed waitpoint token that is a first-class, dashboard-visible object with a timeout, handed to a human or any external system, and completed with a validated payload.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.gate/ctx.human blocks a step; turning the pending gate into an addressable token makes it shareable (paste the approval link in Slack), inspectable (a queue of everything awaiting humans across all runs), expirable, and completable by CI or a webhook as easily as by a person.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Container checkpoint-restore as an alternative to replay for surviving long waits — freeze the process, thaw it later, no re-execution of prior statements.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's determinism gate exists precisely because replay re-executes; for the specific case of a long human gate, checkpointing the step process instead would let weft relax determinism rules for gate-bounded steps and eliminate the 'code before the gate runs twice' class of bug entirely.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Named queues with per-queue concurrency limits, priorities, and per-task machine sizing.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft fans out worktree write steps in parallel; a queue abstraction would let 'expensive Opus review steps' and 'cheap lint steps' have independent concurrency ceilings, and bound how many worktrees exist on disk at once.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A run explorer with one-click replay of any historical run using its original payload, plus tag-based search and alerting across run history.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's journal already stores every input; a 'replay this run' button plus cross-run search ('show every run where the test-fix step failed validation twice') turns the log from a recovery mechanism into a debugging and analytics product.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Realtime run subscriptions with React hooks (`useRealtimeRun`) that stream both run status and LLM output to a frontend.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon UI is bespoke; publishing the run stream as a subscribable API with hooks would let teams embed weft run progress in their own dashboards rather than only viewing it in weft's UI.

projects.name: LlamaIndex Workflows (TypeScript)
projects.license: MIT (per repo; verified as MIT on the package, license file not independently re-read)
projects.popularity: 257 stars, 22 forks, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24 — and **the repository is archived** (`archived: true`, last updated 2026-08-05). Included as a negative data point: the event-driven, DSL-free TS workflow approach was tried at small scale and shelved.
projects.positioning: "Simple, event-driven and stream oriented workflow for TypeScript." The TS sibling of LlamaIndex's Python Workflows: no graph DSL, no builder — steps subscribe to event types and emit event types, and the topology emerges from which events flow where. Marketed as "an event-driven orchestration layer for building multi-agent systems in plain Python or TypeScript, without requiring a separate domain-specific language." Now archived; the Python implementation continues.

features.durability: Minimal. The workflow context can be snapshotted/serialized for pause-resume, but there is no journal, no crash recovery story, no pluggable durable backend. Effectively in-memory execution with an escape hatch. Treat as none for production durability purposes.
features.schemaValidation: Events are typed TypeScript classes/objects and the handler signature is type-checked at compile time, but there is no runtime schema validation of step outputs and no repair loop. Zod is not central.
features.humanInTheLoop: No dedicated primitive. The pattern is to emit an event, let the workflow's stream deliver it to the host application, and send a response event back in — workable, but the pause is only as durable as your own storage of the context snapshot.
features.parallelism: Natural to the model: multiple steps can subscribe to the same event and all run concurrently, and a collector step waits for N events of given types before proceeding (the event-driven equivalent of fan-out/fan-in). Genuinely elegant. In-process only.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: Model calls are whatever you write inside a step, typically LlamaIndex.TS or an SDK directly. No routing abstraction.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: Stream-based: the workflow emits events as a consumable stream, so progress is observable by subscribing. No dashboard, no tracing integration of its own, no run history. LlamaTrace/Arize integration exists on the Python side; TS coverage unknown.
features.testing: Steps are pure functions from event to event, which makes them unusually easy to unit test without any harness — arguably the model's best property. No shipped mocking or replay tooling.
features.authoringModel: Event-driven, DSL-free: a step declares which event types it accepts and which it emits, and the runtime routes. Control flow is implicit in event topology rather than written as a program — which means it avoids a DSL but also avoids readable linear control flow, arguably the worst of both worlds for a long coding pipeline.

strengths: Genuinely DSL-free and tiny — the whole model is 'steps consume events and emit events', learnable in minutes.
Steps are pure event→event functions, making them trivially unit-testable with no framework support required.
Fan-out/fan-in falls out of the event model naturally: many steps subscribing to one event, and a collector awaiting N event types.
Stream-oriented output makes progress observable without a separate tracing layer.
weaknesses: Archived as of 2026-08 — do not build on it. The clearest signal in this cluster that a minimal event-driven TS workflow library is hard to sustain against Mastra/WDK.
No real durability, no crash recovery, no checkpointing backend.
No runtime schema validation, no human-in-the-loop primitive, no cost controls, no observability dashboard.
Implicit control flow: reading the code does not tell you the order of execution, which gets worse as workflows grow.
Tiny adoption (257 stars) and the TS port always trailed the Python original.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Collector steps that wait for N heterogeneous event types before firing — declarative join conditions rather than an explicit await of a known tuple.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.parallel joins a fixed set of known steps; a 'proceed once the type-check result AND any two of three review results have arrived' join would express partial-consensus coding patterns that a fixed tuple await cannot.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Steps as pure event→event functions, testable with zero framework scaffolding.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's zero-model-call harness is engine-driven; keeping individual step *functions* independently callable with a plain input and asserting the Zod-validated output — no engine, no journal — would give users a fast inner test loop underneath the full replay harness.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A negative lesson worth internalizing: minimal event-driven TS workflow libraries without durability, validation, or an inspector UI did not survive 2026.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Confirms weft's bet — the defensible surface is exactly the parts this project lacked (journaled durability, runtime schema validation, human gates, an inspector), not the authoring-model elegance it had.

cluster: Durable execution / workflow-as-code engines (the durability lineage weft draws on)

projects.name: Temporal (server + TypeScript SDK + AI/agent integrations)
projects.language: Go (server); TypeScript SDK; also Java/Go/Python/.NET/Ruby/PHP SDKs
projects.license: MIT (both temporalio/temporal and temporalio/sdk-typescript — verified on GitHub 2026-08-24)
projects.popularity: 22,502 stars on temporalio/temporal and 899 stars on temporalio/sdk-typescript, verified via the GitHub API on 2026-08-24. The reference implementation of durable execution; largest enterprise adoption in this cluster.
projects.positioning: The canonical event-sourced durable execution platform. Workflow-as-code where the whole workflow function is deterministically re-executed against a persisted Event History. General-purpose (not coding-agent-specific), but pushing hard into AI agents: the OpenAI Agents SDK integration (Python) went GA in March 2026, and an official TypeScript package `@temporalio/ai-sdk` (AiSDKPlugin + temporalProvider) for Vercel AI SDK shipped January 2026.

features.durability: Event sourcing, not step memoization. Every command (activity scheduled/completed, timer started/fired, signal received, child workflow started) is appended to a per-execution Event History persisted by the Temporal Service in Cassandra/MySQL/PostgreSQL. On worker loss another worker replays the entire history through the workflow function to rebuild in-memory state, then continues issuing new commands. History size/count limits force `continueAsNew` for long-lived runs.
features.schemaValidation: None at the engine level. Payloads pass through a pluggable `DataConverter` (JSON by default) with optional PayloadCodecs for encryption/compression. Type safety is TypeScript compile-time only; there is no runtime schema enforcement of step outputs and no repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: Three distinct primitives, all durable because they are history events rather than in-process state: Signals (`defineSignal` + `setHandler`, fire-and-forget input), Queries (read-only, must not mutate), and Workflow Updates (`defineUpdate`, synchronous request/response with an optional validator; GA in TS SDK v1.9.0). `condition(predicate)` blocks until a predicate holds; `sleep()` creates a durable timer. No approval UI, forms, approver identity, or N-of-M — you build all of that yourself.
features.parallelism: `Promise.all` over `proxyActivities<typeof activities>()` calls and `startChild`/`executeChild` child workflows. Horizontal fan-out is via task queues and worker fleets, tuned with `maxConcurrentActivityTaskExecutions`/`maxConcurrentWorkflowTaskExecutions`. Nexus provides typed cross-namespace calls (GA since 2025).
features.gitIsolation: None. No worktrees, patch capture, or integration step — anything touching a repo is an ordinary Activity with no isolation guarantees from the engine.
features.multiProvider: Nothing at the engine level. Provider abstraction exists only in the AI integrations: `@temporalio/ai-sdk`'s `temporalProvider.languageModel()` wraps any Vercel AI SDK model so the call executes as an Activity, and the Python OpenAI Agents SDK integration wraps model calls and tools as Activities. Per-step routing is per-Activity options, not a first-class provider router.
features.costControl: None for tokens or USD. Resource governance is namespace-level and task-queue-level rate limiting plus Temporal Cloud billing. There is no per-run budget, no hard ceiling, and no budget inheritance to child workflows.
features.observability: Temporal Web UI shows the full Event History per execution, pending-activity state, and stack traces of blocked workflows; Visibility (Elasticsearch) plus custom Search Attributes for querying runs; OpenTelemetry interceptors and SDK metrics; `temporal` CLI. Temporal Cloud adds usage/limits dashboards. The per-run event history is the single best forensic artifact in this cluster.
features.testing: Best-in-class. `@temporalio/testing` provides `TestWorkflowEnvironment.createTimeSkipping()`, an in-memory test server that fast-forwards durable timers so a 30-day sleep completes instantly, plus `testEnv.sleep()` for manual clock control. Activities are mocked by passing `Partial<typeof activities>` to the Worker. Separately, `Worker.runReplayHistory()` / `runReplayHistories()` feed recorded production histories through new code and throw `DeterminismViolationError` on divergence — a genuine CI gate for 'is this edit replay-safe'.
features.authoringModel: Plain async TypeScript functions in a `workflows.ts` module, bundled by Webpack v5 when the Worker starts. Control flow is ordinary `await`/`Promise.all`; side effects are reached exclusively through typed activity proxies. Determinism enforcement: the bundle runs inside a Node `node:vm` context (`VMWorkflowCreator` / `ReusableVMWorkflowCreator` in packages/worker/src/workflow/; `reuseV8Context` is on by default, giving one V8 context per worker thread with per-workflow objects swapped in and out per Workflow Task). Inside the sandbox `Math.random()` is replaced by a seeded PRNG that reproduces the same sequence on replay, `Date.now()`/`new Date()` return the last Workflow Task completion time, timers are routed to durable Temporal timers, `WeakRef`/`FinalizationRegistry` are removed (non-deterministic GC), and a curated safe global set is injected (URL, URLSearchParams, TextEncoder/TextDecoder, AbortController, an AsyncLocalStorage shim, a replay-aware console). Note the contrast with weft: Temporal replaces globals and catches violations at REPLAY time via command-sequence mismatch, with no static/AST pre-flight gate.

strengths: The most battle-tested event-sourced replay implementation in existence; the Event History is the authoritative, inspectable record of every decision a run made.
Determinism violations fail loudly (`DeterminismViolationError`) instead of silently corrupting state — a hard guarantee weft's tolerant salvage deliberately trades away.

Two complementary, mature answers to mid-run code edits: `patched('id')` / `deprecatePatch('id')` markers written into history, and Worker Deployment Versioning (GA; min Server v1.29.1) with Pinned vs Auto-Upgrade behaviors, Deployment Versions, percentage ramping and instant rollback.
Time-skipping test server plus replay-from-recorded-history CI harness — nothing else in this cluster tests durable code this well.

Real multi-tenancy: namespaces are isolated by default, cross-namespace traffic is only possible through Nexus endpoints with explicit service contracts, and per-namespace rate limits prevent noisy-neighbour effects.
Signals / Queries / Updates give three genuinely different human-input shapes, including validated synchronous updates.
weaknesses: The workflow sandbox is a hard cage: no Node built-ins, no fs, no network, no child processes in workflow code. Every real action must be an Activity — heavyweight and awkward for coding-agent steps that want to shell out.
Non-determinism is only detected during replay; there is no authoring-time static analysis equivalent to weft's AST determinism gate.
`patched()` leaves permanent conditional scar tissue in workflow source; the alternative (Pinned versioning) requires keeping old worker fleets alive.
Zero git awareness — no worktree isolation, patch capture, or integrate step.
No schema validation or in-session repair of step outputs; a malformed model response is just an opaque value.
Operationally the heaviest option: server + persistence store + Elasticsearch, or pay for Temporal Cloud.
History size limits mean long agent loops must `continueAsNew`, which fragments the run's narrative across executions.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `Worker.runReplayHistory()` as a CI gate: replay every recorded production journal against the new code and fail the build on divergence.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's edit-tolerant replay silently salvages, which means a semantically breaking edit can pass unnoticed. A `weft replay-check ./journals/*` command that reports which recorded runs would now diverge turns tolerance from a hope into a tested property.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Author-declared `patched('change-id')` markers persisted in the journal, with a `deprecatePatch` retirement phase.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Content-addressed salvage infers compatibility. An explicit, journaled branch point lets an author say 'this change is intentional and here is the old path', which is auditable and survives cases where hashing can't tell semantic change from cosmetic change.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Pinned vs Auto-Upgrade as a per-workflow versioning policy, with percentage ramping and instant rollback of the Current Version.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has one replay policy. Some coding workflows (a long review loop) want to be pinned to the code they started on; others want to pick up fixes immediately. Making that a declared policy per workflow, with a ramp, is strictly more expressive.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Workflow Update (`defineUpdate` with a validator function) — a synchronous, validated, durable request/response channel into a running workflow.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's ctx.human.ask/approve are specific shapes. A generic validated update channel would let a daemon UI, a CLI, or an MCP client inject typed corrections mid-run and get a typed answer back, with rejection before anything is journaled.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Namespace isolation with Nexus endpoints as the only cross-boundary path.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has no multi-tenancy at all. Namespaces-plus-explicit-contracts is the proven shape for one engine serving many teams/repos without shared-fate.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A time-skipping test server that fast-forwards durable timers and gates.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's zero-model-call harness handles agent calls, but a workflow with a 24h gate or a backoff sleep is still slow to test. Skipping durable time makes long-horizon workflows testable in seconds.

projects.name: Restate
projects.language: Rust (server); SDKs in TypeScript, Java/Kotlin, Python, Go, Rust
projects.license: Server: Business Source License 1.1 (verified from the repo LICENSE; Change License is Apache 2.0 after 4 years) — NOT OSI open source today. TypeScript SDK: MIT.
projects.popularity: 4,338 stars on restatedev/restate, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24. Well-funded, fast-moving, strong AI-agent marketing push through 2026.
projects.positioning: A single-binary durable execution server that sits in front of ordinary functions running in your own process. Restate owns the journal, the scheduler, the timers and an embedded K/V store; your handlers stay plain, unsandboxed code. Positions itself explicitly against Temporal's determinism cage.

features.durability: Every SDK interaction is journaled by the Restate Server (Rust, RocksDB-backed log and K/V, Raft-replicated in cluster mode): `ctx.run` results, sleeps, RPC calls, state get/set, awakeable completions. On failure the handler is re-invoked and journal entries are fed back so completed operations return their recorded value rather than re-executing. Handlers SUSPEND rather than block on long waits, so a run parked on a human costs nothing on FaaS/serverless.
features.schemaValidation: No engine-level validation of step results. The TS SDK gives typed service definitions and pluggable serde. There is no Zod-style validate-and-repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: `ctx.awakeable()` returns an id plus a promise; hand the id to a human, a webhook, or another system, and `ctx.resolveAwakeable(id, payload)` / `ctx.rejectAwakeable(id, reason)` resumes the suspended handler from any process. Workflow handlers additionally get `ctx.promise(name)` — named durable promises resolvable by any other handler in the service. Durable `ctx.sleep()` for timeouts. No approval UI, forms, or approver identity.
features.parallelism: `ctx.run` returns futures; `RestatePromise.all` / `.any` combinators; durable one-way (`send`) and request/response RPC to other services via `ctx.serviceClient` / `ctx.objectClient`. Virtual Objects enforce a single-writer-per-key guarantee, which is effectively a durable distributed mutex.
features.gitIsolation: None. No worktrees, patches, or integration semantics.
features.multiProvider: None built in. The vendor's own durable-AI-agent guidance is 'wrap whichever SDK's model call in `ctx.run`', so provider routing is entirely user code.
features.costControl: None for tokens or USD. No budget, ceiling, or inheritance.
features.observability: Restate UI lists invocations and renders the actual journal entry-by-entry for each invocation, plus a state inspector for Virtual Object K/V. CLI verbs (`restate invocations …`, `restate deployment describe <id> --extra` to count in-flight invocations). OpenTelemetry trace export. The per-invocation journal viewer is the standout debugging surface.
features.testing: Weakest of the top tier. No time-skipping test server and no replay-divergence harness. Practice is running a local `restate-server` (or testcontainers) and doing integration tests.
features.authoringModel: Plain unsandboxed TypeScript async handlers registered as one of three shapes: Services (stateless handlers), Virtual Objects (keyed, with isolated K/V state and single-writer serialization), and Workflows (run-once per id, with `ctx.promise`). No bundler, no vm, no global replacement — you can use any npm package.

strengths: The journal is a first-class, human-inspectable artifact rendered per invocation in the UI — the closest analogue to weft's append-only event log as a product surface.
No sandbox and no determinism cage: ordinary Node code, any library, any Node built-in. Durability comes from wrapping side effects in named `ctx.run` blocks, not from banning language features.
Awakeables are an elegant, externally-addressable HITL primitive: an opaque id that anyone holding it can resolve, from anywhere, at any time.
Virtual Objects' single-writer-per-key guarantee is exactly the primitive weft would need for 'only one agent may hold this repo/branch', and it comes free with the programming model.
Suspension means a run blocked on a human holds zero compute and zero memory.
Single Rust binary with an embedded store — no external database, Redis, or Elasticsearch to operate.
weaknesses: BSL 1.1 server is not open source (Apache 2.0 only after the 4-year Change Date) — a hard blocker for many teams and for embedding.

Restate's answer to mid-run edits is immutable deployments, and the vendor's own blog concedes 'very long running handlers are still a headache' — precisely the case a multi-day coding workflow occupies.
No edit-tolerant replay: an in-place edit that reorders, adds, or removes SDK calls yields error RT0016 on replay.
No static determinism gate; non-determinism only surfaces as a replay mismatch after the fact.
No time-skipping or deterministic test harness worth the name.
No schema validation, no cost budgets, nothing git-aware, no agent-provider abstraction.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Awakeables: `ctx.awakeable()` mints an opaque id + promise; `resolveAwakeable(id, payload)` from any process completes it.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's ctx.gate presumably resolves through the engine/daemon. An awakeable-style id turns a gate into something a Slack bot, a GitHub Action, or a curl from a reviewer's laptop can complete with no access to weft's internals — and the payload can be schema-validated on arrival.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Virtual Objects: keyed entities with a single-writer guarantee and isolated K/V state, serialized by the engine.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's write steps run in isolated worktrees but nothing prevents two concurrent workflows from racing on the same branch or `ctx.integrate()` target. A per-repo/per-branch virtual object would serialize integrations without weft building a lock manager.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `restate invocations pause <id>` then `restate invocations resume <id> --deployment <new-id>` as explicit operator verbs.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Moving a specific stuck run onto fixed code should be a deliberate, auditable command, not only an implicit consequence of replaying with edited source. Weft's salvage would benefit from the same verb pair for the case where an operator knowingly wants a run migrated.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Suspension-on-wait: a handler parked on a timer or awakeable holds no process at all and is re-invoked on completion.
ideasWorthStealing.why: If weft's gates hold a Node process (or a worktree) open for days, cost and resource pressure scale with pending human reviews. Suspend-and-rehydrate makes an arbitrarily large backlog of pending human steps free.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The per-invocation journal viewer as the primary debugging UI, showing each journal entry in order with its recorded value.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already has the journal; rendering it entry-by-entry (rather than a run summary) is what makes 'why did this resume here' answerable without reading raw event-log files.

projects.name: DBOS Transact (TypeScript)
projects.license: MIT (verified on the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24)
projects.popularity: 1,328 stars on dbos-transact-ts and 1,550 on dbos-transact-py, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24. Smaller than the platform players but with real production adoption and an unusually low adoption barrier.
projects.positioning: A library, not a server. Durable workflows implemented as checkpoint rows in YOUR Postgres. Lowest operational footprint in the cluster — no broker, no separate orchestrator process, no sandbox. Increasingly marketed at agentic workflows.

features.durability: Checkpointing, not event sourcing. `DBOS.registerWorkflow()` makes a function durable; `DBOS.runStep(fn, { name })` writes each step's output to the DBOS system database (Postgres; SQLite in some SDKs). On restart the workflow function re-executes from the top and each already-completed step returns its checkpointed value instead of running. Workflow status, inputs, and step outputs are ordinary relational rows you can query with SQL and join against your own application data — and step checkpoints can be transactionally atomic with your own writes.
features.schemaValidation: None built in. No runtime validation of step outputs, no repair.
features.humanInTheLoop: `DBOS.send(destinationID, message, topic)` / `DBOS.recv(topic, timeoutSeconds)` provide durable messaging into a running workflow; `DBOS.setEvent(key, value)` / `DBOS.getEvent(workflowID, key, timeout)` let a running workflow publish typed progress keys that external code reads with a timeout. `DBOS.sleep()` records its wake time in Postgres so it survives restarts. No approval UI, forms, or approver identity.
features.parallelism: `DBOS.startWorkflow(fn, { queueName })` returns handles for background execution; queues carry concurrency limits, rate limits, priority, and partition keys. Steps can be parallelized with `Promise.allSettled` provided they are STARTED in deterministic order.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: None built in.
features.costControl: None for tokens or USD. Queue-level concurrency and rate limits only.
features.observability: DBOS Conductor / DBOS Console — a hosted-or-self-hosted UI listing workflows and their steps with cancel / resume / FORK actions, including bulk fork across many runs (shipped 2026). OpenTelemetry export. Because state is plain Postgres, ad-hoc SQL is a first-class debugging tool.
features.testing: Weakest harness in the cluster. Ordinary Jest/Vitest against a local Postgres; no time-skipping, no mock-step engine, no replay-divergence detection.
features.authoringModel: Plain TypeScript functions plus `DBOS.registerWorkflow` and `DBOS.runStep` (a decorator-based class API also exists). No sandbox, no bundler, no global replacement. Determinism is a documented CONVENTION only: the docs state a workflow 'if called multiple times with the same inputs, should invoke the same steps with the same inputs in the same order' — with zero enforcement, no static gate, and no divergence error.

strengths: Radically simple operations: a library plus a Postgres schema. No orchestrator process, no message broker, no sandbox — by far the easiest thing here to embed inside another product.

`DBOS.forkWorkflow(workflowID, startStep, { newWorkflowID, applicationVersion, queueName, replacementChildren })` is the most direct, operator-legible answer in this entire cluster to 'I fixed the bug, re-run this stuck run from step N on the new code' — and it is explicit rather than inferred.

`applicationVersion` is by default a HASH OF WORKFLOW SOURCE CODE, stamped on every run; recovery only picks up workflows whose version matches the running app, so old-code runs are never silently resumed by new-code workers.
Bulk fork from the Conductor UI turns 'we shipped a bug and 4,000 runs are wedged at step 7' into a UI action rather than a migration script.
The journal is queryable relational data — joinable with domain tables, analysable with plain SQL, and transactable with application writes.
MIT, small surface area, minimal conceptual overhead.
weaknesses: Determinism is entirely honor-system: no sandbox, no static rules, no replay-mismatch detection. Reorder two steps and a run silently receives the wrong checkpointed value.
Step identity is name/position based rather than content-addressed, so code edits are markedly more fragile than under weft's salvage scheme.
No schema validation or repair of step outputs.
No time-skipping, no deterministic simulation, no replay tests — the weakest testing story here.
Nothing git-aware, no token/USD budgets, no agent-provider abstraction.
Postgres is both the strength and the throughput ceiling; there is no separate scale-out execution tier.
Human-in-the-loop is send/recv and setEvent/getEvent primitives, with no approval semantics on top.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `DBOS.forkWorkflow(id, startStep, { applicationVersion, replacementChildren })` — resume an existing run from a chosen step under a chosen code version, optionally substituting child-run results.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is weft's edit-tolerant replay exposed as an operator verb with explicit knobs. Weft should let a human say 'salvage steps 0..N, discard the rest, run under this commit' from the CLI/daemon UI instead of relying purely on automatic content-addressed inference. `replacementChildren` is the sub-workflow analogue weft would need too.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Deriving `applicationVersion` from a hash of the workflow source code and fencing recovery to matching versions, with `getLatestApplicationVersion()` / `setLatestApplicationVersion()` for controlled cutover.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already content-addresses steps; hashing the whole workflow definition and stamping it on the journal gives free detection of 'this journal was written by different code', which is exactly the signal a salvage decision should be conditioned on — and it enables blue/green by running two versions side by side.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Bulk fork from the observability UI: multi-select failed runs and fork them all from the failing step onto the fixed version.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Single-run recovery is a demo; fleet recovery after a bad deploy is the real operational need, and weft's daemon UI is the natural place for it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Storing the journal as ordinary queryable relational rows rather than an opaque append-only file.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Free ad-hoc analysis ('which steps burn the most tokens', 'which repair loops fire most often'), free joins with domain data, and the option of transactionally atomic step checkpoints alongside application writes.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `DBOS.setEvent(key, value)` / `DBOS.getEvent(workflowID, key, timeout)` — a running workflow publishes typed progress keys that external readers poll with a timeout.
ideasWorthStealing.why: A cheap durable progress channel distinct from gates: weft's daemon UI and MCP server could read live per-step progress without the workflow having to pause or the UI having to tail the journal.

projects.name: Inngest (+ AgentKit)
projects.language: Go (server/executor); TypeScript SDK (also Python, Go); AgentKit is TypeScript
projects.license: Server and CLI: Server Side Public License with delayed open source publication (DOSP) to Apache 2.0 — source-available, not OSI-open. All SDKs: Apache 2.0. AgentKit: Apache 2.0 (verified from LICENSE.md 2026-08-24).
projects.popularity: 5,761 stars on inngest/inngest and 922 stars on inngest/agent-kit, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24.
projects.positioning: Event-driven durable step functions delivered over HTTP, designed to run on serverless/edge. AgentKit layers a real multi-agent abstraction (Agent / Network / State / Router) on top of that durability — the only entry in this cluster that ships both a durable engine and a multi-agent framework.

features.durability: Step memoization over HTTP re-invocation. Inngest calls your function endpoint repeatedly; the SDK hashes each step's declared id together with an occurrence counter (so steps inside loops get distinct stable hashes), looks the hash up in the run's managed state store, and returns the memoized value without executing if present. Otherwise the step runs, reports its result back to Inngest for persistence, and execution halts; Inngest re-invokes with the accumulated state. The function body itself re-executes from the top on every invocation — only step bodies are protected.
features.schemaValidation: Event payloads can be typed and validated via `EventSchemas` (Zod schemas supported for event data), giving end-to-end typed clients. Step RETURN values are not schema-validated and there is no repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: `step.waitForEvent(id, { event, timeout, match })` suspends a run until a matching event arrives or the timeout fires; `step.waitForSignal()` targets a specific run rather than an event pattern; `step.sleep` / `step.sleepUntil` support waits up to a year. Approvals are built by having your UI emit an event. No approval forms, approver identity, or N-of-M.
features.parallelism: `Promise.all` over multiple `step.run` / `step.invoke` promises; `step.invoke` calls another Inngest function and awaits its typed result; `step.sendEvent` for fan-out. The distinguishing layer is flow control: concurrency with DYNAMIC KEYS (e.g. `{ key: 'event.data.userId', limit: 1 }`) for multi-tenant fairness, throttling, rate limiting, debounce, and priority — all declared per function.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: The closest analogue to weft's AgentProvider. `step.ai.infer()` speaks to OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/etc. through Inngest's own inference proxy; `step.ai.wrap()` wraps any existing SDK call as a step. AgentKit adds model adapters (`openai()`, `anthropic()`, `gemini()`, …) with per-Agent model override, plus MCP servers as tool sources.
features.costControl: No hard token or USD ceiling. Token usage plus full prompt/response are captured in traces for `step.ai.*` calls, so cost is observable but not enforceable. Flow control governs concurrency and rate, not spend.
features.observability: Inngest Dev Server ships a local UI with run traces and a step-by-step timeline; the Cloud dashboard adds run traces with per-step input/output, AI prompt/response and token counts inline in the trace, metrics, and bulk Replay of historical runs.
features.testing: `@inngest/test` — `InngestTestEngine` with `t.execute()` (run the whole function, steps and all) and `t.executeStep()` (execute one step). Jest-compatible mocks for step tooling, function inputs, and PRIOR step state (`MockedStep`), then assertions over the resulting `state` object including resolved values and thrown errors. A genuine zero-network, zero-model unit harness for durable functions.
features.authoringModel: `inngest.createFunction({ id, concurrency, throttle, ... }, { event: 'x' }, async ({ event, step }) => { ... })` — plain TypeScript with explicit `step.*` calls and explicit step ids. AgentKit is declarative: `createAgent`, `createNetwork`, `createTool`, and a Router that is code-based by default with an optional LLM/ReAct router, over a shared typed `State`.

strengths: The mid-run-edit philosophy is the closest match to weft's edit-tolerant replay anywhere in this cluster, and Inngest publishes the compatibility rules as a contract: change a step's BODY while keeping its id → in-flight runs use the memoized result; ADD a step → in-flight runs execute it when they reach it; REMOVE a step → orphan state is ignored; REORDER steps → a warning is logged but memoized values still return by hash; CHANGE a step's id → it re-executes. Deliberately NO version pinning.
AgentKit is the only durable-engine-plus-multi-agent-framework combination here, with deterministic code-based routing over shared typed State and MCP tooling.

`step.ai.infer()` offloads the model call to Inngest's infrastructure so the serverless function is neither running nor billed during inference, and prompt/response/token counts land in the trace automatically.
Flow control is genuinely multi-tenant aware: concurrency limits keyed by arbitrary event data (per user, per account, per repo), plus throttle, rate limit, debounce and priority.
`@inngest/test` provides per-step mocking and mid-run state injection — the only true unit-test harness for durable functions in this cluster besides weft's own.
Bulk Replay of past runs from the dashboard.
weaknesses: The flip side of no pinning: a reordering edit returns memoized values in the wrong logical position with only a warning — silent wrongness where Temporal would hard-fail.
Non-deterministic code OUTSIDE `step.run` is a documented footgun with no sandbox and no static detection.
The function body re-executes from the top on every step, so any top-level work is repeated once per step in the run.
Server/CLI are SSPL with delayed Apache publication — self-hosting is source-available, not OSI-open.
Zero git awareness: no worktrees, patch capture, or integration semantics.
No hard spend ceiling; token accounting is observability only.
AgentKit's State is a conversation plus a typed state machine, not schema-validated per-step contracts with repair.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Publish the edit-compatibility matrix as an explicit contract (body change = safe, add = runs on reach, remove = ignored, reorder = warn, id change = re-run), with a warning channel for the risky cases.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's content-addressed salvage is a better mechanism than id-hashing, but its BEHAVIOUR is currently implicit. Documenting and instrumenting the same five cases — and surfacing 'this replay salvaged 4 steps, skipped 1, and detected a reordering' — makes tolerance auditable rather than magical.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Hashing step id together with an occurrence counter so repeated steps inside loops get stable, distinct identities.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Content-addressing by input hash collides for identical iterations of a loop. An occurrence counter alongside the content hash disambiguates them cheaply and is complementary rather than competing.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `step.ai.infer()`: the ENGINE, not the workflow process, performs the model call.
ideasWorthStealing.why: If weft's Engine owned the provider call instead of the step body, the run would hold no process during inference, prompt/response/tokens would be journaled centrally by construction, and the budget ceiling would have exactly one enforcement point — which is where weft's token/USD ceilings actually belong.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Flow control with dynamic concurrency keys (`concurrency: { key: 'event.data.repoId', limit: 1 }`) plus throttle/rate-limit/debounce/priority.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's ctx.parallel has no notion of fairness. One daemon serving several repos or several users needs per-key limits so a single fan-out cannot starve everyone else — and per-repo limit:1 also doubles as an integration lock.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `InngestTestEngine.executeStep()` with injected prior-step state via `MockedStep`.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's zero-model-call harness presumably runs workflows end to end. Being able to test ONE step with a synthetic journal prefix — 'given these three prior results, does step 4 do the right thing' — is a much tighter test loop.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: AgentKit's Network + Router split: a shared typed State plus a code-based router that decides the next agent, with an LLM router as opt-in.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's ctx.parallel/ctx.pipeline are static topologies. A durable, journaled router step that picks the next agent from typed state gives dynamic multi-agent topologies without giving up determinism.

projects.name: Trigger.dev (v3/v4)
projects.license: Apache 2.0 (verified on the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24)
projects.popularity: 16,108 stars, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24 — the second most-starred project in this cluster and the most-starred TypeScript-native one.
projects.positioning: Managed (and self-hostable) platform for long-running TypeScript tasks and AI agents, with no timeouts. Fundamentally different durability mechanism from everything else here: CRIU process checkpoint/restore rather than journaled step replay, which means zero determinism constraints on user code.

features.durability: CRIU-based checkpoint/restore of the ENTIRE PROCESS. When a run reaches a waitpoint — `triggerAndWait()`, `wait.for()`/`wait.until()` beyond roughly 60 seconds, `wait.forToken()`, `inputStream.wait()` — the run engine snapshots memory, CPU registers and open file descriptors, compresses the snapshot to disk, and releases the machine; on the resume event the process is restored and continues at the exact instruction. There is NO journal of step results to replay, so no code in a task ever needs to be deterministic. Failure handling is task retries plus `retry.onThrow`; idempotency keys dedupe repeated triggers.
features.schemaValidation: `schemaTask({ id, schema: z.object({...}), run })` validates task PAYLOADS at the boundary before the run starts, with Zod, ArkType, Yup, Valibot and others supported. Outputs are typed but not runtime-validated and there is no repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: The most complete approval primitive in this cluster. `wait.createToken({ timeout, tags })` returns a token carrying an id, a webhook URL and a browser-safe `publicAccessToken`. The run calls `wait.forToken(token)` (returning `{ ok, output | error }`, or `.unwrap()` to throw on timeout) and checkpoints, holding zero compute. Anyone then calls `wait.completeToken(id, output)` — from backend code, from an external service POSTing the webhook URL, or from a browser using the public token with CORS. React Realtime hooks render the pending-approval UI, and token tags make pending approvals filterable in the dashboard.
features.parallelism: `batch.trigger` / `batch.triggerAndWait`, `Promise.all` over `triggerAndWait`, child tasks, and queues with per-queue concurrency limits. Machine presets are configurable per task.
features.gitIsolation: No git-aware isolation, but every run executes in its own isolated container/microVM whose image is customizable through `build.extensions` (apt packages, Python, ffmpeg, Playwright). That is the closest thing in this cluster to weft's per-step sandbox — at the process/container level rather than the repository level.
features.multiProvider: No AgentProvider-style routing abstraction; the AI-agent product wraps whatever framework or SDK you bring. The dashboard does ship a Models page cataloguing models by provider with per-model usage, cost, and cache-hit sparklines derived from your actual traffic.
features.costControl: Organization-level SPEND CAP that pauses execution across every environment when hit — new runs keep queueing rather than failing — plus budget alerts at 75/90/100/200/500% of the monthly budget and spike alerts up to 100x. This is platform compute spend and observed model cost, not a per-run token ceiling shared with sub-workflows.
features.observability: Best-in-class run UI. An OpenTelemetry-powered live trace view renders each run's span tree as it executes, with logs, per-step inputs/outputs, run tags and filters, and a replay button. The Realtime API plus React hooks (`useRealtimeRun`, run streams) push run state and streaming model output into your own application. An MCP server exposes platform operations (e.g. `list_runs`) so an agent can introspect its own executions.
features.testing: `trigger dev` runs the same run engine locally against the same dashboard; a past run can be replayed onto the latest version. There is no time-skipping harness and no mock-step unit engine comparable to `@inngest/test`.
features.authoringModel: `task({ id, run: async (payload, { ctx }) => { ... } })` in `trigger/*.ts`, with `schemaTask` for validated payloads. Plain TypeScript, no sandbox, no restricted globals — `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, timers, network and child processes are all fine anywhere.

strengths: CRIU checkpointing removes determinism constraints entirely: no banned globals, no sandbox, no replay-safety discipline. The opposite end of the design space from weft's AST determinism gate, and it works.

The waitpoint token system (`createToken` / `forToken` / `completeToken` + webhook URL + browser-safe public token + timeout + tags + Realtime hooks) is the most complete human-in-the-loop story anywhere in this cluster.
Run observability is exceptional: live OTel trace view, span tree, per-step IO, tags, and realtime streaming into the customer's own UI.
`schemaTask` applies a Zod-family validator at the input boundary — the same instinct as weft, on the other side of the step.
Build extensions give declarative per-task container customization (system packages, browsers, toolchains), which matters a lot for coding agents.
Apache 2.0 and genuinely self-hostable, unlike the BSL/SSPL/AGPL alternatives.
Spend caps that PAUSE and queue rather than fail, plus percentage-of-budget alerting.
weaknesses: Zero edit tolerance by design: a run locks to the environment's latest version when it starts and never changes version, including across retries and delayed executions. The only recourse for an in-flight run on broken code is a Replay — a brand-new run with the same inputs from the beginning, discarding every completed step.
No journal of step results, so no content-addressed salvage, no fork-from-step-N, and no partial recovery of expensive work.
Checkpoint/restore is infrastructure-heavy (CRIU, snapshot storage, machine lifecycle) and materially harder to self-host than a library; it is also essentially impossible to reimplement.
No deterministic replay tests and no mock-step harness — weaker than Temporal and Inngest on testing.
Output schema validation and repair are absent; only payloads are validated.
No agent-provider routing abstraction and no git/worktree/patch semantics.
The spend cap is org-level and coarse; there is no per-run or per-sub-workflow token budget with inheritance.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `wait.createToken()` → { id, webhook URL, browser-safe publicAccessToken } with a timeout and dashboard tags, completed by `wait.completeToken(id, output)` from literally anywhere, and `.unwrap()` to convert timeout into a throw.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the reference design for weft's ctx.gate / ctx.human.approve. Weft already has Zod, so the completion payload could be schema-validated on arrival — giving a durable human step that a webhook, a Slack action, a CI job, or a React app can satisfy, with a first-class timeout branch.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Realtime run subscriptions plus React hooks (`useRealtimeRun`, output streams) as a public API.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's daemon web UI is a single consumer of run state. Exposing the same stream as an API turns 'approve this diff' and 'watch the agent think' into things a user's own product can host, instead of features locked inside weft's UI.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `schemaTask` — validating the workflow's INPUT boundary with the same validator library used for outputs.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft validates every step's return value but a workflow's own inputs are the most common source of garbage-in. Same Zod, same repair machinery, other side of the boundary.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `build.extensions`: declarative per-task container customization (apt packages, Playwright, Python, ffmpeg).
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's write steps run in git worktrees but presumably inherit the host toolchain. Different repos need different toolchains; declaring the image per step is the natural extension of per-step isolation.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An org-level spend cap that PAUSES execution and keeps runs queued rather than failing them, plus alerts at 75/90/100/200/500% of budget.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has hard ceilings; the missing half is graceful degradation. Pausing-and-queueing at the ceiling (rather than aborting the run) preserves the journal and lets a human raise the budget and resume, which is exactly the behaviour a half-finished coding workflow wants.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A Models page showing per-model usage, cost, and cache-hit-rate sparklines derived from actual traffic.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already meters tokens and USD for its budgets. Aggregating that across runs into per-model/per-provider trends is nearly free and directly informs the per-step routing decisions weft's AgentProvider already exposes.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An MCP server exposing the platform's own run data (`list_runs`, run details).
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already ships an MCP server; exposing weft's OWN journals and run history through it lets a coding agent inspect and reason about its previous runs — self-observability as a tool surface.

projects.name: Windmill
projects.language: Rust (server + workers), Svelte (UI); user scripts in TypeScript, Python, Go, Bash, SQL, PHP, Rust, C#, Java
projects.license: AGPL-3.0 for the community edition (some subdirectories Apache-2.0); Enterprise Edition features under a commercial license (verified on the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24)
projects.popularity: 17,661 stars, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24 — the most-starred project in this cluster. Explicitly markets itself as an open-source alternative to both Retool and Temporal.
projects.positioning: A self-hostable developer platform where scripts become webhooks, flows and auto-generated UIs. The flow engine is a declarative DAG advanced through Postgres, not replayed user code — so it sits at the 'orchestrator' end of this cluster rather than the 'workflow-as-code' end, but it has by far the richest human-approval feature set.

features.durability: Postgres is the only datastore — job queue, flow state, scripts, schedules, everything (no Redis, no broker). A flow is a declarative JSON/YAML DAG (`FlowValue` / `FlowModule`) encoding steps, branches, loops, retry policies and suspend semantics. Stateless API servers advance flow state in Postgres between steps while stateless workers pull individual job rows and run each step as a separate OS process, so a flow resumes mid-flow after a worker or server restart. Dead workers are detected via heartbeat rows in `worker_ping`, and a background reaper marks their in-flight jobs failed for retry.
features.schemaValidation: Every script's typed function signature is parsed into a JSON Schema, which then drives argument validation, the auto-generated input UI, approval-form rendering, AND the tool schema an LLM sees for agent steps. Step-to-step data flow itself is expression-based (`results.step_id`) rather than schema-checked.
features.humanInTheLoop: The richest in this cluster. Any step can be marked Suspend/Approval: the flow parks, and `wmill.getResumeUrls()` (`get_resume_urls()` in Python) yields signed resume / cancel / approval-page URLs to deliver by email, Slack or Teams. Configurable: number of REQUIRED APPROVALS before proceeding, timeout-to-auto-cancel, 'continue on disapproval' which passes a typed error object downstream for branching instead of failing, schema-based APPROVAL FORMS whose fields arrive as `resume['field']`, restriction to logged-in users or specific groups, prohibition of self-approval, and a recorded `approvers` array. Interactive Slack and Microsoft Teams approvals are native.
features.parallelism: For-loops with 'run in parallel' plus an explicit `parallelism` cap on simultaneous iterations, and a 'squash' option to run all iterations on one worker to avoid cold starts. Branch-all (parallel branches) and branch-one (conditional). Sub-flows. Worker groups/tags pin particular steps to particular worker pools.
features.gitIsolation: None at the flow level. Windmill does have git-sync of the workspace itself (scripts and flows pushed to a repo via the CLI), and each job runs in an isolated process with a shared directory, but there is no worktree-per-step or patch-capture model.
features.multiProvider: AI agent steps inside flows support multiple model providers, and any Windmill script or MCP server can be exposed as a tool — Windmill reads the script's typed function signature and generates the tool JSON Schema the LLM sees, so tool definitions never drift from implementations.
features.costControl: None for tokens or USD.
features.observability: Full web UI: run list, per-flow graph view with per-step arguments/logs/results (including per-iteration results inside loops), step-level re-run and debugging, schedules, audit logs. Enterprise adds SSO/SAML, audit log retention, distributed workers/worker groups and autoscaling.
features.testing: Individual steps and whole flows can be test-run from the editor with saved test payloads. No deterministic replay harness, no mock-step unit engine, no time skipping.
features.authoringModel: Primarily a visual flow editor over a JSON/YAML DAG where each node is a real script in the language of your choice, with full LSP/autocomplete. A secondary 'workflows as code' mode expresses the same logic as a single TypeScript or Python file. Flows are versioned deployable artifacts, git-syncable via CLI. Determinism: none required and none enforced — each step is a fresh process whose result is persisted, so there is no replayed user code to be non-deterministic. Mid-run edits: an executing flow uses the flow definition captured at launch, so editing a flow never mutates in-flight runs; there is no fork-onto-new-version verb comparable to DBOS.

strengths: The most complete human-approval feature set anywhere in this cluster: N-of-M required approvals, schema-backed approval forms, group restrictions, no-self-approval, disapproval-as-a-branch, timeouts, recorded approver identity, and native Slack/Teams inline approval.
Postgres-only architecture with heartbeat-based worker reaping — no broker, no Redis, no Elasticsearch.
Typed script signatures automatically generate JSON Schemas, which are then reused for input UIs, approval forms, AND LLM tool schemas — one source of truth, three consumers.
Very broad platform: schedules, webhooks, apps/UIs, worker groups, git-sync, multi-language steps, agent steps.
Largest user base of any self-hostable engine here.
No determinism cage — steps are ordinary processes in any language.
weaknesses: The primary authoring model is a visual/declarative DAG with expression-based data flow (`results.x`), not typed code with `await` as the edge; 'workflows as code' is a secondary mode. This is the direct antithesis of weft's thesis.
Coarse durability: the unit of resume is a step job row, not a content-addressed journal entry. No salvage across code edits, no fork-from-step, no per-step content addressing.
AGPL-3.0 plus Enterprise gating on the scale features (distributed workers, autoscaling, SSO, audit retention) — a real constraint for embedding or commercial redistribution.
No token/USD budgets, no agent-provider routing abstraction, no git worktree/patch/integrate model.
No deterministic replay tests and no zero-model-call harness.
Agent steps are a feature bolted onto a general automation platform, not the design center; nothing about it is specific to coding agents.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The full approval-step configuration matrix: required-approval count (N-of-M), timeout-to-cancel, 'continue on disapproval' producing a typed error object for downstream branching, restriction to specific groups, prohibition of self-approval, and a recorded `approvers` array on the run.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's ctx.human.approve is effectively a boolean by comparison. Every one of these is a real requirement the moment a coding workflow lands changes in a shared repo, and all of them are journalable facts rather than UI decoration.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Schema-backed approval forms: the reviewer fills a typed form on the approval page and its fields become `resume['field']` in the flow.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already defines every step's contract in Zod. Rendering a Zod schema as the human's input form — and validating the human's answer with the same schema and repair path as a model's answer — makes ctx.human.ask structurally identical to any other validated step, which is a genuinely elegant unification.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `getResumeUrls()`: signed resume / cancel / approval-page URLs mailable to a reviewer who never touches the engine UI, plus native Slack and Teams interactive approvals.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Adoption of a human gate is gated on how little the human has to install. A signed URL in an email or a Slack button is the lowest possible friction, and it composes with weft's journal because the resume is just a step completion.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Generating LLM tool JSON Schemas automatically from typed function signatures.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's steps already carry Zod schemas. Deriving the agent's tool surface from those same schemas means tool definitions can never drift from the implementations, and adding a step automatically extends what an agent can call.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: For-loop `parallelism` cap plus a 'squash onto one worker' locality option.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.parallel presumably fans out unbounded. A max-in-flight cap is necessary for rate-limited providers, and an explicit locality option matters when N iterations should share one warm worktree/toolchain rather than paying N setup costs.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Worker groups/tags routing particular steps to particular machine pools.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Coding workflows are heterogeneous — a cheap planning step and a heavy build-and-test step should not need the same machine. Tagging steps to pools is the minimal version of that and slots naturally into per-step routing weft already has for providers.

projects.name: Hatchet
projects.language: Go (engine); SDKs in TypeScript, Python, Go and Ruby; React dashboard
projects.license: MIT (verified on the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24) — the README emphasizes '100% MIT-licensed'
projects.popularity: 7,785 stars, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24. Strong recent growth on the back of AI-agent positioning.
projects.positioning: A Postgres-backed distributed task queue that grew into a durable-execution and DAG orchestrator, now explicitly targeting long-running AI agents. Its real differentiator is the scheduling layer (fairness, concurrency keys, rate limits, priorities), not the durability model.

features.durability: Postgres is both queue and durability layer, and full task history is RETAINED after completion rather than discarded — enabling replay and post-hoc debugging. Two task flavors: ordinary tasks (retried, results persisted, individually replayable) and durable tasks, which receive a `DurableContext`. Every call to `ctx.sleepFor`, `ctx.waitFor` / `ctx.waitForEvent`, `ctx.memo` or `runChild` writes a checkpoint into a durable event log; on resume Hatchet replays that log up to the last checkpoint, skipping completed operations, and continues from there.
features.schemaValidation: The TypeScript SDK types task input/output via generics; the Python SDK uses Pydantic models for input and output validation. No runtime repair loop and no validation of intermediate step results in TS.
features.humanInTheLoop: Durable event waits. `ctx.waitFor(conditions)` accepts `UserEventCondition` and `SleepCondition`, with arrays meaning AND and `Or(...)` meaning first-of. A run parks until an external event with a matching key/expression is pushed. `ctx.waitForEvent(EVENT_KEY)` is the shorthand. No approval UI, forms, approver identity, or N-of-M semantics — an approval is 'someone pushed an event with this key'.
features.parallelism: Declarative DAGs via `workflow.task({ parents: [...] })`, plus runtime-dynamic child spawning so the DAG can be built as an agent decides. Fan-out/fan-in, worker slot control. The scheduling layer is the standout: concurrency keys with FAIRNESS strategies (e.g. round-robin across tenant/user keys rather than a plain global limit), rate limits as declarative consumable resources, priorities, and sticky assignment.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: None built in.
features.costControl: None for tokens or USD. Rate limits and concurrency limits only.
features.observability: Self-hosted React dashboard with run and DAG visualizations, per-task inputs/outputs/logs, retry history, per-task replay, metrics and alerting; OpenTelemetry export. Because history is retained in Postgres, any past run can be replayed.
features.testing: Ordinary language-native testing against a local Hatchet (docker compose). No time-skipping, no mock-step harness, no replay-divergence detection.
features.authoringModel: Plain TypeScript: `hatchet.task({ name, fn })`, `hatchet.workflow()` with `.task({ parents: [...] })` to declare DAG edges, and `hatchet.durableTask()` for durable context. Note that edges are DECLARED via `parents`, not inferred from `await` — the opposite of weft's 'await = edge'. Determinism: no sandbox, no static gate, no divergence error. Durable tasks replay their own checkpoint log so the usual sequence-stability caution applies, but Hatchet publishes no formal edit-compatibility contract, no version pinning of in-flight runs, and no fork-from-step verb — the weakest versioning story in this cluster.

strengths: Genuinely MIT and self-hostable with a single Postgres dependency — no BSL, SSPL or AGPL asterisk, unlike Restate, Inngest, Golem and Windmill.

The best queueing and scheduling layer here: concurrency keys with fairness strategies, declarative rate-limit resources, priorities, sticky assignment and worker slots. These are exactly the multi-tenant scale features weft has none of.
`ctx.waitFor(Or(UserEventCondition(...), SleepCondition('24h')))` composes event waits and timeouts into one durable primitive.
Full task history retained by default rather than deleted on success, with per-task replay from the dashboard.
Runtime-dynamic child spawning lets a DAG be constructed as the agent decides while the parent stays durable.
Good DAG visualization in the dashboard, and four language SDKs.
weaknesses: No versioning or pinning story for in-flight runs and no fork-from-step; deploying mid-run is essentially undefined behaviour you must reason about yourself. This is the biggest gap relative to weft, Temporal, DBOS, Restate and Trigger.dev.
No determinism enforcement of any kind — no sandbox, no static gate, no replay-mismatch error.
Human-in-the-loop is only 'wait for an event with this key': no tokens, forms, approver identity, N-of-M, or approval UI.
DAG edges declared as `parents: [...]` are more verbose and less refactor-safe than deriving edges from `await`.
No schema repair, no cost budgets, no git/worktree/patch semantics, no agent-provider abstraction.
No deterministic test harness.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `ctx.waitFor(Or(UserEventCondition(...), SleepCondition('24h')))` — composable AND/OR wait conditions as a single durable primitive.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's gates would gain 'approve, or auto-escalate/auto-decide after T' for free, expressed as one journaled wait rather than a hand-rolled race between a gate and a timer.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Concurrency keys with explicit fairness strategies (round-robin across tenant keys) rather than plain global limits.
ideasWorthStealing.why: One weft daemon serving several repos or users needs fairness, not just a cap: without it a single 200-way fan-out starves everyone else. This is the correct primitive and weft has nothing equivalent.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Rate limits modelled as declarative named resources that steps consume, rather than as per-function settings.
ideasWorthStealing.why: 'At most N Claude calls per minute across every workflow on this daemon' is a shared resource, not a per-workflow property. Making it a first-class consumable resource is the right shape, and it pairs naturally with weft's token/USD budgets.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Retaining full run history for every task by default and exposing per-task replay from the dashboard.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft journals everything already; surfacing 'replay just this one step with the same inputs' as a UI action is a cheap, high-value debugging affordance for iterating on a prompt without re-running the whole workflow.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `ctx.memo` — an explicitly memoized value inside a durable task, distinct from a full checkpointed step.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Not every cached intermediate deserves the weight of a schema-validated journaled step. A lighter memo tier keeps the journal readable while still surviving replay.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Runtime-dynamic child spawning that builds the DAG as execution proceeds, with the parent remaining durable.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.parallel/ctx.pipeline are declared up front. Agentic coding workflows frequently discover their fan-out (one sub-workflow per file the agent decided to touch), which needs durable spawn-as-you-go.

projects.name: Resonate HQ
projects.language: Rust (server); SDKs in TypeScript and Python
projects.popularity: 656 stars on resonatehq/resonate and only 57 on resonate-sdk-ts, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24 — by far the smallest project in this cluster, and the TS SDK is very thin.
projects.positioning: 'Distributed async await'. Durable execution modelled as an addressable SET of durable promises rather than an ordered event log — a deliberate theoretical alternative to the Temporal/Restate log-replay model. Explicitly agent-native and programmatic-first, with docs that argue for CLI/API surfaces over dashboards.

features.durability: Object-set, not log. Every `ctx.run` / `ctx.rpc` / `ctx.sleep` creates a durable promise in the Resonate Server's promise store, addressed by an id derived deterministically from the parent execution id (`${ctx.id}.<seq>`). On recovery the function re-executes and each promise id is looked up: completed promises return their stored value, unknown promises trigger real invocation. Because promises form an UNSEQUENCED SET rather than an ordered log, there is no positional matching that an edit can violate.
features.schemaValidation: None built in.
features.humanInTheLoop: The cleanest primitive in this cluster. `ctx.promise()` mints a durable promise with a stable, RECONSTRUCTABLE id — `${ctx.id}.<seq>` by default, or a caller-chosen id such as `${orderId}.approval`. The workflow yields it and suspends; anything that knows the id (a webhook handler, a CLI, a Slack button, another process on another machine) resolves it and the workflow resumes, possibly in a completely different process. Documented as the canonical human-in-the-loop pattern with a shipped example.
features.parallelism: Two engines. Generator engine: `yield* ctx.run(...)` for sequential, `yield ctx.beginRun(...)` to start work and collect the future later with `yield future`; exponential-backoff retries by default. Async engine: `ctx.run(...)` is eager and returns an awaitable handle; retries require an explicit `retryPolicy`. `ctx.rpc()` makes durable calls to functions registered on other nodes.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: None built in.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: Deliberately API- and CLI-first rather than dashboard-first; `resonate dev` runs a local server and the promise store is queryable. Weakest UI story in this cluster, and that is an explicit design stance rather than an oversight.
features.testing: Deterministic Simulation Testing applied to the SERVER and to EVERY SDK. The server ships a public differential tester and the TypeScript SDK ships a public simulation harness that drives the SDK through randomized interleavings and injected failures to surface edge cases before production. No other project in this cluster tests its own engine this way.
features.authoringModel: `resonate.register(name, fn)`; workflows are generator functions (`function*(ctx, ...) { yield* ctx.run(...) }`) or async functions. Identical code runs local-only (single process, `resonate dev`) or against a remote Resonate Server by passing a `url`. Determinism: Resonate's published argument is that with a log-based system 'your workflow code needs to be deterministic to make the system happy', whereas with an object-set system 'your workflow code needs to be deterministic to make your use-case happy'. There is no sandbox, no static gate, and no divergence error — a mismatch after an edit simply causes different promise ids to be looked up, and missing ones get invoked. Correctness under edits is entirely the developer's responsibility.

strengths: The promise-SET model is structurally more edit-tolerant than an ordered log: inserting, removing or reordering calls produces different id lookups rather than a positional mismatch error. This is the closest theoretical cousin to weft's content-addressed step salvage, and Resonate has published the clearest argument for why it works.
Deterministically-derived, externally-addressable promise ids make human-in-the-loop and cross-process resumption trivial — an operator can resolve `${orderId}.1` with a single curl.
Deterministic Simulation Testing of both server and SDKs, with the harnesses public — a testing philosophy the rest of this cluster lacks entirely.
Local-vs-remote symmetry: the same workflow code runs fully in-process for development or against a server in production.
Apache 2.0 throughout — no license asterisk.
An unusually rigorous published account of where determinism constraints actually come from, which is directly useful reading for weft's design rationale.
weaknesses: By far the smallest adoption and ecosystem here (656 / 57 stars); the TypeScript SDK is thin and its API has churned between generator and async engines, which is a real risk for anyone depending on it.
Explicitly de-prioritizes dashboards, so observability is minimal next to Temporal, Trigger.dev and Windmill.
No determinism enforcement and no divergence detection at all — a semantically breaking edit silently re-runs or skips work with no signal.
No versioning or pinning story for in-flight executions.
No schema validation, no budgets, no git awareness, no agent-provider abstraction, no gates beyond raw promises.
Recent marketing has pivoted hard toward AI-generated/agent framing, which makes it harder to assess the underlying engineering maturity from the outside.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Deterministically-derived, externally-addressable durable-promise ids (`${parentId}.<seq>`, or a caller-chosen id like `${orderId}.approval`) that ANY party who can compute the id may resolve.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's steps are already content-addressed internally. Exposing a stable, computable public handle for a gate means an external reviewer, a CI job, or an MCP client can complete a human step without weft handing out an opaque token first — the id is derivable from facts the caller already knows.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The promise-set (rather than ordered-log) recovery model as the formal justification for edit tolerance.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's edit-tolerant replay is its most unusual claim and currently reads as a heuristic. Resonate has published the theory that makes it principled — unsequenced addressable results rather than positional log matching — which is both a design check and a credible citation for weft's own docs.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Deterministic Simulation Testing of the ENGINE itself: randomized interleavings, injected crashes and message loss, all replayable from a seed.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's zero-model-call harness tests user workflows. DST would test weft's own journal/replay/salvage/budget logic — precisely the code where a subtle bug silently corrupts a customer's run and is nearly impossible to reproduce otherwise.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A public differential tester that compares two implementations against the same workload.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft runs the same Engine behind a CLI, an MCP server and a daemon web UI. A differential harness asserting all three produce identical journals for identical workflows would catch surface-specific drift before users do.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Local-vs-remote symmetry: identical workflow code runs entirely in-process for development or against a server for production, chosen by one constructor argument.
ideasWorthStealing.why: It makes the dev loop for durable workflows as cheap as a script, which is exactly what weft needs for coding workflows that people iterate on constantly.

projects.name: Golem Cloud
projects.language: Rust (worker executor + services); user code in any language compiling to WASM components — Rust, TypeScript/JS, Python, Go, Scala, MoonBit
projects.license: Business Source License 1.1 (verified from the repo LICENSE 2026-08-24; converts to Apache 2.0 after the Change Date) — NOT OSI open source today. Note this is a change from Golem's earlier Apache 2.0 licensing.
projects.popularity: 1,535 stars, verified via the GitHub API 2026-08-24. Small but distinctive; has repositioned heavily around 'agent-native' runtime framing.
projects.positioning: An 'agent-native' durable computing platform that makes the WASM RUNTIME durable rather than journaling user-declared steps. Durability lives below the application, at the WASI host-function boundary, so user code needs no determinism discipline whatsoever. Relevant to weft as the strongest counter-example to banning non-deterministic APIs.

features.durability: The most transparent mechanism in this cluster.
