User code compiles to a WASM component; Golem's worker executor supplies durable implementations of the WASI host interfaces and records EVERY host-function interaction — I/O, HTTP, clocks, randomness, RDBMS calls, authorization decisions — into a per-worker OPLOG. Recovery replays the oplog against a fresh WASM instance, feeding recorded results back for effects already performed, so execution resumes at the exact point of interruption, on a different machine if necessary. Idle workers suspend to zero memory and are resurrected by oplog replay. Persistence level and ATOMIC REGIONS are configurable through `golem:api` host functions (mark a region atomic so it replays all-or-nothing, or lower persistence for cheap effects), and idempotence mode controls whether an interrupted external call is retried or fails the worker.
features.schemaValidation: WIT (WebAssembly Interface Types) defines every component's exported and imported interfaces, and the platform enforces those types at the ABI boundary — a genuinely strong, language-agnostic contract. But it validates interface SHAPE, not LLM output semantics, and there is no repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: No dedicated primitive. Workers are addressable, long-lived, stateful entities invoked by name, so 'wait for a human' is modelled as the worker blocking on an invocation or an external call. No gates, tokens, forms, timeouts-as-branches, or approver identity.
features.parallelism: The worker IS the unit of concurrency: cheap (megabyte-scale), suspend-to-zero when idle, individually addressable and invocable. Fan-out means spawning many workers and invoking them. There is no in-language parallel/pipeline combinator at the engine level.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: None built in.
features.costControl: None for tokens or USD.
features.observability: The oplog IS the observability surface — a durable journal of every input, effect and decision for a worker, inspectable via CLI and API. There is a Golem Desktop app and worker-metadata APIs. No trace-style run UI comparable to Trigger.dev or Temporal.
features.testing: Language-native testing plus a local Golem. No time-skipping harness and no replay-divergence tooling documented.
features.authoringModel: Ordinary code in your language of choice, compiled to a WASM component with a WIT interface. No workflow DSL, no `step.run` wrappers, no decorators — durability is invisible because it lives under the host boundary. Determinism: user code needs NO determinism discipline at all, because randomness, clocks and network results are recorded and replayed rather than banned. This is the exact inverse of weft's AST determinism gate (which bans Date.now/Math.random/timers/network) and reaches the same guarantee by recording instead of prohibiting.

strengths: Durability is achieved below the application at the WASI host boundary, so no code changes, decorators or step wrappers are required and no determinism rules apply to user code — the cleanest separation of concerns in this cluster.
Randomness and clocks are RECORDED rather than banned, which is the strongest available argument that weft's AST prohibition list could be relaxed into interception.

Snapshot-based worker update is a genuinely different answer to mid-run code changes: the old component version implements `golem:api/save-snapshot` and the new one `golem:api/load-snapshot`; the update is ENQUEUED like an invocation and applied only when the worker goes idle, state is serialized to bytes, the worker restarts on the new version and loads it — with automatic revert to the old version if `load-snapshot` fails. Golem also offers an automatic update mode that continues the existing oplog against the new component version, documented as only safe when changes are minor or touch code paths that have not yet run.
Configurable persistence levels and atomic regions let you trade oplog volume against recovery granularity, per region of code.
Per-agent suspend-to-zero makes very large numbers of long-lived idle agents cheap.
Language-agnostic via the WASM component model, with WIT-typed interfaces enforced at the ABI.
weaknesses: BSL 1.1 — not open source, which constrains adoption and embedding, and is a downgrade from its earlier Apache 2.0 licensing.

Everything must compile to a WASM component. The TypeScript/JS path works but the tooling burden is real, and — decisively for weft's use case — there are no arbitrary native Node modules and no direct child processes, so a coding agent cannot simply shell out to git, a package manager, or a test runner.
No human-in-the-loop primitives at all, no schema-validated step contracts in the LLM sense, no budgets, nothing git-aware.
Observability is oplog-centric rather than a run/trace UI.
Automatic update is explicitly best-effort and can fail; snapshot update requires you to write and maintain serialization for the worker's entire state.
Smallest practical ecosystem among the platform-scale entries here, with heavy conceptual and infrastructural onboarding.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Record-and-replay of non-determinism instead of banning it: intercept `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, timers and even network results, journal their outcomes, and feed them back on replay.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the single most valuable idea for weft in this cluster. Weft's determinism gate currently BANS these APIs via AST rules plus replaced globals in a node:vm sandbox — which is safe but makes ordinary workflow code awkward and forces contortions. Weft already replaces those globals; making the replacements journal-and-replay rather than throw would preserve the guarantee while deleting most of the friction, and turn a prohibition list into a capability.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `save-snapshot` / `load-snapshot` as a developer-authored migration hook, applied only when the run is idle, with automatic revert if the load fails.
ideasWorthStealing.why: A principled complement to automatic content-addressed salvage: when weft's replay cannot infer how to carry state across an edit, let the workflow author WRITE the migration, run it only at a quiescent point, and roll back safely if it throws. That converts 'salvage failed, start over' into 'salvage failed, run the author's migration'.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Configurable persistence levels and explicit ATOMIC REGIONS — per-region control over how much is journaled and whether a region replays all-or-nothing.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft journals every step uniformly. Cheap idempotent steps bloat the log and slow replay, while multi-effect sequences (write worktree, run tests, capture patch) really want all-or-nothing replay semantics. Region-level policy gives both.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Idempotence mode as an explicit per-call policy: on interruption, either retry the external call or fail the run.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft makes this decision implicitly today. For an agent step that already spent tokens and may have had side effects, whether replay re-invokes or hard-fails should be a declared property of the step, not a hidden engine default.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Treating a version update as an ENQUEUED INVOCATION applied only when the worker is idle.
ideasWorthStealing.why: It guarantees a code change is never applied mid-step. Weft's edit-tolerant replay currently reacts to whatever source is present at resume time; scheduling the version swap as a journaled event at a quiescent point makes the transition an auditable entry in the log rather than an ambient condition.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Suspend-to-zero for idle runs.
ideasWorthStealing.why: A workflow parked at a human gate for three days should consume no memory and no process. Combined with Restate's suspension model, this makes an unbounded backlog of pending human reviews essentially free.

cluster: Python agent orchestration frameworks (weft's competitors by mindshare, different language)

projects.name: LangGraph
projects.license: MIT for the core library. The API server package `langgraph-api` (what `langgraph dev` runs, and the basis of self-hosted LangGraph Platform) is Elastic License 2.0, not OSI-open-source — so the 'MIT' claim covers the graph runtime only, not the deployment layer.
projects.popularity: 40.4k stars, read off the GitHub repo page on 2026-08-24 (GitHub REST API was blocked by the session proxy, so this is a rendered-page reading, not an API-verified number). Clearly the mindshare leader in this cluster; README cites Klarna, Replit, Elastic.
projects.positioning: "Low-level orchestration framework for building stateful agents." Deliberately unopinionated graph runtime beneath LangChain's `create_agent`, Deep Agents, and LangSmith. Sells durability + human-in-the-loop + memory as the three pillars.

features.durability: Checkpointer writes a `StateSnapshot` (channel values, pending node set, run config, parent-checkpoint pointer) at every superstep boundary, keyed by thread_id. Checkpointer interface is minimal: `put`, `get_tuple`, `list`. Implementations: InMemorySaver, SqliteSaver, PostgresSaver/AsyncPostgresSaver, MongoDBSaver. Three durability modes selectable per run: `exit` (persist only at graph exit), `async` (persist concurrently with the next step), `sync` (persist before the next step starts). Resume = re-invoke with the same thread_id; nodes before the resume checkpoint are NOT re-run, nodes at/after it re-run in full. The Functional API (`@entrypoint` / `@task`) memoizes completed task results in the checkpoint so replay restores them instead of recomputing — the entrypoint body itself always replays from the top. Crucially, granularity is the node/task, not the line: any code inside a node before an interrupt or crash re-executes, and docs explicitly tell you to make it idempotent. Time travel: `update_state()` writes a new checkpoint on the parent, and invoking with a `checkpoint_id` forks an alternate timeline. No code-change tolerance story — replay assumes the same graph topology.
features.schemaValidation: Not enforced at the graph-step level; state is a TypedDict/Pydantic model with reducer-annotated channels and is validated only as far as the state schema goes. Structured output lives one layer up in `create_agent(response_format=...)`, which picks `ProviderStrategy` (native constrained decoding on OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/xAI) or `ToolStrategy` (schema as a tool call) automatically. ToolStrategy has an in-loop repair path: on a Pydantic validation error the agent feeds the specific error back to the model and retries, configurable via `handle_errors` (bool / custom message / exception types / callback). Result lands in the `structured_response` state key.
features.humanInTheLoop: `interrupt()` raises a special exception caught by the runtime, which persists the checkpoint and returns the interrupt payload to the caller; you resume with `Command(resume=value)` and that value becomes the return of the original `interrupt()` call. The whole node re-executes on resume — this is the documented sharp edge, with recommended workarounds (side effects after the interrupt, upserts, or a separate node). Multiple interrupts in one node are matched to resume values strictly by index. Static `interrupt_before`/`interrupt_after` breakpoints exist but docs say they're for debugging, not production.
features.parallelism: Pregel/BSP supersteps: all nodes with pending messages in a superstep run concurrently, then state is reduced via channel reducers before the next superstep. Fan-out via multiple edges from one node or `Send` objects for dynamic map. The Functional API returns futures from `@task` calls that you `.result()` / `await`. `defer=True` nodes wait for all branches. Node-level caching via `CachePolicy(cache_key=fn, ttl=...)` at graph compile time.
features.gitIsolation: None. No worktree, sandbox, or patch-capture concept. Coding-agent work happens through whatever filesystem tools you hand the agent; the sibling `deepagents` package adds a virtual/backed filesystem abstraction but no git-level isolation or staged-patch integration point.
features.multiProvider: Inherited from LangChain's `init_chat_model` / BaseChatModel — every major provider, plus per-node model choice since a node is just a function. There is no first-class 'route this step to Claude Code vs Codex CLI' abstraction; agents are chat-model+tools, not CLI coding agents.
features.costControl: None built in. `usage_metadata` on AIMessage carries token counts and LangSmith aggregates cost, but there is no budget object, no hard ceiling, no abort-on-spend, and nothing propagated into subgraphs. Verified in multiple 2026 comparison writeups: budget enforcement is left to application code at the model-integration level.
features.observability: LangSmith is the first-party path (traces, token/cost, evals, datasets) and is a paid SaaS. OSS side: `stream_mode` of values/updates/messages/debug/custom, `get_state_history()` for checkpoint walking, plus OpenTelemetry via community instrumentation (OpenInference, Langfuse, Arize). The LangGraph Studio debugger ships with `langgraph dev` under Elastic License 2.0.
features.testing: No zero-model-call harness in core. Practice is FakeListChatModel / FakeChatModel stubs plus LangSmith `evaluate()` over datasets with LLM-as-judge. Checkpoint replay gives you a form of deterministic re-execution but it is not packaged as a test fixture.
features.authoringModel: Code-as-graph, but explicitly a graph: `StateGraph(State).add_node(...).add_edge(...).add_conditional_edges(...)`, compiled to a Pregel runtime. The Functional API (`@entrypoint`/`@task`) is the closest analogue to weft's 'await = edge' model — plain imperative Python where awaited tasks become checkpointed units — but it is the secondary, less-documented API and gives up the introspectable topology.

strengths: Deepest and most battle-tested checkpoint/resume implementation in the cluster: durability modes, thread history, fork/time-travel, and production Postgres/Mongo savers all exist and are used at scale.
Interrupt/resume is a genuine first-class primitive, not a callback — the pause survives process death and can last arbitrarily long.
Two authoring surfaces (explicit graph, and imperative Functional API) covering both 'I want to see the topology' and 'I want plain code'.
Enormous ecosystem gravity: supervisor and swarm prebuilts, Deep Agents, LangSmith, every observability vendor has an integration.
Structured-output repair loop with configurable error handling is close to weft's in-session repair, and picks native constrained decoding when the provider supports it.
weaknesses: Node-level replay granularity means every node body must be hand-written to be idempotent; the docs put the burden on you rather than the runtime. Weft's content-addressed step salvage is a strictly finer-grained answer.
No determinism enforcement whatsoever — nothing stops `Date.now()`-equivalents inside a node, and nothing detects that a replay diverged.
Replay is not edit-tolerant: change the graph and old checkpoints are at best unreliable, at worst unusable.
No cost ceilings, no budget propagation to subgraphs.
The deployment/UI layer (server, Studio) is Elastic-licensed, so the 'fully OSS' story breaks exactly where a daemon/web-UI comparison with weft would happen.
No git isolation or patch-staging — nothing that makes multi-agent code-writing safe by construction.
Boilerplate-heavy for simple flows; state channels + reducers are a real learning cliff.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Explicit, selectable durability modes (`exit` / `async` / `sync`) as a per-run knob.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft journals every step; letting the caller trade fsync latency for crash-window size on a per-run basis is a cheap knob that matters for fast CI-style runs vs long overnight ones.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `update_state()` + fork-from-checkpoint as an explicit alternate-timeline API, with the original run left untouched.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already has an append-only journal; exposing 'rewind to step N, edit the value, branch a new run' turns the journal into a debugging and what-if tool, not just a crash-recovery mechanism. This is the highest-leverage idea on this list.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Node-level `CachePolicy(cache_key, ttl)` — memoize a step keyed by a user-supplied hash of inputs.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Complements content-addressed salvage: salvage handles replay, a cache handles *repeat* runs across different workflow invocations (e.g. re-running the same lint step across 20 PRs).

ideasWorthStealing.idea: ProviderStrategy vs ToolStrategy auto-selection for structured output.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft repairs after the fact; using native constrained decoding when the provider supports it means fewer repair rounds and fewer wasted tokens.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `stream_mode` as a first-class enum (values/updates/messages/debug/custom) rather than one event firehose.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's daemon web UI and CLI want different granularities off the same journal; naming the modes makes the contract explicit.

projects.name: CrewAI
projects.license: MIT (the OSS framework). The AMP / Enterprise control plane is commercial.
projects.popularity: 57.6k stars, 8.2k forks, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24. Highest raw star count of any code-first framework here; heavily marketed, large but shallow user base.
projects.positioning: "Open-source Python framework with high-level abstractions and low-level APIs for building production-ready multi-agent workflows." Two products in one repo: Crews (role-playing autonomous agents that delegate to each other) and Flows (event-driven deterministic control flow). Positioned against LangGraph as 'less boilerplate'.

features.durability: Flows only, and it is state-snapshot persistence rather than an event journal. `@persist` (class- or method-level) writes the Flow's state to `SQLiteFlowPersistence` by default after method execution; state carries an auto-generated `id` UUID. Restore has two distinct modes: `kickoff(inputs={'id': uuid})` resumes under the same flow_uuid and extends history, while `kickoff(restore_from_state_id=uuid)` forks from a snapshot with a fresh `state.id`, leaving the original lineage intact. Crews (the flagship abstraction) have no durable execution — a crash mid-crew loses the run. There is no step-level journal, no replay semantics, and no story for code changes between runs.
features.schemaValidation: Per-task, and reasonably good: `output_pydantic=Model` or `output_json=Model` on a Task, with results exposed as `TaskOutput.pydantic` / `.json_dict` / `.raw`. Guardrails are the repair mechanism: function-based guardrails receive `TaskOutput` and return `(bool, Any)` — returning `(False, error_message)` feeds the message back to the agent and retries, bounded by `guardrail_max_retries` (default 3). LLM-based guardrails accept a plain-English criterion string and let a model judge. Multiple guardrails run sequentially via `guardrails=[...]`. Flow state can be a Pydantic BaseModel (`Flow[MyState]`) or an untyped dict.
features.humanInTheLoop: Two mechanisms. Task-level `human_input=True` pauses after task completion for review/approval in the terminal loop. Flow-level `@human_feedback` decorator pauses, collects feedback, and — when you give it an `emit` list of outcome labels — uses an LLM to classify the free-text feedback into one of those labels, which then triggers the matching `@listen` branch. Feedback is retained on `self.last_human_feedback` / `self.human_feedback_history`. The LLM-classification step is unusual and a bit risky, but it's a genuinely novel affordance.
features.parallelism: `Process.sequential` and `Process.hierarchical` (a manager agent delegates) for Crews; `async_execution=True` on tasks, and `kickoff_for_each_async` for fan-out over inputs. Flows get `or_()` (fire when any upstream emits) and `and_()` (fire when all complete) combinators plus `@router` for conditional branching.
features.gitIsolation: None. CrewAI ships code-execution tools that run in Docker containers (`code_execution_mode='safe'`), which is process isolation, not git isolation — no worktrees, no patch capture, no staged integration point.
features.multiProvider: Via LiteLLM, so ~100+ providers behind one `LLM(model=...)`. Per-agent model assignment is idiomatic (cheap model for the researcher, expensive for the writer). No coding-CLI-agent provider abstraction.
features.costControl: Weakest area, and independently flagged as a production hazard in 2026 comparison writeups (uncapped crew loops reaching $414 in a single run). What exists: `max_iter` per agent (reasoning-loop cap), `max_rpm` (rate limit), and `crew.usage_metrics` reporting tokens after the fact. There is no budget object, no USD ceiling, no abort-on-spend, and nothing shared with sub-crews. CrewAI also carries a documented ~18% token overhead vs LangGraph for equivalent work.
features.observability: An internal event bus you can subscribe to with custom listeners, plus a long list of third-party integrations: Langfuse, MLflow, Langtrace, Arize Phoenix, Opik, Weave, OpenLIT (OTel-native), Portkey, LangDB, Patronus AI. First-party tracing lives in CrewAI AMP (commercial), with a free Crew Control Plane tier.
features.testing: `crewai test` exists as a CLI command that runs a crew N times and scores task outputs with an LLM judge — real, but it is an eval loop, not a deterministic harness. No mock-provider fixture, no replay-based zero-model-call testing.
features.authoringModel: Two DSLs. Crews are largely declarative — YAML `agents.yaml` / `tasks.yaml` with role/goal/backstory strings, wired by a `@CrewBase` class. Flows are decorator-driven Python: `@start()`, `@listen(other_method)`, `@router()`, with `self.state` as the shared mutable object. Control flow is expressed by decorator wiring rather than by `await`, so the call graph is not readable from the code's own structure.

strengths: Fastest time-to-first-demo in the cluster; the role/goal/backstory metaphor is genuinely accessible to non-specialists and drives the star count.
Guardrails with bounded retry and error-message feedback are a clean, well-shaped structured-output repair loop — closer to weft's design than most competitors.
The `@human_feedback` + `emit` labels design (LLM classifies free-text human feedback into a routing decision) is a real product idea, not just an approval gate.
Flows' fork-vs-resume distinction (`restore_from_state_id` vs `inputs={'id'}`) is a thoughtful API detail most frameworks miss.
YAML config separates prompt content from orchestration code, which teams with non-engineer prompt owners actually like.
weaknesses: Durability only covers Flows, not Crews — the headline abstraction is not crash-safe.
Persistence is whole-state snapshotting, not an append-only journal; no per-step provenance, no replay, no salvage across edits.
No cost ceilings at all, combined with autonomous delegation loops — the documented worst-case failure mode of this framework is a runaway bill.
Autonomy-first design makes runs non-reproducible by construction; agents deciding to delegate is exactly what you don't want in a coding pipeline.
No git isolation, no patch staging, no determinism gate.
Reputation among practitioners has drifted toward 'demo framework' as LangGraph and MAF hardened.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: LLM-classified human feedback: `@human_feedback(emit=['approve','revise','escalate'])` lets a reviewer type free prose and a model maps it onto a declared outcome set that drives routing.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's `ctx.human.review` currently needs the human to produce a structured verdict. Letting a reviewer type 'the error handling in the second file is wrong, redo it' and having that classified into a typed branch outcome — while journaling both the raw prose and the classification — is a direct upgrade with no loss of auditability.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Both function-based and prose-based guardrails on the same step, run as an ordered chain.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has Zod validation (structural). A prose guardrail ('the diff must not touch files outside src/') is a semantic gate that Zod can't express, and chaining them gives structural-then-semantic validation with the same repair loop.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Explicit fork-from-snapshot API that assigns a fresh run id while preserving the parent's lineage pointer.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Complements the LangGraph time-travel idea; weft's journal already has everything needed to make 'branch this run from step 12' a one-liner with clean provenance.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `crewai test` — a CLI verb that runs the workflow N times and scores outputs, as a first-class command next to `run`.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has a zero-model-call harness for determinism; a complementary `weft eval` verb for the stochastic dimension would round out the CLI without compromising the deterministic harness.

projects.name: Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF)
projects.language: Python and .NET as first-class peers, plus a Go SDK
projects.popularity: 13.1k stars, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24. Lower than AutoGen's legacy 60.6k but rising fast — this is the successor both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel now point at. 1.0 shipped 2026-04-07; the checkpoints doc I read was last updated 2026-08-10 and describes Python 1.13.0 behavior, so it is under very active development.
projects.positioning: The merged successor to AutoGen (multi-agent orchestration) and Semantic Kernel (enterprise kernel/plugins/connectors). Sells itself as the production-grade path: 'prototype to production' with checkpointing, OpenTelemetry, and Azure deployment. Enterprise-first, Microsoft-shaped.

features.durability: The most rigorously specified checkpointing in this cluster. Workflows execute in supersteps (Pregel-style); a checkpoint is written at the end of each superstep, after every executor in that superstep completes, capturing four things explicitly: all executor states, all pending messages queued for the next superstep, pending requests and responses, and shared state. Python 1.13.0 added an entry checkpoint before the first superstep (recording workflow input) and another when responses to request events are delivered — the stated goal being 'the complete workflow run is replayable'. Storage is a `CheckpointStorage` protocol with three shipped implementations (InMemory, File on local disk, Cosmos DB with `/workflow_name` as partition key); swapping providers requires no executor code changes. Two resume paths: resume in place on the same workflow instance (`workflow.run(checkpoint_id=...)`), or rehydrate into a brand-new instance by passing checkpoint_storage to a freshly built workflow. Executors persist their own state by overriding `on_checkpoint_save()` / `on_checkpoint_restore()` (C#: `OnCheckpointingAsync` / `OnCheckpointRestoredAsync`). Sub-workflows are checkpointed too. The hard constraint, stated bluntly in the docs: a rehydrated workflow must preserve topology AND executor identities — in .NET the executor identity is derived from the agent's `Id` and `Name`, so changing either makes existing checkpoints unresumable, and 'assigning stable values does not repair checkpoints created with different or randomly generated IDs'. No edit tolerance. Separately, Microsoft layers Durable Task Framework / Durable Task Scheduler underneath for the hosted long-running story.
features.schemaValidation: Pydantic on the Python side and strongly-typed messages on the .NET side; executors declare typed message handlers (`@handler` on a typed parameter) and edges are typed, so a type mismatch is a wiring error. Structured output via provider-native response formats. There is no described per-step validate-and-repair loop equivalent to weft's — validation is at the type/serialization boundary, not a retry mechanism.
features.humanInTheLoop: `RequestInfoExecutor` is a built-in executor that emits a request event, and the workflow's pending requests/responses are part of the checkpoint payload. So a workflow can checkpoint mid-request, the process can die, and the response can be delivered later against a rehydrated instance — the docs call out an entry checkpoint written specifically when request responses are delivered. This is a properly durable HITL primitive, comparable to weft's `ctx.gate`.
features.parallelism: Superstep BSP: all executors that received messages in a superstep run concurrently, then a barrier. Edge groups (fan-out, fan-in, switch-case) express topology. Shipped orchestration patterns: sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic (the AutoGen Magentic-One planner-orchestrator ported over).
features.gitIsolation: None. Sandboxing is at the container/Azure Container Apps level, not git. No worktree, no patch capture, no staged integration.
features.multiProvider: Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, and notably the GitHub Copilot SDK; plus A2A and MCP for cross-agent/tool interop. Non-Microsoft providers (Anthropic, Google) are supported but visibly second-class in the docs. There is no per-step router that treats a coding CLI as a provider.
features.costControl: Nothing budget-shaped in the OSS framework. Token usage flows into OpenTelemetry spans (gen_ai semantic conventions) and Azure Monitor / Application Insights handles aggregation and alerting. No ceilings, no abort-on-spend, no propagation into sub-workflows.
features.observability: Best-in-cluster on the standards axis: OpenTelemetry is built in, not bolted on, following the gen_ai semantic conventions, so traces land in any OTel backend (Azure Monitor, Jaeger, Grafana). Plus DevUI — a local interactive web UI for running, inspecting, and debugging workflows, and `SuperStepCompletedEvent` gives you a per-superstep event stream with the checkpoint handle attached. Workflow visualization/graph rendering is built in.
features.testing: No dedicated deterministic harness. Standard pytest/xUnit with mocked chat clients. Checkpoints make manual replay possible but aren't packaged as test fixtures.
features.authoringModel: Code-as-graph via `WorkflowBuilder(start_executor=...).add_edge(a, b).build()`, with executors as classes carrying typed `@handler` methods. More ceremonious than weft's plain-await model, but the typing is genuinely enforced end to end, and the same workflow definition compiles in Python, .NET, and Go.

strengths: The single most precisely specified checkpoint payload in the cluster — pending messages and pending requests/responses are captured, not just state, which is why HITL survives process death correctly.
Explicit entry checkpoints (before first superstep, and on request-response delivery) make the run genuinely replayable end to end rather than only resumable forward.
Executor-controlled serialization (`on_checkpoint_save`/`on_checkpoint_restore`) puts the state contract in the author's hands instead of guessing via reflection.

Treats checkpoint storage as a trust boundary and says so in the docs, with a restricted unpickler and an `allowed_checkpoint_types` allowlist in `module:qualname` form — a security posture nobody else in this cluster has.
OpenTelemetry-native with gen_ai semantic conventions; no vendor lock-in for traces.
Cross-language parity (Python/.NET/Go) with the same workflow model.
Backed by Microsoft with an explicit LTS promise, and both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel now funnel users here.
weaknesses: Checkpoint compatibility is brittle by design: topology and executor identity must match exactly, and the docs admit stale checkpoints cannot be repaired — start a new lineage instead. This is precisely the problem weft's edit-tolerant replay attacks.

Python checkpoints use pickle for non-JSON-native state; the restricted unpickler mitigates but does not eliminate the deserialization risk, and it means checkpoints are not portable or human-inspectable.
No cost budgets or ceilings.
No git isolation or patch-staging for code-writing agents.
No determinism gate — nothing prevents non-deterministic code inside an executor.
Azure gravity is strong; the fully-OSS, non-Microsoft path is workable but underdocumented.
Ceremony-heavy authoring (builder + executor classes + typed handlers) versus plain async code.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Checkpoint the *pending message queue and pending requests/responses*, not just accumulated state.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the difference between 'resume forward' and 'the in-flight human gate survives a crash'. Weft journals step results; explicitly journaling the set of outstanding gates/asks and their correlation ids makes `ctx.human.ask` crash-proof rather than crash-tolerant.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Entry checkpoints: one before the first step recording the workflow input, and one at the moment an external response is delivered.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Bookending the run with input and external-input checkpoints is what makes the whole run replayable rather than only the middle. Cheap to add to an append-only journal and it closes the 'where did this run's inputs come from' gap.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Explicit author-controlled serialization hooks per step (`on_checkpoint_save` / `on_checkpoint_restore`).
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's Zod schemas define the shape of a step's *result*; a separate hook for a step's *internal* resumable state would let long-running steps (a multi-turn agent loop) checkpoint mid-flight instead of being all-or-nothing.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Treat the journal as a trust boundary with a type allowlist (`allowed_checkpoint_types` in `module:qualname` form) and a documented threat model.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal is JSON + Zod so it dodges the pickle problem, but the *framing* is worth copying: say out loud that journal storage is trusted infrastructure, and make the set of deserializable step-result types an explicit, enumerable allowlist. That pairs naturally with the determinism gate as a second security-shaped guarantee.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `SuperStepCompletedEvent` carrying the checkpoint handle inline in the event stream.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's daemon UI could surface 'resume from here' affordances directly on journal events if each event carried its own resume handle.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: DevUI as a shipped local debugging UI, distinct from the production deployment surface.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has a daemon web UI over the Engine; MAF's split between DevUI (author-time) and deployed workflow (run-time) is a useful framing for what each surface should show.

projects.name: AutoGen (microsoft/autogen, legacy)
projects.license: MIT for code, CC-BY-4.0 for docs
projects.popularity: 60.6k stars, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24 — the highest count in this cluster, but it is legacy mindshare. The README carries a prominent banner: 'Maintenance Mode — AutoGen is now in maintenance mode. It will not receive new features or enhancements and is community managed going forward.'
projects.positioning: Historically the conversational multi-agent research framework (v0.4 rearchitected around an actor/event-driven core: AgentChat on top of autogen-core). Now explicitly superseded — the README directs new users to Microsoft Agent Framework and existing users to the migration guide. Included here because its star count still dominates search results and comparison posts.

features.durability: `save_state()` / `load_state()` on teams and agents produce a serializable snapshot you persist yourself. That is the whole story: no automatic checkpointing, no superstep boundaries, no journal, no resume-after-crash without your own plumbing. AutoGen v0.4's actor runtime is event-driven but the events are not durably journaled.
features.schemaValidation: Pydantic-typed messages between agents in v0.4's core; structured output via provider `response_format` on the model client. No validate-and-repair loop as a framework primitive.
features.humanInTheLoop: `UserProxyAgent` — an agent whose 'model' is a human input function. `human_input_mode` of ALWAYS / TERMINATE / NEVER on the classic ConversableAgent. It is an in-process blocking callback, not a durable gate: kill the process and the pending request is gone.
features.parallelism: Team topologies rather than a DAG: RoundRobinGroupChat, SelectorGroupChat (model picks the next speaker), Swarm (handoff-based), MagenticOneGroupChat (ledger-driven planner). Concurrency exists in the actor runtime but is not exposed as a fan-out/fan-in workflow primitive.
features.gitIsolation: None. Code execution via `DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor` (container isolation) or a local executor. No worktrees, no patch capture.
features.multiProvider: OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, and others via `ChatCompletionClient` implementations; per-agent model assignment.
features.costControl: Usage accounting on model clients (`total_usage()`), and `max_turns` / termination conditions bound a conversation. No token or USD budget with a hard ceiling.
features.observability: OpenTelemetry instrumentation in v0.4, plus AutoGen Studio (a low-code prototyping GUI). Third-party tracing via AgentOps, Langfuse, etc.
features.testing: `ReplayChatCompletionClient` — a model client that returns a scripted list of responses instead of calling a provider. This is the closest thing in this whole cluster to weft's zero-model-call harness and it is genuinely useful. No replay-of-recorded-runs facility though.
features.authoringModel: Conversational: instantiate agents with system messages and tools, put them in a team, call `run()` / `run_stream()`. Control flow emerges from speaker selection rather than being written down. Deliberately un-graph-like.

strengths: `ReplayChatCompletionClient` is a clean, minimal answer to deterministic testing without model calls.
The v0.4 actor/event-driven core was a genuinely good rearchitecture — typed messages, async, distributed-capable.
Magentic-One's ledger-driven orchestrator (task ledger + progress ledger, re-planned on stall) is a strong pattern that MAF carried forward.
AutoGen Studio lowered the barrier for non-programmers to prototype agent teams.
weaknesses: Maintenance mode — no new features, community-managed. Should not be chosen for new work in 2026.
No durable execution at all beyond DIY save_state/load_state.
HITL is an in-process blocking callback that does not survive a crash.
Emergent conversational control flow is the opposite of what a coding pipeline wants: non-reproducible, hard to bound, hard to audit.
No cost ceilings, no git isolation, no determinism guarantees.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `ReplayChatCompletionClient`: a provider implementation whose entire behavior is 'return the next item from this list'.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already has a zero-model-call harness; the framing worth copying is making it a *provider* rather than a test mode — a `ReplayAgentProvider` slots into the existing AgentProvider interface, so tests exercise the real routing/budget/journal code paths with zero special-casing.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Magentic-One's two-ledger orchestrator: a task ledger (facts, guesses, plan) plus a progress ledger (is progress being made? who acts next?), with re-planning triggered on detected stall.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's supervisor-shaped workflows currently need the author to hand-code stall detection. A journaled progress ledger — 'no new content-addressed step results in N steps' — is a cheap, deterministic stall signal that the engine could offer, and it composes with budget ceilings as a second abort condition.

projects.name: AG2 (AutoGen fork, ag2ai/ag2)
projects.popularity: 4.9k stars, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24. 5,417 commits, 17 open issues, 16 open PRs — actively maintained but a fraction of the original AutoGen's reach.
projects.positioning: Community fork of AutoGen (by original AutoGen authors) after the Microsoft rearchitecture, self-described as an 'open-source AgentOS'. AG2 v1.0 (`import ag2`) is a hard break: GroupChat and Swarm were replaced by a hub-and-channel 'Network' architecture, with the classic patterns moved to a separate `ag2-classic` repo. So the project is maintaining two incompatible frameworks in parallel.

features.durability: No durable execution primitive found. Conversation history and 'knowledge persistence' / history compaction are documented, but there is no checkpoint-and-resume-after-crash story, no journal, no replay.
features.schemaValidation: Structured outputs listed as a supported advanced concept (Pydantic response models on the LLM config). No validate-and-repair loop as a framework primitive.
features.humanInTheLoop: v1.0 mechanism is `context.input()` called from inside a tool, plus a customizable `hitl_hook` for approval workflows — so HITL is a tool-level concern rather than a graph-level gate. Classic AG2 retains `UserProxyAgent` and `human_input_mode`. In-process, not durable.
features.parallelism: v1.0's Network is a hub-and-channel message topology; agents publish/subscribe rather than sit on a DAG. Classic AG2 has GroupChat and Swarm handoffs. No explicit fan-out/fan-in workflow combinators.
features.gitIsolation: None. Docker-based code execution inherited from AutoGen.
features.multiProvider: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Cohere, Ollama, Bedrock via LLM config lists — including per-agent config lists with fallback ordering.
features.costControl: Inherited AutoGen usage accounting and `max_turns`/`max_consecutive_auto_reply` bounds. No budget ceiling.
features.observability: Third-party integrations (AgentOps, Langfuse). No first-party OTel-native story comparable to MAF's.
features.testing: Standard pytest; no shipped replay/mock provider harness of note in v1.0 docs.
features.authoringModel: Conversational agents plus, in v1.0, a network/channel topology. Control flow is emergent from message routing, not written as code structure.

strengths: Apache-2.0 and genuinely community-governed, with the original AutoGen authors involved.
Kept a maintained home for the classic AutoGen patterns (`ag2-classic`) after Microsoft moved on — real value for the large installed base of AutoGen v0.2 code.
`hitl_hook` as a pluggable, framework-level approval interception point is a cleaner seam than AutoGen's per-agent `human_input_mode`.
Hub-and-channel Network is arguably a better fit than group chat for many-agent systems.
weaknesses: Splitting into two incompatible frameworks (v1.0 Network vs ag2-classic) fragments an already small community.
No durable execution, no journal, no crash recovery.
Materially less mindshare than either AutoGen's legacy footprint or MAF's forward momentum — a real 'which fork do I bet on' risk.
No cost ceilings, git isolation, determinism gate, or structured-output repair loop.
Documentation is thinner than the incumbents'.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A single pluggable `hitl_hook` that intercepts every human-input request framework-wide, rather than per-call configuration.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has `ctx.gate` / `ctx.human.ask/approve/review` as distinct call sites. One engine-level interception hook would let the CLI, the MCP server, and the daemon web UI each supply their own delivery mechanism without any workflow code changing — the same workflow file runs headless in CI (auto-approve policy), interactively in the terminal, or via the web UI.

projects.name: Google ADK (Agent Development Kit)
projects.language: Python (sibling adk-java, adk-go); docs at adk.dev
projects.popularity: 21.3k stars, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24. Bi-weekly release cadence, Python 3.10+. Strong and growing, driven by Google Cloud/Vertex distribution.
projects.positioning: "A flexible and modular framework that applies software development principles to AI agent creation." Code-first, model-agnostic in principle but Gemini/Vertex-optimized in practice. Ships the full lifecycle: build, evaluate, deploy (Cloud Run / Vertex AI Agent Engine), with a Task API for structured agent-to-agent delegation and A2A protocol support.

features.durability: Two layers. (1) Session persistence: `SessionService` implementations — InMemory (lost on restart), Database (SQLite locally, Cloud SQL in production), and VertexAiSessionService. Sessions are an append-only chronological list of `Event` objects; state is mutated via state deltas carried on events, with key prefixes controlling scope (`app:` app-wide, `user:` across a user's sessions, `temp:` never persisted). That event-list-plus-deltas shape is structurally the closest thing in this cluster to weft's append-only journal. (2) Resumability, added in ADK Python 1.16+: set `is_resumable=True` via `ResumabilityConfig` on the `App`, then resume a stopped run by its Invocation ID (found in the event history). On resume, ADK replays previously completed steps from the logged events — results of successfully executed tools and completed agents are restored rather than re-run, while incomplete tools are re-executed and partially-complete agents restart from their last checkpoint. Per workflow-agent type: SequentialAgent resumes at the next sub-agent, LoopAgent continues from the last completed iteration, ParallelAgent skips already-completed sub-agents. The documented guarantee is deliberately weak and honest: 'the Resume feature ensures that the Tools in an agent are run at least once, and may run more than once' — at-least-once, so destructive tools need your own idempotency. Documented limits: you cannot modify the workflow before resuming, custom agents must implement resumability manually via their own state classes and checkpoints, and resume is not supported from `adk web` or the CLI.
features.schemaValidation: `output_schema` (a Pydantic model) on an LlmAgent constrains the final response, and `input_schema` constrains input; `output_key` writes the result into session state. Note the significant ADK constraint: an agent with `output_schema` set cannot also use tools or transfer to other agents. Tool arguments are schema-validated from function signatures/OpenAPI specs. No documented repair-retry loop on validation failure.
features.humanInTheLoop: Long-running tools: a tool declared as long-running returns a pending marker, the invocation yields, and the result is supplied later — combined with resumability this survives process restarts and webhook-driven resumption (Google's own blog frames it as 'pause for human approvals and resume via webhooks'). Plus a `tool_confirmation` flow for explicit per-tool approval. Callbacks (`before_tool_callback` / `after_tool_callback`) provide an interception point for approval policy.
features.parallelism: Three shipped workflow agents composing deterministically: `SequentialAgent`, `ParallelAgent` (concurrent sub-agent fan-out), `LoopAgent` (bounded iteration with an escalation exit). These sit alongside LlmAgent (model-driven routing) and custom agents, so you mix deterministic structure with model-driven delegation. Multi-agent hierarchies compose by nesting agents as sub-agents; the Task API adds structured multi-turn agent-to-agent delegation.
features.gitIsolation: None. Artifacts (`ArtifactService`) give versioned binary/file storage keyed to a session or user, which is adjacent — you get versioned file blobs — but there is no git worktree, no patch object, and no staged-integration boundary.
features.multiProvider: Gemini/Vertex first-class; others via LiteLLM (`LiteLlm(model=...)`) covering Anthropic, OpenAI, and the rest. Per-agent model assignment. No coding-CLI-agent provider abstraction.
features.costControl: None in the framework. Token counts land in traces/Vertex telemetry; no budget object, no ceiling, no propagation to sub-agents.
features.observability: `adk web` dev UI with an event timeline, state inspector, and trace view; OpenTelemetry export with vendor integrations (Datadog has a first-party ADK integration; LangWatch, Maxim, Phoenix, Weave all support it). Cloud Trace/Cloud Logging on Vertex.
features.testing: The strongest evaluation story in this cluster, and it has a piece nobody else has. Standard eval: `*.test.json` files (single session, multiple turns — unit-test grain) and evalset files (multiple multi-turn sessions — integration grain), scored on `tool_trajectory_avg_score` (exact match of the tool-call sequence), `response_match_score` (ROUGE-1), `final_response_match_v2` (LLM judge), plus rubric-based metrics for tool-use correctness, safety, and hallucination. Runnable three ways: `adk web` eval tab, `adk eval` CLI, and `AgentEvaluator.evaluate()` under pytest for CI. The distinctive piece: **`adk conformance`** — record a scenario once into `generated-recordings.yaml` + `generated-session.yaml` golden baselines, then run in Replay Mode (the default) where the tool compares live LLM requests, responses, and tool calls against the recording and *fails the command* on deviation; Live mode re-records. It is designed to sit in CI and block a PR that changes agent behavior. There is a separate `google/adk-conformance` repo holding the test artifacts.
features.authoringModel: Code-first Python: agents are objects (`LlmAgent(model=..., instruction=..., tools=[...], sub_agents=[...])`) composed into a tree, with `SequentialAgent`/`ParallelAgent`/`LoopAgent` supplying deterministic control flow. Also an 'Agent Config' YAML path for no-code definition. Control flow is expressed by composing agent objects rather than by `await`.

strengths: Session = append-only event list + state deltas with scope prefixes is a genuinely well-designed persistence model, and closer in spirit to weft's journal than anyone else's snapshot-based approach.
`adk conformance` record/replay against golden LLM-interaction baselines, wired to fail CI on deviation, is the single best testing idea in the cluster.
Evaluation is unusually complete: trajectory scoring (not just final answer), three grains of runner (UI / CLI / pytest), and rubric metrics for when no reference answer exists.
Honest documentation about weak guarantees — the at-least-once tool execution caveat and the explicit list of resumability limitations are the kind of thing most frameworks bury.
Deterministic workflow agents (Sequential/Parallel/Loop) sitting alongside model-driven agents lets you put structure exactly where you want it.
Artifact service gives versioned file storage as a first-class, session-scoped concept.
Multi-language (Python/Java/Go) with A2A protocol support.
weaknesses: Resumability is at-least-once, not exactly-once — destructive tools need application-level dedup, which is the same burden LangGraph imposes.
'You cannot modify the workflow before resuming it' — no edit tolerance at all, the exact gap weft targets.
Custom agents must hand-roll their own resumability via state classes and checkpoints; only the built-in workflow agents get it free.
Resume is not exposed through `adk web` or the CLI — it is an API-only capability, which undercuts the operator story.
The `output_schema` restriction (an agent with structured output cannot use tools or transfer) is a sharp and surprising limitation.
No cost budgets or ceilings.
No git isolation, no determinism gate.
Gemini/Vertex gravity: non-Google providers work via LiteLLM but are visibly second-class.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `adk conformance`: record a run's LLM requests/responses/tool calls into a golden YAML baseline, then default to Replay Mode where any deviation fails the command — designed to run on every PR and block merges.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the highest-value idea in the entire cluster for weft. Weft's journal *already contains* exactly this recording, and the determinism gate already guarantees the non-model parts replay identically. A `weft conformance` verb that pins a run's journal as a golden file and fails CI when a workflow edit changes the agent-interaction trace would be near-free to build on existing infrastructure and would be a category-defining feature for a coding-workflow engine.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: State key scope prefixes (`app:`, `user:`, `temp:`) that determine persistence lifetime declaratively at the key.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft journals everything; a `temp:` equivalent — values explicitly marked as never-journaled — gives authors a sanctioned escape hatch for secrets and huge blobs without weakening the journal's guarantees or forcing them to smuggle state out of band.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Trajectory-based evaluation (`tool_trajectory_avg_score`) — scoring the *sequence of steps taken*, not just the final output.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal is a step sequence by construction. Scoring 'did this run take the expected path through the workflow' is a metric weft can compute exactly and cheaply where everyone else has to reconstruct it from traces.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-composite-agent resume semantics spelled out explicitly (Sequential → next sub-agent; Loop → last completed iteration; Parallel → skip completed branches).
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has `ctx.parallel` and `ctx.pipeline`; documenting (and testing) the precise resume semantics of each combinator, as a table, is exactly the kind of specificity that earns trust for a durability claim.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A versioned artifact service — session-scoped, versioned binary/file storage as a first-class service.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's write steps produce patches. A companion versioned artifact store for the non-patch outputs (build logs, coverage reports, screenshots) would give those the same durable, addressable treatment that code changes already get.

projects.name: LlamaIndex Workflows (llama-index-workflows / run-llama/workflows-py)
projects.popularity: 442 stars on the standalone workflows-py repo, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24 — but this badly understates reach, since the workflow engine is the orchestration layer inside llama_index (51.8k stars, read 2026-08-24) and ships as the `llama-index-workflows` PyPI package (1.0 released 2026-06-30). Note: the repo README has been rebranded toward 'LlamaAgents' / document-centric agents, so the packaging story is in flux.
projects.positioning: "An event-driven, async-first, step-based way to control the execution flow of AI applications like agents." Explicitly anti-DSL: 'branch, loop, parallelize, persist state, recover from failures, all in plain Python with no DSL.' Now positioned around document-centric agents (LlamaParse integration), with three deployment modes: library, `llama-agents-server` (REST + streaming + persistence), and `llamactl` CLI.

features.durability: Two mechanisms. (1) Context serialization: `Context.to_dict()` / `Context.from_dict()` snapshots the whole workflow context — state, event queues, in-flight step data — so you can persist and rehydrate a run. This is what powers HITL resumption across process boundaries. (2) `WorkflowCheckpointer` wraps a workflow and records a checkpoint after each step completes, letting you list checkpoints and `run_from(checkpoint=...)` to re-run from any of them. Durability backends are pluggable — file or database. It is checkpoint-per-step (finer-grained than LangGraph's superstep) but it is state snapshotting, not a content-addressed journal, and there is no edit-tolerance story.
features.schemaValidation: Events are Pydantic models, so the message passing between steps is schema-validated by construction — a step declares the event type it accepts and the type(s) it returns, and a mismatch is a validation error. `ctx.store` is typed via a Pydantic state model. This is arguably the cleanest typed-edge design in the Python cluster. But it validates the *event envelope*, not the *model output*; structured LLM output uses LlamaIndex's `structured_predict` / output parsers with retry, separately.
features.humanInTheLoop: `InputRequiredEvent` emitted from a step, consumed by the caller from the event stream; the caller sends back a `HumanResponseEvent` via `ctx.send_event()`. Because the Context is serializable, the workflow can be snapshotted while waiting and rehydrated later in a different process — so this is genuinely durable HITL, not an in-process callback.
features.parallelism: `ctx.send_event()` fans out multiple events; `ctx.collect_events(ev, [TypeA, TypeB, ...])` is a buffering join that returns `None` until all expected event types have arrived, then returns them together — a clean fan-in idiom. `@step(num_workers=N)` bounds concurrent instances of a step. Steps are async by default.
features.gitIsolation: None. No worktrees, no patch capture, no sandbox.
features.multiProvider: All LlamaIndex LLM integrations (300+ packages on LlamaHub), so effectively every provider. Workflows themselves are provider-agnostic — a step is just an async function, so you can call anything.
features.costControl: None. Token counting via the LlamaIndex `TokenCountingHandler` callback, but no budget, no ceiling, no propagation.
features.observability: `ctx.write_event_to_stream()` plus `handler.stream_events()` for live streaming; instrumentation via LlamaIndex's dispatcher/span system, with integrations to Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, TruLens, W&B. `llama-agents-server` exposes REST endpoints for run monitoring.
features.testing: No dedicated zero-model-call harness. Standard pytest with async fixtures; checkpoints allow re-running from a point but aren't framed as test infrastructure.
features.authoringModel: Closest philosophical match to weft in this cluster: a class with `@step`-decorated async methods, where the *type annotations* define the topology — a step accepting `EventA` and returning `EventB` implicitly creates the edge. No graph builder, no explicit `add_edge`. `ctx.store` holds shared state. Control flow is expressed by which event type you return.

strengths: Type-driven implicit topology (edges inferred from event type annotations) is elegant and genuinely DSL-free — the workflow reads as plain Python.
Pydantic events mean every edge in the workflow is schema-validated by construction, which is a stronger structural guarantee than any state-dict-based framework offers.
`collect_events` is the nicest fan-in primitive in the cluster: a buffering join that reads as ordinary code.
Full Context serialization makes durable HITL work across process boundaries with no special machinery.
Checkpoint-per-step is finer-grained than superstep-based competitors.
Very small dependency surface if you install just `llama-index-workflows` — you are not buying the whole LlamaIndex stack.
weaknesses: Small standalone community (442 stars); most users encounter it as an implementation detail of llama_index rather than choosing it deliberately.
Branding/packaging churn — the repo README now reads as 'LlamaAgents' with a document-agent framing, which muddies what the product actually is.
No edit-tolerant replay; checkpoints assume the same workflow class.
No cost control, no determinism enforcement, no git isolation.
Event-type-driven routing gets hard to follow at scale — with many event types the topology lives in the type system and is not visible in one place.
Structured *model output* validation is a separate LlamaIndex concern, not a workflow-step guarantee.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Type-inferred topology: a step's accepted and returned event types *are* the edges — no explicit wiring call at all.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already uses `await` as the edge, which is the same instinct. The addition worth stealing is deriving a *static, renderable graph* from the type signatures — weft could extract a topology diagram from its TypeScript step signatures at build time, giving the daemon UI a real map of a workflow that has never been run.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `ctx.collect_events(ev, [TypeA, TypeB])` — a buffering join that returns `None` until all expected inputs have arrived.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's `ctx.parallel` handles structured fan-out where you know the branches up front. A type-keyed buffering join handles the harder case: heterogeneous branches finishing at different times, joined by what they produced rather than by how they were launched.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Whole-context serialization (`to_dict`/`from_dict`) as an explicit public API, separate from the checkpoint mechanism.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal is the source of truth, but a single serialize/deserialize call for 'the entire live run state' is what makes handing a paused run to a different process (CLI → daemon → MCP client) a one-liner rather than a replay.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `@step(num_workers=N)` — bounded concurrency declared at the step, not at the call site.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's budget ceilings bound cost; a per-step concurrency cap bounds resource contention (e.g. at most 3 concurrent worktree builds) and belongs in the same declarative family.

projects.name: Pydantic AI (+ pydantic-graph, + Temporal / DBOS / Prefect / Restate durability)
projects.popularity: 19.5k stars, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24. Fastest-growing of the type-safety-first frameworks; carries the Pydantic brand's credibility with the Python typing community. Docs moved from ai.pydantic.dev to pydantic.dev/docs/ai.
projects.positioning: "How Python does AI: agents, realtime voice, image generation, embeddings. Every model, every interface, typed end to end." FastAPI-for-agents positioning: type safety, dependency injection, and a composable 'capabilities' model where features snap on. Notably, it does NOT try to own durability — it integrates with real durable-execution engines instead.

features.durability: The most intellectually honest approach in the cluster: don't build a checkpointer, integrate with engines that already solved this. Four integrations. **Temporal**: the agent run loop lives in deterministic workflow code, and everything I/O-bound is offloaded to activities — every model request is its own activity, tools requiring I/O (FunctionToolset, MCPToolset) are activities unless marked `metadata={'temporal': False}`, MCP server communication is an activity, and event-stream handlers can be activities. Temporal's replay gives exactly-once semantics for activity results. **DBOS**: in-process library, no separate worker — 'functions remain normal Python functions but are checkpointed into a database' (Postgres or SQLite); pydantic-ai wraps model requests, MCP communication, event-stream handlers, and dynamic/MCP toolsets as DBOS steps, but tool functions registered directly on the agent are NOT auto-wrapped (you add `@DBOS.step` yourself). DBOS also supplies durable queues with concurrency limits, rate limits, timeouts, and prioritization. **Prefect** and **Restate** are further options; Temporal and Prefect support per-tool activity configuration, DBOS does not. The API is capability-based: attach `TemporalDurability` / `DBOSDurability` to any `Agent` and the same agent runs normally outside a workflow (the older `TemporalAgent` wrapper is deprecated). Separately, `pydantic-graph` has its own `BaseStatePersistence` (FullStatePersistence in memory, FileStatePersistence to disk) snapshotting node-by-node.
features.schemaValidation: The whole point of the library, and the closest analogue to weft's guarantee in Python. `output_type=Model` gives a validated Pydantic instance; validation failure triggers an automatic `ModelRetry` that feeds the specific validation error back to the model for repair, bounded by `retries`. Output modes: tool-call, native structured output, and prompted JSON. Tool arguments are schema-validated from the function signature. `@agent.output_validator` adds custom post-validation that can also raise `ModelRetry`. Typed dependencies via `deps_type` and `RunContext[DepsT]` make the whole thing statically checkable with mypy/pyright.
features.humanInTheLoop: Deferred tools, and it is a well-designed mechanism. A tool marked `requires_approval=True` (static) or raising `ApprovalRequired` (dynamic, based on args/context) causes the run to *terminate* with a `DeferredToolRequests` output containing `approvals`, `calls`, and `metadata`. The caller resolves these externally and resumes by calling `agent.run()` again with the original `message_history` plus a `DeferredToolResults` mapping tool-call IDs to booleans (approve/deny), result values, or exceptions (`ModelRetry` / `ToolFailed`). The resumed run gets a fresh `run_id` but keeps continuity via `conversation_id`. There is also an inline alternative — a `HandleDeferredToolCalls` capability that resolves within the same run. Because resumption is just message history plus results, HITL composes naturally with the durable-execution integrations.
features.parallelism: Concurrent tool calls within a turn; agents are async so ordinary `asyncio.gather` works. `pydantic-graph` has no built-in fan-out combinator. Durable parallelism comes from the underlying engine (Temporal child workflows, DBOS queues with concurrency limits).
features.gitIsolation: None. No sandbox, no worktree, no patch capture.
features.multiProvider: Best-in-cluster breadth with a genuinely uniform interface: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google/Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, Groq, Mistral, Cohere, xAI, Ollama, HuggingFace, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. `FallbackModel` chains providers on failure. Model set per-agent or per-run. Still chat-models-and-tools, not coding-CLI agents.
features.costControl: `UsageLimits(request_limit=..., input_tokens_limit=..., output_tokens_limit=..., total_tokens_limit=...)` passed to `run()` raises `UsageLimitExceeded` when breached — this is the ONLY framework in this cluster with an actual enforced token ceiling that aborts a run. It is per-run and token-based; there is no USD conversion and no automatic propagation to sub-agent runs (you thread it through yourself). Logfire tracks cost.
features.observability: Logfire is first-party and OpenTelemetry-native — traces, spans, token/cost tracking, and a real-time debugging UI, with the instrumentation being plain OTel so any backend works. `InstrumentationSettings` controls granularity. Because it emits standard gen_ai OTel semantics, Langfuse/Phoenix/Braintrust all consume it.
features.testing: The best DIY-testing story short of ADK's conformance mode. `TestModel` auto-generates schema-valid responses and calls every tool without hitting a provider — zero model calls, and it exercises your real validation code. `FunctionModel` gives full scripted control over what the 'model' returns. `ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS=False` is a global kill-switch that makes any accidental real API call raise. `capture_run_messages()` asserts on the exact message exchange. Separately, `pydantic-evals` provides datasets, evaluators (including LLM judges), and experiment tracking.
features.authoringModel: Plain Python: `Agent(model, deps_type=..., output_type=..., system_prompt=...)`, tools as decorated functions, run with `await agent.run()`. Multi-step control flow is just Python control flow. `pydantic-graph` is the optional state-machine layer — `BaseNode` subclasses as dataclasses whose `run()` return type annotations define the outgoing edges, with `GraphRunContext` carrying state and deps, `End` terminating, `graph.iter()` for stepwise control, and mermaid rendering. The docs explicitly discourage it for general use: 'Graphs are a powerful tool, but they're not the right tool for every job' — heavy generics, for advanced users, overkill unless you genuinely need a formal state machine.

strengths: Structured output with automatic ModelRetry repair is the closest thing in Python to weft's schema-validated-step-with-in-session-repair, and it is the library's central, best-executed feature.
`UsageLimits` with hard token ceilings that raise and abort — uniquely, nobody else in this cluster enforces a budget.
`TestModel` / `FunctionModel` / `ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS=False` is a genuine zero-model-call testing harness, including a global guard against accidental real calls.

Refusing to build its own durability and instead integrating Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate is the right architectural call — you inherit exactly-once semantics from engines that have spent a decade on it.
Deferred tools give durable HITL with a clean resume contract (message history + results), and it composes with every durability backend.
Type safety is real, not aspirational — mypy/pyright check agent deps and outputs end to end.
Logfire is OTel-native so there is no lock-in, and the DX is excellent.
`FallbackModel` for provider failover is a small feature that matters a lot in production.
weaknesses: Durability is entirely borrowed: Temporal means running a separate worker fleet and accepting 2MB payload limits, serializable-deps requirements, and a stable-agent-name constraint (renaming an agent breaks in-flight workflow replay). DBOS needs Postgres. Out of the box, pydantic-ai has no durability at all.

Determinism constraints are inherited and enforced by the *underlying engine*, not by pydantic-ai — and Temporal's sandbox catches accidental I/O, but nothing catches `Math.random`-style nondeterminism inside a tool that you forgot to make an activity.
`pydantic-graph` is officially discouraged and generics-heavy, so multi-step orchestration has no blessed answer between 'plain Python' and 'adopt Temporal'.
No fan-out/fan-in workflow combinators — parallelism is raw asyncio.
`UsageLimits` is token-only, per-run, and does not automatically propagate into sub-agent runs.
No git isolation, no patch staging.
Multi-agent topologies (supervisor/swarm/handoff) are not shipped as prebuilts; you compose them yourself.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS=False` — a global kill-switch that makes any real provider call raise, so an under-mocked test fails loudly instead of silently burning tokens.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's zero-model-call harness works when you use it correctly; a global guard makes it fail closed. One env var / test-setup flag on the AgentProvider layer, and no weft test can ever accidentally hit Claude or Codex.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `TestModel` that auto-generates *schema-valid* responses from the declared output schema, rather than requiring hand-written fixtures.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft steps already declare Zod schemas. Auto-deriving a plausible valid value from the Zod schema means a new step is testable the moment it is written, with zero fixture authoring — this is a direct, cheap win from infrastructure weft already has.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Capability-based durability attachment: `TemporalDurability` / `DBOSDurability` snap onto an ordinary Agent, and the same agent still runs normally outside a workflow.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft owns its journal, but the composability pattern generalizes: making journaling, budget enforcement, and the determinism gate independently attachable capabilities rather than baked-in engine behavior would let the same workflow file run in a fast unjournaled dev mode and a fully-journaled production mode without edits.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `FallbackModel` — an ordered provider chain that fails over automatically.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft routes steps to Claude or Codex per-step. A declarative fallback chain ('try Codex, fall back to Claude on 5xx or rate-limit') is a natural extension of the existing per-step routing and turns provider outages from a run failure into a logged degradation.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Deferred-tool resumption keyed by tool-call ID, where the resume payload can carry an *exception* (`ModelRetry` / `ToolFailed`) as well as a value.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's human gates are approve/reject-shaped. Letting a human reviewer return a structured failure that re-enters the model's retry loop as feedback — rather than terminating the step — makes `ctx.human.review` a repair mechanism, not just a checkpoint.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Delegating durable execution to Temporal/DBOS rather than owning it — and specifically DBOS's in-process, Postgres-checkpointed model with no separate worker.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Not to replace weft's journal, but as an *export target*: a weft workflow that can be hosted on DBOS or Temporal inherits enterprise operational tooling (retries, queues, rate limits, prioritization) that weft will not build itself, and it is a credible answer to 'how does this run in my company's infrastructure'.

projects.name: Burr (Apache Burr, DAGWorks)
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (now an Apache incubating project — donated from DAGWorks)
projects.popularity: 2.5k stars, read off the GitHub repo page 2026-08-24. ~975 commits. Small but with a coherent, well-defended point of view; the move under the Apache umbrella is a credibility signal.
projects.positioning: Build decision-making applications (chatbots, agents, simulations) as explicit state machines, with a strong bias toward monitoring, tracing, and infrastructure-agnosticism. Deliberately framework-agnostic — Burr orchestrates, you bring whatever LLM library you like. The pitch is 'your application is a state machine, so write it as one'.

features.durability: State-machine persistence via pluggable persisters. `BaseStatePersister` / `AsyncBaseStatePersister` interfaces, with `SQLLitePersister` built in and a `b_<database-library>` naming convention for others (Postgres, Redis, Mongo). Three identifiers carry the whole model: `app_id` (unique run, auto-UUID if unset), `partition_key` (grouping — e.g. user id), and `sequence_id` (position in the state-change sequence). `with_state_persister()` persists state *after each action* — per-action grain, not per-superstep. Loading uses `initialize_from()` with a `StateInitializer` and options `resume_at_next_action`, `default_entrypoint`, and `default_state`. The distinctive feature is **forking**: `fork_from_app_id` + `fork_from_partition_key` + `fork_from_sequence_id` rewinds to a specific point in a *previous* run and starts a new app from there, leaving the original untouched. And the tracking/telemetry system doubles as a persister, so you can resume a run directly from its tracked trace during local development. Still state snapshots, not content-addressed step results, and no edit tolerance.
features.schemaValidation: Typed state via a Pydantic-backed typing system (`State` can be parameterized by a Pydantic model, giving IDE and mypy support on state fields). Actions declare `reads` and `writes` — the set of state keys they consume and produce — which Burr validates statically at graph-build time. That reads/writes contract is the interesting bit: it is a data-dependency declaration, not just a type. No LLM-output repair loop (Burr doesn't own the LLM call).
features.humanInTheLoop: No dedicated gate primitive. The pattern is: an action returns, the application halts at a designated action (`halt_before` / `halt_after` on `app.run()`), the caller collects human input, and then `app.run()` continues with the input threaded into state. Because state is persisted per action, the pause is genuinely durable and can span processes — the mechanism is just less packaged than LangGraph's `interrupt()`.
features.parallelism: `MapStates` / `MapActions` recursive-application constructs for fan-out over collections, plus subgraph/recursive applications. Async actions supported. Less developed than the checkpoint/tracking story.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.multiProvider: Not Burr's concern by design — Burr never calls an LLM. You call whatever you want inside an action, so every provider works and none is integrated. Hooks provide a vendor-integration seam.
features.costControl: None. You could implement it in a hook, and the hook system is the right shape for it, but nothing ships.
features.observability: Burr's strongest suit and its actual reason for existing: a self-hosted open-source tracking server and UI (`burr` CLI launches it) showing every state transition, the state before and after, action inputs/outputs, streaming, and errors — with no external dependency and no SaaS. This is the only genuinely OSS, self-hosted, first-party observability UI in the cluster (LangSmith is SaaS, MAF's DevUI is dev-only, Logfire is SaaS). OpenTelemetry integration exists both ways (Burr can emit OTel, and can ingest OTel from libraries used inside actions).
features.testing: Because the tracker doubles as a persister, you can load any tracked run's state at any sequence_id and re-run an action against it — effectively replay-from-production-trace as a debugging and test-fixture mechanism. Actions are plain functions of `(state, **kwargs) -> (result, state)`, which makes them trivially unit-testable in isolation. No mock-LLM harness (out of scope by design).
features.authoringModel: Explicit state machine: `@action(reads=[...], writes=[...])`-decorated functions returning `(result, new_state)`, wired with `ApplicationBuilder().with_actions(...).with_transitions(('from', 'to', condition))`. Control flow is declared as transitions with conditions, fully separate from the action bodies. The most explicitly 'this is a state machine' authoring model in the cluster.

strengths: Per-action persistence with `(app_id, partition_key, sequence_id)` as the addressing scheme is a clean, obvious, resumable model — much simpler to reason about than superstep semantics.
Forking from an arbitrary `(app_id, sequence_id)` into a new application is a first-class API, not an afterthought.
The tracker-as-persister trick — resume or replay directly from a recorded trace — collapses debugging and durability into one mechanism.
Fully OSS self-hosted observability UI with no SaaS dependency; genuinely differentiated in a field where everyone else's good UI is a paid product.
`reads`/`writes` declarations validated at build time catch data-dependency errors before the first LLM call.
Deliberately framework-agnostic — no lock-in to a particular LLM library.
Actions as pure `(state, inputs) -> (result, state)` functions are trivially testable.
Apache governance reduces single-vendor risk.
weaknesses: Small community and limited mindshare; you will be an early adopter.
No HITL primitive — `halt_before`/`halt_after` plus manual state threading works but requires assembly.
No LLM integration at all means no structured-output enforcement, no repair loop, no cost tracking, no provider routing — all of which weft treats as core.
Parallelism constructs are the least developed part of the framework.
No determinism gate, no git isolation.
Explicit transition declarations are verbose relative to `await`-as-edge; adding a step means touching actions, transitions, and reads/writes.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `(app_id, partition_key, sequence_id)` as the universal addressing triple for any point in any run, with fork-from-triple as a first-class API.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal entries are already addressable; adopting an explicit, user-facing, stable triple makes 'fork run X at step 12', 'diff run X against run Y', and 'resume this run under a new id' all expressible in the CLI and MCP surface with one consistent vocabulary.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The tracking/telemetry store doubling as the state persister — replay a production run directly from its recorded trace.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal already *is* both. What Burr does that weft should copy is expose it that way in the product: a `weft replay <run-id> --from-step N` that pulls a real production run into a local debugging session is the same infrastructure with a much better story attached.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `reads=[...]` / `writes=[...]` declarations on each step, validated statically before any execution.
