Prompt management with versioning, deployment *labels* (production/staging), client-side caching so fetch latency is memory-speed, and — critically — trace linkage, so you can slice quality and cost by prompt version
Cost accounting with a maintained pricing table plus custom model pricing, aggregated up the trace tree and sliceable by user/session/tag/prompt version
Human annotation queues and score configs put human review, LLM-judge scores, and user feedback into one comparable score store
Datasets seeded directly from production traces closes the loop from incident to regression test
Environments as a first-class dimension keeps dev/staging/prod telemetry separate without separate projects
weaknesses: Observability only: it records what happened but cannot make an application durable, resumable, or replayable — the traces are a copy, not the source of truth
Non-trivial self-host footprint (Postgres + ClickHouse + Redis + S3 + web + worker) compared with a single-process engine
`ee` folders are commercially licensed, so some features (notably parts of RBAC/SSO/enterprise governance) are gated
Cost is observed, never enforced — no ceilings, no hard stop
SDK churn has been significant (Python v2→v3, JS v3→v4→v5, all rebasing on OTel), so integration guides age quickly
No structured-output or validation capability at all — purely the telemetry/eval layer

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Emit a proper OTel span tree — one span per step, typed as generation/span/event, with nested context propagation — instead of a single span per run
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the single largest identified gap in weft. Weft already journals every step with inputs, outputs, model, and token counts; mapping that journal onto nested OTel GenAI spans is close to mechanical and would immediately make weft runs viewable in Langfuse, Phoenix, Opik, or any OTLP backend — buying an entire trace UI for near-zero build cost.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Prompt management as versioned server-side artifacts with deployment labels (production/staging), client-side stale-while-revalidate caching, and explicit linkage from each generation back to the prompt version that produced it
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's prompts are inline in TypeScript, so changing one requires a deploy and there is no way to ask 'did quality drop when we changed the review step's prompt?'. Prompt-version linkage in the journal would make weft's edit-tolerant replay far more meaningful — you could distinguish 'the code changed' from 'the prompt changed'.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A model-pricing table with user-definable custom model entries, with cost aggregated up the trace tree and sliceable by tag/user/session/prompt version
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft enforces token/USD ceilings but attribution matters as much as enforcement. Per-dimension cost rollups would tell a team *which step, which prompt version, which sub-workflow* is burning the budget — turning a hard ceiling into an actionable one.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Annotation queues + score configs: route selected runs to humans, capture typed scores, and store human, LLM-judge, and end-user scores in one comparable place
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's humans are durable steps that gate execution. Langfuse's humans grade *completed* runs asynchronously. Weft has no post-hoc quality signal at all; adding a score store keyed by journal id would let review gates double as a labelled dataset.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Creating dataset items directly from production traces, then re-running the workflow over the dataset and diffing versions
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journals are already complete recordings of real runs. Promoting a failed journal to a regression case — replayable through the existing zero-model-call harness, or with real models as an experiment — is a near-free capability given weft's existing journal + replay machinery.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: 'Environment' as a first-class telemetry dimension
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft runs the same workflows from CLI, MCP, and daemon; tagging journals by environment would keep experimental local runs from polluting production statistics.

projects.name: LangSmith (OSS surface only)
projects.language: Python and JavaScript/TypeScript (SDK); Go collector proxy
projects.license: MIT for the SDK. The LangSmith platform/server itself is NOT open source.
projects.popularity: langsmith-sdk: 1.0k stars on the GitHub repo page as of 2026-08-24 (seen directly). Platform adoption is large but proprietary and unverifiable; treat as unknown. Latest release version unknown.
projects.positioning: The commercial counter-example in this cluster: a mature, deeply integrated tracing/eval platform whose *client* is open source and whose *server* is not. Self-hosting is an Enterprise-plan add-on requiring a contract with LangChain — there is no free self-host path.

features.authoringModel: Not a workflow authoring tool (that is LangGraph, a sibling). Instrumentation is `@traceable` (Python) / `traceable()` (JS), a manual `RunTree` API for constructing trace trees by hand, `wrap_openai`-style client wrappers, and automatic capture for LangChain/LangGraph.
features.costControl: Cost accounting per run using a model price map; no enforcement or ceilings. Platform-level usage limits are billing controls, not runtime budget ceilings.
features.durability: Durable telemetry storage on the hosted platform. LangGraph (separate product) is where durable execution lives — with checkpointers persisting graph state between super-steps, thread-scoped state, time-travel, and interrupt/resume — which is architecturally the closest thing in the LangChain world to weft's journal. LangSmith itself does not make your app resumable.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Annotation queues for human review of traces, feedback scores attached to runs, and a UI for manual labelling. (Runtime human gates live in LangGraph's `interrupt()`, not LangSmith.)
features.multiProvider: Provider-agnostic. Traces anything via `@traceable`; end-to-end OpenTelemetry support means any OTLP emitter can ship spans in, and `LANGSMITH_OTEL_ENABLED=true` lets an app emit OTel spans once and fan them out through a Collector to LangSmith *and* other backends simultaneously. The langsmith-collector-proxy accepts OTLP over HTTP in both JSON and protobuf.
features.observability: Very mature: nested run trees with typed run types (llm/chain/tool/retriever/prompt), token and cost per node, latency waterfalls, filtering and saved views, threads for multi-turn sessions, online evaluation rules that score a sampled fraction of production traffic, alerting, and a prompt hub/playground. End-to-end OTel support was added specifically so LangSmith stops being a closed telemetry island.
features.parallelism: Run trees model concurrent branches; context propagation handles nesting across async boundaries.
features.schemaValidation: None — not a structured-output tool.
features.testing: Strong: `evaluate()` (and `aevaluate()`) runs a target function over a dataset with a list of evaluators (custom code, LLM-as-judge, or built-ins), producing an experiment with per-example results and aggregate scores; supports pairwise/comparative experiments, repetitions for variance, and summary evaluators over the whole run. Datasets are versioned with splits, and examples can be added from production traces. Pytest/Vitest integrations let evals run in CI.

strengths: The most polished trace UI and eval workflow in the category, with years of production hardening
End-to-end OTel support plus a Go collector proxy means you can emit spans once and fan out to LangSmith and other backends — no vendor lock at the telemetry layer
`evaluate()` with summary evaluators, repetitions for variance, and pairwise experiments is a more complete statistical harness than most OSS equivalents
Online evaluators score a sampled slice of live production traffic continuously, not just offline datasets
Framework-independent `@traceable`/RunTree works fine without any LangChain code
Pytest/Vitest integration puts evals in CI naturally
weaknesses: The platform is closed source; self-hosting is Enterprise-only, contract-gated, and demands a Kubernetes cluster (reported minimums around 16+ vCPU / 64+ GB RAM plus managed databases) — disqualifying for anyone wanting weft-style local-first operation
Only the thin SDK is MIT; the valuable part is not available to read or fork
Cost is reported, never enforced
Strongest ergonomics still assume LangChain/LangGraph; standalone use is supported but second-class
Durable execution lives in a different product (LangGraph), so the observability and durability stories are split across two systems

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Emit OTel spans once and let a Collector fan them out to multiple backends (the LANGSMITH_OTEL_ENABLED + collector-proxy pattern)
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft should never require a specific observability vendor. Emitting standard GenAI spans from the journal and letting operators route them wherever means weft's telemetry story is 'works with everything' rather than 'one span, and you're on your own'.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Online evaluators: sample a percentage of production runs and score them continuously with an LLM judge, with alerting on score regressions
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's budget ceilings catch cost regressions but nothing catches *quality* regressions. Sampling completed journals for automated scoring would give weft a production quality signal it currently lacks entirely.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Summary evaluators and repetitions — running each dataset example N times to measure variance, and scoring the experiment as a whole rather than only per-example
ideasWorthStealing.why: Coding agents are high-variance. A weft eval that runs a workflow once per case would be badly misleading; measuring variance across repetitions is the difference between a real regression signal and noise.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: LangGraph's checkpointer + interrupt()/resume model as a comparison point for weft's journal
ideasWorthStealing.why: LangGraph persists graph state between super-steps and resumes from a checkpoint after a human interrupt. Weft's content-addressed step salvage with edit-tolerant replay is more ambitious, but LangGraph's thread-scoped state and time-travel (fork a run from any past checkpoint) is a capability weft should match — replaying a journal from step N with a changed input is a natural extension of salvage.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Pytest/Vitest-native eval integration so experiments are just tests
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already has a zero-model-call harness; letting the same declarations run as model-backed evals in CI, under Vitest, would unify the two testing modes under one authoring surface.

projects.name: Arize Phoenix
projects.language: Python (server and SDK) with TypeScript/JavaScript client support
projects.license: Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2) — source-available, not OSI open source; free to self-host but you may not offer it as a managed service
projects.popularity: 11.2k stars on the GitHub repo page as of 2026-08-24 (seen directly). Latest release version unknown.
projects.positioning: The OpenTelemetry-purist observability platform: everything is OTel spans following OpenInference semantic conventions, so Phoenix is a *backend* for a standard rather than an SDK you must adopt. Runs as a single local process (`phoenix serve`, or in a notebook) as easily as a cluster — the most weft-like local-first posture in this cluster.

features.authoringModel: Not a workflow tool. `arize-phoenix-otel` is described as 'a lightweight wrapper around OpenTelemetry primitives with Phoenix-aware defaults' — `register()` configures a tracer provider and OTLP exporter in one call; 40+ auto-instrumentors then patch libraries automatically. Manual spans use the plain OTel API plus OpenInference attribute helpers.
features.costControl: Token counts are captured per span via OpenInference attributes and cost is computed from a model pricing table, aggregated per trace/project. Accounting only — no enforcement, no ceilings.
features.durability: Durable trace and dataset storage (SQLite for local/single-user, Postgres for deployments). Telemetry durability, not execution durability — Phoenix cannot resume your application.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Human annotations on spans and traces (typed labels/scores with explanations), annotation configs, and the ability to curate examples into datasets by hand from the trace view. Human and LLM-judge annotations share the same store.
features.multiProvider: Fully provider-agnostic through OpenInference: instrumentors exist for OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral, Groq, LiteLLM, plus frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, DSPy, Vercel AI SDK, smolagents, and more) across Python, TypeScript, Java and Go. Any OTLP source works.
features.observability: Excellent, and the most standards-clean. Ingests OTLP directly (gRPC and HTTP), so it is a drop-in OTLP backend. Spans are typed by OpenInference span kind — LLM, CHAIN, TOOL, AGENT, RETRIEVER, EMBEDDING, RERANKER, GUARDRAIL, EVALUATOR — which gives the UI enough structure to render a purpose-built view per node type (retrieved documents for RETRIEVER, tool arguments for TOOL, messages/params/tokens for LLM) rather than a generic timeline. Projects separate applications; sessions group multi-turn traces. Latency, token, and cost rollups per span and per project.
features.parallelism: Standard OTel nesting and context propagation.
features.schemaValidation: None at generation time. `arize-phoenix-evals` includes evaluators that check output conformance, but Phoenix does not constrain or repair generation.
features.testing: Versioned datasets of examples (inputs, optional reference outputs, metadata), created manually, uploaded, or curated from production spans. `run_experiment(dataset, task=fn, evaluators=[...])` executes the task over every example and applies evaluators; each experiment run is stored, traced (the task's own spans are captured), and comparable side by side against other runs over the same dataset version. `arize-phoenix-evals` ships prebuilt LLM-judge templates (hallucination, QA correctness, RAG relevance, toxicity, summarization) that return a label *plus an explanation*, and can run with concurrency and rate-limit handling. The prompt playground allows editing a prompt and replaying it across a whole dataset to compare before/after.

strengths: Pure OTel/OpenInference: adopting Phoenix costs nothing beyond emitting standard spans, and leaving costs nothing either — the strongest anti-lock-in position in the cluster
Typed span kinds (LLM/CHAIN/TOOL/AGENT/RETRIEVER/EMBEDDING/RERANKER/GUARDRAIL/EVALUATOR) give the UI real semantics, so each node renders meaningfully instead of as an opaque blob
Runs locally as a single process or in a notebook, with SQLite — matches weft's local-first, daemon-on-your-machine posture better than Postgres+ClickHouse+Redis stacks
Experiments capture the task's own traces, so a failing eval example links straight to the trace that produced it
LLM judges return explanations alongside labels, which makes eval results debuggable rather than just numeric
`arize-phoenix-evals` is usable standalone as a library, independent of the Phoenix server
40+ instrumentors across four languages, including a TypeScript story and Vercel AI SDK support
weaknesses: ELv2 is source-available, not OSI open source — a licensing consideration for anyone embedding or offering it
Prompt management is present but less developed than Langfuse's (labels, caching, and SDK fetch semantics are thinner)
Python-centric server and ecosystem; TS/Java/Go get instrumentation but not the full authoring experience
Observability only — no durable execution, no cost enforcement, no orchestration
OpenInference conventions overlap and partially conflict with the official OTel GenAI conventions, so you must pick a dialect

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Typed span kinds (LLM / CHAIN / TOOL / AGENT / RETRIEVER / GUARDRAIL / EVALUATOR) so a trace UI can render each node according to what it is
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already knows the kind of every journaled step — write step in a worktree, gate, human ask, sub-workflow, integrate, repair attempt. Stamping an OpenInference-style span kind on each would make weft's daemon UI (and any external backend) render a genuinely structured run view rather than a flat list, essentially for free.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Experiments whose task execution is itself traced, linking each eval result to the trace that produced it
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal is already the trace. Running a dataset of cases through weft would naturally produce one journal per case; linking eval scores to journal ids gives instant drill-down from 'this case regressed' to 'here is exactly what every step did'.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: LLM-judge evaluators that emit an explanation alongside the label
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's ctx.human.review is a human judgement with no machine counterpart. An explained LLM judge could pre-screen review gates — auto-approving clear passes and surfacing only ambiguous cases with a written rationale to the human, cutting gate latency.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Local-first single-process deployment with SQLite, scaling to Postgres only when needed
ideasWorthStealing.why: Validates weft's daemon design and suggests the journal store should be swappable the same way — SQLite by default, Postgres for team deployments — without changing the Engine API.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The prompt playground replaying an edited prompt across an entire dataset
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft can replay journals. Extending replay so a step's prompt can be edited and re-run across many stored journals at once would turn edit-tolerant replay from a crash-recovery feature into a prompt-development feature.

projects.name: Braintrust (OSS components)
projects.repo: https://github.com/braintrustdata/braintrust-sdk (JS/TS, being split into braintrust-sdk-javascript and braintrust-sdk-python); https://github.com/braintrustdata/autoevals; https://github.com/braintrustdata/braintrust-proxy; https://github.com/braintrustdata/agentbehavior
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (SDKs, autoevals, agentbehavior); the Braintrust platform itself is proprietary
projects.popularity: braintrust-sdk (JS) repo page showed 27 stars as of 2026-08-24 (seen directly) — low because the repo was recently split into language-specific repos, so this understates adoption. From search results and NOT directly verified: autoevals ~990 stars, braintrust-proxy ~408, agentbehavior 292 (agentbehavior's 292 was seen directly on its repo page). Platform adoption: unknown.
projects.positioning: An eval-first commercial platform (evals as the primary artifact, tracing secondary) that open-sources its client SDKs, its scorer library, its LLM proxy, and — newest and most interesting — an open *standard* for specifying agent behaviour. The proprietary part is the app.

features.authoringModel: `Eval()` is the core authoring primitive: a named experiment declaring `data` (dataset), `task` (the function under test), and `scores` (a list of scorer functions). Run via the `braintrust eval` CLI over `.eval.ts`/`.eval.py` files — evals are source files in your repo, versioned in git, not UI config. Tracing uses `wrapOpenAI`/`traced`/`startSpan`. agentbehavior specs are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter.
features.costControl: Cost accounting per span from token usage; the braintrust-proxy can enforce caching and provides a single key across providers. No runtime budget ceilings in the OSS pieces.
features.durability: None for execution. The proxy is stateless apart from its cache; the SDK buffers and flushes spans. Experiment results are durable on the (proprietary) platform.
features.gitIsolation: None — but evals-as-code in the repo means eval definitions are versioned with the code they test, which is the closest analogue.
features.humanInTheLoop: Human review/annotation and score overrides exist on the platform; the OSS surface contributes the score model those reviews write into. agentbehavior is explicitly a human-authored artifact: written behaviour specs that reviewers, rubrics, and scorers are all measured against.
features.multiProvider: braintrust-proxy is the standout OSS piece: a unified API over OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Llama, Bedrock and others behind one key, deployable on Cloudflare Workers/edge, with response caching and automatic logging. Effectively a self-hostable multi-provider gateway you can put in front of anything.
features.observability: SDK emits nested spans with inputs, outputs, scores, and metadata, and supports OTel export; the trace UI, experiment comparison views and monitoring are proprietary. The OSS half gives you emission, not visualization.
features.parallelism: Evals run concurrently across dataset rows with configurable concurrency; tracing spans nest normally.
features.schemaValidation: Not a structured-output library. autoevals includes scorers that check JSON/schema validity and structural diffs, but validation is a scoring concern, not a generation-time guarantee.
features.testing: This is the whole point and it is the strongest CI-shaped story in the cluster. `Eval()` declarations live as source files, run through a CLI, and there is a first-party GitHub Action ('Braintrust eval') that runs evals on every PR and comments the score diff versus the base branch — evals as a required check. **autoevals** is a standalone Apache-2.0 scorer library usable with no Braintrust account: heuristic scorers (Levenshtein, exact match, numeric diff, JSON diff, embedding similarity) and model-graded scorers (Factuality, ClosedQA, Battle/pairwise, Humor, Security, Summarization, Translation) with prompts written using chain-of-thought and returning reasoned verdicts. **agentbehavior** is a newer open standard: Markdown+YAML specs that describe how an agent should gather context, decide, act, and recover from uncertainty across a whole trajectory, with a discovery model and validation rules — explicitly 'the standard before any reviewer, rubric, scorer, or eval measures it', supervising the *process* rather than only the outcome.

strengths: Evals-as-code in the repository, run by a CLI, gated by a GitHub Action that comments score deltas on PRs — the most natural fit with an engineering workflow of anything in this cluster
autoevals is genuinely standalone and Apache-2.0: a library of both heuristic and model-graded scorers you can use without adopting the platform
braintrust-proxy is a self-hostable, edge-deployable multi-provider gateway with caching and a single API key — useful infrastructure independent of the product
agentbehavior tackles trajectory-level behaviour specification, which is exactly the coding-agent problem (was the *process* right?) and which no scorer-only approach addresses
Model-graded scorers use chain-of-thought and return reasons, so failures are explicable
Clean separation: the pieces you might want to embed are open, the app you'd rather buy is not
weaknesses: The platform — trace UI, experiment comparison, monitoring, human review — is proprietary; the OSS pieces alone give you no visualization
Repo splitting has fragmented the SDK story and makes adoption signals hard to read
No durable execution, no runtime cost ceilings, no orchestration
agentbehavior is very new and its ecosystem/tooling is unproven
Star counts for autoevals and braintrust-proxy came from search snippets, not from the repo pages — unverified

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Evals as versioned source files (`*.eval.ts`) run by a CLI and enforced by a CI action that comments score diffs on the PR
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft is a TypeScript engine with a CLI and a zero-model-call harness. Adding a model-backed eval mode that runs `.eval.ts` files and posts a score delta on PRs would make weft workflow changes reviewable the same way code changes are — and it fits weft's existing CLI surface exactly.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: agentbehavior: trajectory-level behaviour specs (Markdown + YAML) describing how an agent should gather context, decide, act, and recover — supervising the process, not just the final artifact
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the single most weft-relevant idea in the cluster. Weft's write steps produce patches judged at ctx.integrate(); nothing evaluates *how* the agent got there. Weft's journal is a complete, structured trajectory — it is uniquely positioned to check a run against a declared behaviour spec ('did it read the tests before editing?', 'did it escalate when the schema was ambiguous?') as a journaled, gate-able assertion.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A standalone scorer library mixing cheap heuristics (Levenshtein, JSON diff, exact match, embedding similarity) with model-graded judges (Factuality, ClosedQA, pairwise Battle)
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has no notion of output quality beyond schema validity. A tiered scorer set — heuristics first, model judge only when heuristics are inconclusive — would give weft quality signals while respecting its budget ceilings.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Pairwise/Battle comparison scoring rather than absolute scores
ideasWorthStealing.why: Absolute quality scores for coding output are nearly meaningless; 'is patch A better than patch B' is answerable. Weft could run a write step twice in two worktrees and use pairwise judging to pick which patch reaches ctx.integrate().

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An open, self-hostable multi-provider proxy with caching in front of the providers
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's AgentProvider abstracts Claude and Codex in-process. Putting a caching proxy underneath would make replay of model-backed runs cheap and would let the determinism gate extend to model calls — a cached response is a deterministic response.

projects.name: Opik (Comet)
projects.language: Java backend, TypeScript/React frontend, Python and TS/JS SDKs
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (full platform, including self-hosting, with no commercial licensing required)
projects.popularity: 21.6k stars on the GitHub repo page as of 2026-08-24 (seen directly). Latest release version unknown.
projects.positioning: The most permissively licensed full platform in this cluster: Apache-2.0 end to end, self-hostable via Docker Compose or Helm with no feature gating, backed by Comet (an established ML-experiment-tracking company). Covers tracing, evals, prompts, guardrails, and — uniquely — automated prompt/agent optimization.

features.authoringModel: Not a workflow tool. `@track` decorator (Python) and SDK spans; 60+ framework integrations (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google ADK, Flowise, CrewAI, DSPy and more); plus first-party OTel ingest so any language with an OTel SDK can send traces without an Opik SDK.
features.costControl: Token and cost tracking per trace/span from provider usage and a pricing table, aggregated per project. Accounting only, no enforcement.
features.durability: Durable trace/dataset/experiment storage (ClickHouse + MySQL + Redis in the standard deployment). Telemetry durability, not execution durability.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Human feedback scores on traces and spans, annotation queues, and SME review workflows; human scores share a store with automated metrics so they can be compared and used as ground truth for calibrating LLM judges.
features.multiProvider: Provider-agnostic. 60+ integrations plus first-party OTel ingest — explicitly 'any language with an OpenTelemetry SDK can send traces', which is the key property for a TypeScript engine like weft.
features.observability: Strong and agent-focused. Multi-step agent traces capture LLM calls, tool executions, and retrieval steps as a nested tree with an agent-graph view; production dashboards with latency/cost/volume; and **online evaluation rules** that apply LLM-judge metrics to a sampled slice of live production traces continuously, feeding scores back onto the traces. Native OTel ingest means no SDK lock-in.
features.parallelism: Nested spans with context propagation; evaluations run concurrently over datasets.
features.schemaValidation: Not a generation-time validator. **Opik Guardrails** provides input/output checks (PII, topic restriction, safety) that can run inline and block or flag — closer to Guardrails AI than to Zod, but present in the same platform as the tracing.
features.testing: Complete: datasets and experiments; a large built-in metric library including LLM-as-judge metrics (Hallucination, Moderation, AnswerRelevance, ContextPrecision/Recall, **G-Eval** — the chain-of-thought-generated-criteria judge) alongside heuristic metrics; custom code metrics; and a **pytest integration** so evaluations run on every commit as ordinary tests. The **Opik Agent Optimizer** SDK is the differentiator — it programmatically improves prompts and agents against a dataset and metric (in the DSPy tradition) but wired into the same trace/eval store.

strengths: Apache-2.0 for the entire platform with no paid-tier gating on self-hosting — the most permissive full-featured option in this cluster
First-party OTel ingest as a peer to the native SDKs, so a TypeScript engine can integrate with zero Opik-specific code
G-Eval implemented as a built-in metric: the judge generates evaluation criteria via chain-of-thought from a task description, then scores against them — far more transferable than fixed rubrics
Online evaluation rules score sampled production traffic continuously, not just offline datasets
Agent Optimizer brings DSPy-style automated prompt improvement into an observability platform, closing the loop from trace → dataset → optimized prompt → trace
pytest integration makes evals a normal CI concern
Guardrails, tracing, evals, prompt versioning, and optimization in one Apache-2.0 system reduces the number of tools to run
weaknesses: Self-hosting needs ClickHouse + MySQL + Redis + Java backend — heavy next to a single-process local daemon
Cost is observed, never enforced
No durable execution, no orchestration, no git/worktree awareness
Breadth over depth: many features, several of them less mature than the single-purpose leaders (prompt management is thinner than Langfuse's, OTel conventions less rigorous than Phoenix's)
Python SDK is clearly first-class; the TS/JS SDK trails

ideasWorthStealing.idea: G-Eval: an LLM judge that first generates evaluation criteria from a task description via chain-of-thought, then scores the output against those generated criteria
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft steps have Zod schemas but no quality rubric. G-Eval derives a rubric from the step's own description — so weft could auto-generate a quality check for any step from its existing declaration, with no per-step rubric authoring, and surface the result at a review gate.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: First-party OTel ingest treated as a peer of the native SDK, not an afterthought
ideasWorthStealing.why: Confirms that weft's correct integration strategy is to emit standard GenAI spans rather than write per-vendor exporters — one properly instrumented span tree lands in Opik, Phoenix, Langfuse, and any OTLP backend at once.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Online evaluation rules: sample a fraction of production traces and score them with LLM judges continuously, writing scores back onto the trace
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has no continuous quality signal. Sampling completed journals for automated scoring — with the sampling rate itself under the budget ceiling — would give weft production quality monitoring that respects its cost model.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An Agent Optimizer that reads the trace/eval store and programmatically improves prompts against a metric
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journals are an exceptionally rich optimization corpus (every step's input, output, validation failures, repair attempts, and human gate decisions). Mining them to improve step prompts is a capability weft is better positioned for than any observability vendor, since its journal is the execution itself rather than a copy.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Inline guardrails (PII, safety, topic) in the same system as tracing, able to block as well as flag
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft steps run models over private repositories. A blocking pre-integration check for secrets or license-incompatible content, journaled as a step, is a natural extension of ctx.integrate().

projects.name: Helicone
projects.popularity: helicone/helicone: 6.1k stars; helicone/ai-gateway: 624 stars — both seen directly on their GitHub repo pages as of 2026-08-24. IMPORTANT CURRENT STATE: Helicone was acquired by Mintlify, announced 2026-03-03 (confirmed on helicone.ai/blog/joining-mintlify and mintlify.com/blog/mintlify-acquires-helicone); founders Justin Torre and Cole Gottdank joined Mintlify. The product is in maintenance mode — security updates, bug fixes, and new model support continue, but active feature development has ended, and Mintlify is supporting customers migrating to alternatives. Reported lifetime scale: ~16,000 organizations, ~14.2 trillion tokens (vendor figures, unverified).
projects.positioning: The gateway-first take: sit in the request path rather than instrument the code. Change your `baseURL` and you get logging, caching, rate limiting, cost accounting, routing, and failover across 100+ models with one API key. 'The NGINX of LLMs.'

features.authoringModel: Zero-code-change integration: point the OpenAI SDK's `baseURL` at the gateway and add a header. No decorators, no spans to author. An async logging path via OpenLLMetry exists for teams who refuse a proxy in the hot path.
features.costControl: The strongest *enforcement* story in this cluster and the one weft should study. Rate limits are configurable per user, per team, and globally, and — critically — can be expressed in request counts, **token usage, or dollar amounts**. That is actual runtime budget enforcement at the gateway, not after-the-fact accounting. Backed by what the project calls the largest open-source API pricing database, covering 300+ models.
features.durability: Request/response logs are durably stored; the gateway itself is stateless apart from its cache. No execution durability.
features.gitIsolation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Minimal — user feedback capture on requests; no annotation queues or review workflows of the depth Langfuse/Phoenix/Opik offer.
features.multiProvider: Best-in-class at the transport layer. One API key over 100+ models across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, AWS Bedrock and 20+ providers, all speaking the OpenAI shape. Routing strategies include model-based latency routing (pick the fastest model), provider latency routing via P2C + PeakEWMA, weighted distribution, and cost-optimized routing, with automatic fallback on provider failure. Reported gateway characteristics: <5ms P95 added latency, ~64MB memory, ~3,000 req/s, ~30MB binary.
features.observability: Request-level logging with cost, latency, token counts, user attribution, and custom properties; dashboards over that. OpenTelemetry support for logs/metrics/traces is built in. Because it is a proxy, it sees only the LLM call boundary — it cannot see your application's internal structure, so traces are flat request logs rather than nested application traces. This is the fundamental trade-off versus SDK instrumentation.
features.parallelism: N/A at the application level; the gateway handles concurrent requests.
features.schemaValidation: None.
features.testing: Prompt versioning with production data, prompt experiments (run a new prompt version against logged production requests), and eval support through integrations such as RAGAS. Weaker than the dedicated eval platforms.

strengths: Rate limits and budgets expressible in dollars and tokens, enforced at the gateway per user/team/globally — real spend enforcement, not just reporting
An open pricing database covering 300+ models, independently useful to anyone doing cost accounting
Zero-code-change integration: a baseURL swap gets you logging, caching, cost tracking, and failover for any client in any language
Sophisticated routing: latency-aware P2C+PeakEWMA provider selection, weighted split, cost-optimized routing, automatic failover
Rust gateway with very low overhead (<5ms P95, ~64MB RSS) and a small self-hostable binary
Response caching with Redis and S3 backends, claimed to cut cost and latency by up to 95% on cacheable traffic
Apache-2.0 throughout, including the gateway
weaknesses: Acquired by Mintlify (2026-03-03) and now in maintenance mode with feature development ended — a serious adoption risk, and Mintlify is actively helping customers migrate off
Proxy-only visibility: it sees LLM calls, not your application's step structure, so no nested application traces
Weak eval and human-review capabilities relative to Langfuse/Phoenix/Opik
A proxy in the request path is an availability dependency and a data-residency consideration
No structured output, validation, orchestration, or durability

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Budgets expressed in dollars and tokens and *enforced* at multiple scopes — per user, per team, global — not merely reported
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft already has token/USD ceilings shared with sub-workflows, so this validates the design; the extension worth stealing is the scoping. Per-user and per-team ceilings (not just per-run) would matter as soon as weft's daemon serves more than one person.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An open, maintained model-pricing database as a standalone artifact
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft must price every model call to enforce its USD ceiling. Pricing drifts constantly across Claude and Codex model versions; depending on a maintained open pricing table rather than hard-coded constants makes weft's ceilings correct rather than approximately correct.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Latency- and cost-aware routing with automatic provider failover (P2C + PeakEWMA), as a policy rather than call-site logic
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's per-step routing is author-declared and static. Runtime-adaptive routing — send this step to whichever of Claude/Codex is currently fastest or cheapest, falling back on error — would improve both wall-clock and spend without changing workflow code, and the routing decision itself is journalable.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Response caching keyed on the request, with pluggable backends
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft replays journals for crash recovery. A cache at the model-call boundary makes *fresh* runs cheap when steps repeat — and makes model calls behave deterministically under replay, which is directly aligned with weft's determinism gate.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An OpenAI-compatible ingress requiring only a baseURL change
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's CLI + MCP + daemon all sit on one Engine. An OpenAI-shaped endpoint would let arbitrary existing clients benefit from weft's budget enforcement and journaling with no integration work at all.

projects.name: OpenInference (Arize)
projects.popularity: 1.2k stars on the GitHub repo page as of 2026-08-24 (seen directly). 30+ instrumentation packages published to PyPI/npm. Latest release version unknown.
projects.positioning: A specification plus instrumentation libraries that layer AI-specific conventions on top of OpenTelemetry. Explicitly complementary to OTel — spans are ordinary OTel spans with OpenInference attributes, so they land in any OTLP backend, not just Phoenix. The de-facto convention with the widest *shipping* instrumentation coverage today.

features.authoringModel: Auto-instrumentation packages that monkey-patch client libraries (`openinference-instrumentation-openai`, `-anthropic`, `-langchain`, `-llama-index`, `-dspy`, `-crewai`, `-vercel-ai`, and 30+ more), plus helper APIs and decorators for manual spans that stamp the right attributes.
features.costControl: Defines token-count attributes (prompt/completion/total, with variants) so backends can compute cost. Specifies nothing about pricing or enforcement.
features.durability: N/A — a convention plus instrumentation, not a store.
features.gitIsolation: N/A.
features.humanInTheLoop: N/A, though it defines an EVALUATOR span kind and conventions for annotations/scores attached to spans, which is where human and automated judgements attach.
features.multiProvider: Broad: instrumentors for OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, VertexAI, Mistral, Groq, LiteLLM and more, across four languages. Transport- and format-agnostic (usable over JSON, protobuf, or DataFrames).
features.observability: This *is* the observability layer. Its defining contribution is the **span kind** taxonomy — LLM, CHAIN, TOOL, AGENT, RETRIEVER, EMBEDDING, RERANKER, GUARDRAIL, EVALUATOR — which gives a backend enough type information to render each node purposefully. Attribute families cover llm.model_name, llm.invocation_parameters, llm.input_messages / llm.output_messages (indexed message structures with role/content/tool_calls), llm.token_count.*, tool.name/description/parameters, retrieval.documents.* (with per-document id/score/content), embedding.embeddings.*, and input/output value+mime_type on every span. Also standardizes span-level attribute-masking/privacy controls so message content can be redacted at instrumentation time.
features.parallelism: Inherits OTel context propagation; concurrent work nests correctly.
features.schemaValidation: N/A.
features.testing: N/A, though the EVALUATOR span kind and score conventions let eval results ride the same telemetry pipeline as traces.

strengths: The span-kind taxonomy is the single most useful abstraction for rendering agent traces, and no other convention ships one as complete
Very wide shipping instrumentation coverage — 30+ packages across Python, TS, Java, Go — so it works today rather than aspirationally
Pure OTel underneath: spans go to any OTLP backend, so adopting the conventions does not tie you to Phoenix
Rich, structured message and document attributes (indexed messages, per-document scores) that generic OTel span attributes cannot express
Built-in privacy controls for masking sensitive span attributes at instrumentation time — important when spans carry source code
Apache-2.0 with a public spec
weaknesses: A competing dialect to the official OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions; attribute names differ, so backends must translate and adopters must choose
Governed by a single vendor (Arize) rather than a neutral foundation, despite the open license
Convention only — no storage, UI, cost model, or enforcement
Convergence with the official OTel GenAI conventions is expected but incomplete, so today's choice carries migration risk

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The span-kind taxonomy — LLM / CHAIN / TOOL / AGENT / RETRIEVER / GUARDRAIL / EVALUATOR — as the vocabulary for typing every node in a run
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's journal already distinguishes step kinds (write step in a worktree, gate, human ask, sub-workflow, integrate, repair). Mapping those onto OpenInference span kinds when emitting telemetry means weft runs render correctly in Phoenix, Langfuse, and Opik with no per-vendor work — the fastest path out of weft's one-span-per-run situation.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Indexed structured message attributes (llm.input_messages.N.role / .content / .tool_calls) rather than a single opaque JSON blob
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's steps exchange rich structured values. Emitting messages as indexed attributes lets a trace UI diff turn-by-turn and lets backends filter on message content — which a stringified blob makes impossible.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Attribute masking/privacy controls applied at instrumentation time
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's spans would carry source code, diffs, and possibly secrets from private repositories. Redaction has to be a first-class, configurable property of weft's span emission from day one, not a downstream backend setting.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Shipping instrumentation as separate per-library packages rather than one monolith
ideasWorthStealing.why: If weft ever exposes its telemetry to other tools, a small `@weft/otel` package that maps journal events to spans — decoupled from the Engine — keeps the convention dialect swappable as OTel GenAI stabilizes.

projects.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions
projects.repo: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai (split out of open-telemetry/semantic-conventions); docs at https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/ now redirect there
projects.language: YAML models compiled with Weaver into Markdown docs and codegen; language-agnostic
projects.popularity: 279 stars on the semantic-conventions-genai repo page as of 2026-08-24 (seen directly). Star count is a poor signal here — this is the vendor-neutral standard the whole ecosystem is converging on. Latest release version unknown.
projects.positioning: The official, vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry standard for GenAI telemetry. As of 2026 it has been split out of the main semantic-conventions repo into its own repository, with Weaver managing the dependency on core conventions — a signal the GenAI surface grew large enough to need its own release cadence. This is the target weft should emit against.

features.authoringModel: Not code — a specification. Conventions are authored as YAML models in `model/` and compiled by Weaver into documentation and code-generated constants for language SDKs.
features.costControl: Defines the token-usage attributes and metrics required to compute cost — input/output tokens broken out by modality (text, image, audio), plus `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.cache_write.input_tokens` and reasoning tokens tracked separately though included in totals. Deliberately does not define pricing or enforcement.
features.durability: N/A.
features.gitIsolation: N/A.
features.humanInTheLoop: N/A.
features.multiProvider: Provider abstraction is the core design. `gen_ai.provider.name` is a discriminator with well-known values across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google (Gemini and Vertex AI), Azure, AWS Bedrock, Cohere, Mistral AI and others, and provider-specific convention documents layer extra attributes on the common core — so consumers can handle any provider generically while still reading provider-specific detail.
features.observability: The specification itself. Span name is `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`. `gen_ai.operation.name` has well-known values `chat`, `generate_content`, `text_completion`, `embeddings`, `retrieval`, `execute_tool`, `fetch_response`, `invoke_agent`, `create_memory`, `search_memory` — note that agent invocation, tool execution, and memory operations are now first-class, not just raw model calls. Required/conditionally-required attributes are `gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.provider.name`, and `gen_ai.request.model`; recommended ones cover temperature, top_p, max_tokens, frequency/presence penalty, stop sequences, and stream mode. Message capture converged on `gen_ai.input.messages` and `gen_ai.output.messages` as **span attributes** carrying a defined JSON structure (structured or JSON-string), rather than the earlier log-events approach — with instrumentations expected to offer filtering/truncation. Metrics and events are defined alongside spans, and MCP (Model Context Protocol) has its own conventions. Stability: the GenAI conventions are in **Development** status; only `error.type` is marked Stable.
features.parallelism: Standard OTel context propagation and span nesting.
features.schemaValidation: N/A for LLM output, but the YAML models are themselves schema-validated and Weaver can generate typed constants and run a live-check against emitted telemetry.
features.testing: Weaver supports validating an instrumentation's emitted telemetry against the conventions, which is effectively a conformance test for telemetry.

strengths: Vendor-neutral and the convergence point: emitting these attributes means every OTLP backend (Langfuse, Phoenix, Opik, Datadog, Grafana, Honeycomb, LangSmith) can read weft's telemetry
Agent, tool-execution, memory, and MCP operations are first-class span types — a much better fit for a multi-agent coding engine than 'LLM call' alone
Detailed token accounting including cache read/write and reasoning tokens broken out — exactly what is needed to enforce a USD ceiling accurately on modern models
Message capture settled on span attributes with a defined JSON structure, resolving a long-running events-vs-attributes ambiguity
Provider-specific conventions layered over a common core, so generic consumers and provider-aware consumers both work
Weaver-based tooling generates constants and can validate emitted telemetry against the spec
Its own repo and release cadence signals sustained investment
weaknesses: Still Development status — attributes may change, so early adopters carry migration cost
Competes in practice with OpenInference, which currently has broader shipping instrumentation; the two dialects have not fully converged
Message-content capture is opt-in and privacy-sensitive by nature; the spec leaves redaction largely to instrumentations
Conventions only — no reference backend, no UI, no cost model
Documentation moved mid-2026, so much existing guidance and many links are stale

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Adopt gen_ai.* conventions for weft's telemetry: one span per step named `{operation} {model}`, with gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, and full token attributes, nested under the run
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the concrete fix for weft's single-span-per-run limitation, and it is the standards-correct version. It costs weft little — the journal already holds every field the spec asks for — and it instantly makes weft legible to every OTLP backend without weft building any UI.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Use `invoke_agent` and `execute_tool` operation names, and the MCP conventions, for the non-LLM parts of a run
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft is a multi-agent engine with an MCP server. Emitting agent-invocation and tool-execution spans under standard names means weft's orchestration structure — not just its model calls — shows up correctly in trace UIs.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Break token accounting out by cache-read, cache-write, and reasoning tokens rather than a single input/output pair
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft enforces hard USD ceilings. Cached input tokens and reasoning tokens are priced very differently from ordinary input tokens; without that breakdown weft's budget arithmetic will systematically misestimate spend on both Claude and Codex.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Weaver-style validation of emitted telemetry against the convention model as a conformance test
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft has a zero-model-call test harness and a determinism gate — both about mechanically enforcing invariants. Adding a telemetry conformance check to that harness would keep weft's span emission correct as the conventions move toward stable.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Instrumentation-level filtering and truncation of captured message content
ideasWorthStealing.why: Weft's steps carry source code and diffs. The spec's expectation that instrumentations offer content filtering is exactly the control weft needs before it emits step inputs/outputs as span attributes from private repositories.

cluster: Open-source coding agent harnesses and multi-agent coding orchestrators (weft's closest competitors by use case)

projects.name: Claude Code (dynamic workflows, subagents, agent teams, hooks, skills, plugins, worktrees)
projects.repo: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code (issue tracker; product docs at https://code.claude.com/docs). Agent SDK: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk
projects.language: TypeScript/Node (CLI distributed as an npm package; the public repo is an issue tracker, currently labelled language Python)
projects.license: Proprietary / source-unavailable CLI under Anthropic Commercial Terms. The public GitHub repo carries NO license field (verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24). Only the Agent SDK wrappers and docs are openly distributed. NOT open source — included because it is the dominant competing harness.
projects.popularity: 142,871 stars on anthropics/claude-code, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24 (issue-tracker repo, so stars measure product mindshare, not code)
projects.positioning: The reference agentic coding harness. As of 2026 it is no longer a single-agent REPL: it ships a full orchestration stack — subagents, agent teams, git-worktree isolation, hooks, skills, plugins, checkpointing — and, most importantly for weft, 'dynamic workflows': a JavaScript orchestration script that the harness executes to fan out to hundreds of subagents deterministically. This is the single closest thing to weft in existence and it is bundled free with the tool weft calls out to.

features.durability: Two independent layers. (1) Session transcripts are append-only JSONL under ~/.claude/projects/{project}/{sessionId}/, with subagent transcripts kept separately at .../subagents/agent-{agentId}.jsonl that survive main-conversation compaction; /resume and --continue rehydrate from them, retained cleanupPeriodDays (default 30). (2) Checkpointing snapshots the file tree before each user prompt (100 most recent per session), stored with the conversation so /rewind works after a resume; offers restore-code, restore-conversation, or both. Workflow runs track each agent's result so a stopped run is resumable — but only within the same process: 'Resume works within the same Claude Code session. If you exit Claude Code while a workflow is running, the next session starts the workflow fresh.' Replay is order-based and brittle: cached results stop at the first agent that did not finish, and every agent that STARTED after it re-runs even if it completed. Checkpointing explicitly does not track bash-mediated file changes, subagent edits (except foreground forked skills), external edits, or symlinked/hard-linked paths.
features.schemaValidation: The workflow agent() call accepts a JSON Schema: agent(prompt, { schema: { type:'object', required:['files'], properties:{...} } }) and resolves to a parsed object. The Agent SDK also exposes structured outputs (docs/en/agent-sdk/structured-outputs). No documented in-session repair loop on validation failure; agent() instead resolves to null on stop or unrecoverable API error, and callers are expected to .filter(Boolean).
features.humanInTheLoop: Rich at the session level, absent inside a workflow. Session-level: permission modes (default/plan/acceptEdits/bypassPermissions/auto), AskUserQuestion, ExitPlanMode, plan-approval requests from agent-team teammates to the lead, and a PermissionRequest hook for programmatic decisions. Workflow-level the docs are explicit: 'No mid-run user input. Only agent permission prompts can pause a run. For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow.' AskUserQuestion is one of the tools automatically stripped from all subagents. So there is no ctx.gate equivalent — a human cannot be a durable step in a workflow.
features.parallelism: Four distinct primitives. (1) Subagents: background by default, own context window, up to 20 concurrent (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS), nesting 3 deep. (2) Dynamic workflows: pipeline(list, fn) fans one agent per item; runtime caps at 16 concurrent agents (fewer on low-CPU/containers) and 1,000 agents total per run; deliberately staggers same-prefix agents up to CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS (default 5000ms) so siblings hit the first agent's prompt cache. (3) Agent teams (experimental, CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1): peer Claude Code processes with a shared file-locked task list at ~/.claude/tasks/{team}/ and JSON mailboxes at ~/.claude/teams/{team}/inboxes/{agent}.json. (4) Worktree-backed parallel sessions.
features.gitIsolation: Best-in-class and enforced, not advisory. `claude --worktree <name>` creates .claude/worktrees/<name> on branch worktree-<name>, base branch controlled by worktree.baseRef ('fresh' = origin default branch, 'head' = local HEAD). Subagents get `isolation: worktree` frontmatter for a per-agent temp worktree. Crucially the harness ENFORCES the boundary with four static checks: it blocks Edit/Write/NotebookEdit targeting the main checkout; blocks Bash/PowerShell/Monitor whose cwd resolves into the main checkout; blocks git redirects via -C, --git-dir, GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE or a preceding cd; and blocks any command shape it cannot statically prove stays inside the worktree (refuses brace expansion and unquoted heredocs). It runs `git worktree lock` while an agent is live and sweeps stale locks. .worktreeinclude (gitignore syntax) copies gitignored files like .env into each new worktree. WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks let non-git VCS replace the logic. But: there is no patch object — work lands as commits on a branch, not as a reviewable diff returned to an orchestrator, and there is no ctx.integrate() gate.
features.multiProvider: Anthropic models only, across Anthropic API / Bedrock / Google Cloud Agent Platform / Microsoft Foundry, plus an LLM-gateway protocol. Per-step routing exists WITHIN that family: subagent frontmatter `model: sonnet|opus|haiku|claude-opus-5|inherit`, per-invocation model param on the Agent tool, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL override, org availableModels allowlist with documented substitution rules. No Codex/GPT/Gemini/OSS provider behind the same interface.
features.costControl: Reporting and advisory warnings only — no hard ceiling. /workflows shows per-agent token usage live; the task panel raises a 'Large workflow' warning past 25 scheduled agents or 1.5M projected tokens, and the docs state plainly: 'The warning is advisory: it doesn't pause or limit the run.' The real bounds are structural (16 concurrent, 1,000 agents/run) plus a workflowSizeGuideline setting (small<5 / medium<15 / large<50) that is 'advice, not a cap'. Agent SDK exposes cost-tracking; Claude apps gateway has org spend limits. Nothing resembling a per-run USD ceiling shared with sub-workflows.
features.observability: Strongest in the cluster. /workflows TUI with phase tree, per-agent token totals, elapsed time, drill-in to any agent's prompt/tool calls/result, filter by status, pause (p), kill agent (x), restart agent (r), save script (s). Agent panel for subagents/teammates with live transcripts. OpenTelemetry via Agent SDK observability; org-level analytics/monitoring pages. Every workflow run writes its script to a file under ~/.claude/projects/ so you can diff the orchestration between runs.
features.testing: No zero-model-call harness. Testing story is the Agent SDK (programmatic driving, hooks, permission callbacks) plus /code-review and ultrareview as agentic review passes. Workflows themselves have no offline/mocked execution mode — every run spends tokens.
features.authoringModel: Uniquely, the script is model-authored rather than human-authored: you type `ultracode: <task>` (or set /effort ultracode) and Claude WRITES the JS orchestration, you approve the phase list, it runs, then you press `s` to save it to .claude/workflows/ as a reusable /command. Body is plain JS with top-level await, `export const meta = {name, description}`, globals agent() and pipeline(), and an `args` global for parameters. Sandbox restrictions: no import() (fails before the run starts), no filesystem or shell access from the script itself — only agents touch the world. Subagents are markdown+YAML frontmatter; skills are markdown; plugins bundle agents/skills/hooks/workflows/commands.

strengths: Dynamic workflows are a direct, shipped, free implementation of weft's core thesis (code-as-orchestration, schema-typed agent calls, fan-out, resumable) and are bundled with the agent weft depends on
Worktree isolation is actually enforced by static command analysis, not just convention — real effort spent closing escape hatches (git -C, GIT_DIR, heredocs, brace expansion)
The workflow is generated by the model and then frozen into a reusable command — removes the authoring burden weft's plain-TypeScript model imposes

Hooks are a genuinely complete interception surface: ~25 events, blocking and non-blocking, with updatedInput mutation on PreToolUse and a uniform JSON contract across command/HTTP/MCP/prompt/agent hook types
Prompt-cache-aware fan-out scheduling (deliberate 5s stagger so siblings share the cached prefix) is a real cost optimization nobody else does
Enormous distribution: 142k stars, bundled subagents/skills/plugins/marketplace ecosystem
weaknesses: Not open source — no license on the repo, closed CLI, Anthropic-only models. Cannot be self-hosted, forked, or audited
Workflow resumability is process-scoped: exiting the CLI loses an in-flight run entirely. There is no crash-durable journal for workflows (only for conversations)

Workflow replay is order-based, not content-addressed: stopping mid fan-out re-runs every agent that started after the first unfinished one, even completed ones. The docs concede this makes stopping 'expensive'
No human-in-the-loop inside a workflow at all — AskUserQuestion is stripped from subagents and mid-run input is impossible; multi-stage sign-off requires splitting into separate workflows
No hard cost ceiling — only advisory warnings and structural agent caps
No multi-provider routing: cannot put Codex or a local model behind the same step interface
No offline/mocked test harness for workflows
Agent teams are experimental, disabled by default, and explicitly do not survive /resume

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Model-authored orchestration: let the model write the workflow script from a natural-language task, show the user the planned phase list for approval, run it, then offer one keystroke to freeze that run's script into a reusable, versioned command
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's biggest adoption tax is that a human must hand-write TypeScript before getting any value. A 'draft me a weft workflow, run it, then save it to workflows/' path converts weft from a framework you commit to into a tool you try once.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Static enforcement of worktree isolation on shell commands, not just file writes: block `git -C`, `--git-dir`, `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`, a preceding `cd` into the main checkout, and refuse command shapes (brace expansion, unquoted heredocs) that cannot be statically proven to stay inside the worktree
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft returns patches from worktrees, but an agent that runs `git -C ../main commit` or a heredoc writing outside the worktree silently breaks the isolation guarantee. This is the same class of static analysis weft already does for the determinism gate, applied to bash.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Prompt-cache-aware fan-out scheduling: when ctx.parallel launches N steps sharing a system-prompt/tool prefix, hold all but the first until the first response begins, then release the rest so they read the shared cache — configurable cap (default ~5s) with an escape hatch to disable
ideasWorthStealing.why: Directly cuts real USD on every fan-out. weft already has budgets and per-step routing, so it knows which steps share a prefix; this is pure margin on top of existing machinery.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A live orchestration TUI with per-agent token/cost/elapsed columns, drill-in to any step's prompt and tool calls, and per-step controls: pause run, kill one step, RESTART one step in place
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has a daemon web UI, but per-step restart-in-place (rather than resume-from-journal) is what you actually want when one step of a 40-way fan-out goes off the rails. It converts a failed run from 'resume the whole thing' into a surgical retry.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Write every run's resolved orchestration to a file under the run directory so runs can be diffed against each other, and give parameterized workflows a single `args` global passed as structured data (not string-parsed)
ideasWorthStealing.why: Makes 'why did today's run behave differently from yesterday's' answerable by diff. weft's journal records events; recording the *program* alongside the events closes the loop for edit-tolerant replay debugging.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A layered concurrency cap that degrades with available CPU (16 concurrent, fewer inside a CPU-limited container) plus an absolute per-run step ceiling (1,000) as a runaway-loop backstop independent of the token budget
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has token/USD ceilings but a runaway loop can burn wall-clock and local resources long before it burns budget, especially with worktrees and containers per step.

projects.name: OpenHands (ex OpenDevin) + software-agent-sdk + Agent Canvas
projects.repo: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands (moved from All-Hands-AI/OpenHands); SDK: https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk; docs https://docs.openhands.dev
projects.language: TypeScript (frontend/Agent Canvas) + Python (agent SDK / agent server)
projects.popularity: 84,976 stars on OpenHands/OpenHands and 1,020 on OpenHands/software-agent-sdk, both verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24
projects.positioning: Pivoted decisively in 2026 from 'autonomous SWE agent' to platform: Agent Canvas is 'the self-hosted developer control center for coding agents and automations', running OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini or any Agent-Client-Protocol agent across local / Docker / VM / cloud backends, with an Automation Server for schedules and webhooks. The software-agent-sdk underneath is the closest structural analogue to weft's engine: a typed event framework with an append-only per-conversation event log.

features.durability: The closest thing in the cluster to weft's journal. Each conversation persists to a directory containing base_state.json (agent config, execution status, stats, secrets, custom agent state) plus an events/ directory of individually-numbered JSON files (event-00000-abc123.json, …). The docs justify the split exactly as weft would: 'Fast event appends: No need to rewrite the entire history.' Resume = construct a new Conversation with the same conversation_id and persistence_dir; base state is restored and the event history is deserialized to reconstruct the trajectory. There is also an explicit pause-and-resume guide. Critically this is state RESTORATION, not deterministic replay — no content-addressed step salvage and no edit-tolerance, so changing the agent definition and resuming has undefined semantics.
features.schemaValidation: Typed event framework (Pydantic models across the SDK) validates the event envelope, and structured tool schemas validate tool arguments. But there is no per-step 'this step must return a value matching schema S, and if it doesn't, repair it in-session' contract — the unit of validation is the tool call, not the step result.
features.humanInTheLoop: Genuinely good and the best-designed risk-gated approval in the cluster. Confirmation policies are first-class objects: AlwaysConfirm(), NeverConfirm(), ConfirmRisky(). With ConfirmRisky, an LLMSecurityAnalyzer runs OUT OF BAND from the main agent and classifies each pending action LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH/UNKNOWN; HIGH triggers confirmation. The conversation enters an explicit WAITING_FOR_CONFIRMATION state that a host loop polls, so approval is a real state machine transition rather than a UI modal. Still: the human gates actions, not a durable named step that can be asked an arbitrary question and have the answer journaled.
features.parallelism: Weak inside a conversation, strong across them. The TaskToolSet delegation to sub-agents is explicitly 'designed for sequential blocking tasks' — sub-agents run one at a time and the parent blocks (returning a TaskObservation with task_id, subagent, status, text, and a `resume` parameter to continue a prior task). Parallelism comes from running many conversations: the Agent Server is a REST API hosting multiple agents per host, and Agent Canvas manages concurrent conversations across backends. Conversations can be branched to explore an alternative path while preserving the original.
features.gitIsolation: Environment isolation rather than git isolation. Workspace is an abstraction with local / Docker / Kubernetes / remote-API implementations; ephemeral Docker or K8s workspaces per agent are the recommended pattern, with volume mounts scoping file access. No git-worktree primitive, no patch-return-then-integrate flow — agents commit and push, or you diff the mounted directory yourself.
features.multiProvider: Best-in-cluster breadth. LiteLLM underneath means effectively any provider; 'bring your own model, any LLM'. Beyond model routing, OpenHands routes whole AGENTS via the Agent-Client Protocol — an ACP Agent can delegate to Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI instead of calling an LLM directly, a strictly more general version of weft's AgentProvider abstraction. Also exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so external chat UIs/IDEs can drive it.
features.costControl: Detailed metrics, thin enforcement. llm.metrics per LLM instance accumulates cost, prompt/completion/cache-read/cache-write/reasoning tokens and latencies; conversation.conversation_stats aggregates across all LLMs including auxiliary ones like the condenser (so the condenser's own spend is counted — a nice detail). Hard budget caps are an OpenHands Cloud org feature (organizations/budgets), not an SDK primitive; the SDK metrics docs describe reporting after execution, not a ceiling that halts a run.
features.observability: OpenTelemetry tracing guide; the event log itself is the audit trail and is queryable per event; Agent Canvas shows conversation history, files, terminals, model config and backend state in one UI; Automation Server records run history for scheduled/webhook-triggered runs.
features.testing: No documented zero-model-call replay harness. Testing is conventional pytest plus SWE-bench-style evaluation harnesses; the event log makes trajectory inspection possible but there is no published 'replay this journal with a stub provider' mode.
features.authoringModel: Python objects and imperative control flow: construct LLM, Agent, Tools, Workspace, Conversation, then send_message()/run(). Sub-agents are registered via a factory function + register_agent(name, factory, description) and invoked through the TaskToolSet. Automations are declarative definitions on the Automation Server (schedule or webhook). Not a DSL, not a graph — closest in spirit to weft's plain-code approach, but Python and without await-as-edge semantics.

strengths: Append-only per-event JSON file store with a base_state.json sidecar — the same durability architecture weft chose, validated independently at scale

ConfirmRisky + out-of-band LLMSecurityAnalyzer is a better default than binary approve-everything/approve-nothing, and WAITING_FOR_CONFIRMATION as an explicit conversation state makes approval resumable
ACP means whole third-party agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) are pluggable, not just models — a superset of weft's AgentProvider idea
Workspace abstraction spans local / Docker / K8s / remote API behind one interface, so the same agent code runs on a laptop or in an ephemeral cloud sandbox
Automation Server (cron + webhooks + run history + dispatch, with Slack/GitHub/Linear/Notion integrations) is the productionization layer most of this cluster lacks
MIT licensed, fully self-hostable, mature (84,976 stars)
weaknesses: Sub-agent delegation is explicitly sequential and blocking — no real fan-out inside a conversation
Resume restores state; it does not deterministically replay, and there is no edit-tolerance or content-addressed salvage when the agent definition changes
No git-worktree isolation and no patch-then-integrate review flow — isolation is container/volume level only
No hard USD/token ceiling in the SDK (only cloud org budgets), so a runaway loop is bounded by iteration limits at best
The 2026 pivot to Agent Canvas has spread the project thin: SDK, legacy app, Agent Server, Automation Server and Canvas are separate surfaces with uneven documentation
No determinism guarantees whatsoever on orchestration code

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Risk-classified approval: an out-of-band LLM security analyzer that scores each proposed action LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH/UNKNOWN, paired with a ConfirmRisky policy so only HIGH-risk actions interrupt the human
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.gate/ctx.human.approve is binary and human-scheduled. Auto-escalating only genuinely risky actions is what makes long unattended runs tolerable, and it composes with weft's journal — the risk classification becomes a journaled attribute of the step.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Make waiting-for-human an explicit, persisted state (WAITING_FOR_CONFIRMATION) that any host loop can poll, rather than a callback the process must be alive to service
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already treats humans as durable steps; an explicit polled state means the CLI, MCP server and web UI can all service the same pending gate, and a crashed daemon doesn't strand it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Agent-Client Protocol: put whole third-party agent binaries behind the provider interface, not just model APIs, so a step can be served by Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or an OpenHands agent interchangeably
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's AgentProvider already abstracts Claude and Codex; standardizing on ACP would make weft compatible with every agent that adopts it instead of requiring a bespoke adapter per vendor.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Count auxiliary LLM spend (context condenser, summarizer, schema-repair calls, security classifier) in the same conversation_stats rollup as the primary agent
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's schema repair and any future compaction are themselves model calls. If they're not on the budget ledger the hard ceiling is a lie — exactly the kind of accounting bug that only shows up on a big run.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An Automation Server layer: cron schedules + inbound webhooks + run history + dispatch, so a workflow can be triggered by a GitHub event or a Linear ticket rather than only by a human at a CLI
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already has a daemon and an Engine class; a trigger surface turns 'a workflow I run' into 'a workflow that runs', which is where journaled durability actually pays off.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Numbered individual event files (event-00000-{hash}.json) plus a separate base_state.json, rather than one growing log file
ideasWorthStealing.why: Confirms weft's append-only choice, and per-event file granularity makes partial reads, external tooling and content-addressed lookup trivial without parsing a whole journal.

projects.name: SWE-agent (+ mini-swe-agent, EnIGMA)
projects.popularity: 20,122 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; actively pushed (2026-08-17). The research-lineage leader — NeurIPS 2024 paper, origin of the 'agent-computer interface' framing
projects.positioning: The benchmark-driven research harness: take a GitHub issue, autonomously fix it, measured on SWE-bench. Entirely config-driven — 'governed by a single yaml file'. Where weft optimizes for a human's production workflow, SWE-agent optimizes for reproducible batch evaluation across thousands of instances, and it is the only project here whose design center is scientific reproducibility.

features.durability: Trajectory files, not a resumable journal. Each run writes <instance_id>.traj JSON containing a `trajectory` array where every turn records response, thought, action, observation, state, and the exact query messages sent to the LM — the most complete per-step record in the cluster. Alongside it: config.yaml sufficient to reproduce the exact run, plus level-separated log files. But there is no crash-resume: an interrupted batch leaves missing patches, and the remedy is a post-hoc `sweagent merge-preds` utility that stitches partial preds.json outputs together. Trajectories are consumed forward as demonstrations for future runs, not replayed to restore a run.
features.schemaValidation: Tool/action parsing validated against the configured action parser (function-calling or a text format), with parse-error retries built into the loop. The unit is the action, not the step result — there is no typed contract on 'what this phase returns'.
features.humanInTheLoop: Minimal by design. There is a human-in-the-loop / interactive mode for stepping through an agent, but the product is unattended batch evaluation. No approval gates, no review flow, no durable human steps.
features.parallelism: `run-batch --num_workers N` runs instances concurrently, each in its own Docker container via SWE-ReX. Notably includes `--random_delay_multiplier` (default 0.3) to stagger worker startup and ease CPU pressure during container init — a real operational detail born of running thousands of containers. Parallelism is across INSTANCES (embarrassingly parallel), never within one task: a single instance is a strictly sequential ReAct loop.
features.gitIsolation: Docker container per instance via SWE-ReX (the execution runtime), each with its own checkout. Output is a unified diff patch per instance collected into preds.json as {instance_id: patch} — so it does produce patches as first-class artifacts, but for scoring rather than for human review-then-integrate.
features.multiProvider: LiteLLM underneath: 'your language model of choice', GPT/Claude/local models. Per-run model config in YAML; no per-step routing because there are no differentiated steps.
features.costControl: The best hard ceiling in this cluster. `--agent.model.per_instance_cost_limit` is a real enforced cap that stops an instance when exceeded, plus total-run limits and step limits. Because the workload is thousands of instances, cost enforcement had to be genuinely load-bearing rather than advisory.
features.observability: Trajectory inspector/viewer for browsing runs; exhaustive .traj files containing the literal LM input at each step; multi-level logs; exit-status records per instance. Reproducibility-grade rather than operations-grade — no live dashboard.
features.testing: Strongest evaluation story anywhere here, but it's benchmark evaluation, not unit testing: SWE-bench, SWE-smith (training-data generation), and the trajectory format as a stable artifact. No mock-provider replay harness for the orchestration itself.
features.authoringModel: Declarative YAML: the agent, its tools, the action parser, templates and history processors are all config. mini-swe-agent is the counter-statement — a deliberately minimal (~100 line) harness reported at ~65% on SWE-bench, arguing most harness complexity is unnecessary.

strengths: Enforced per-instance USD cost limits that actually stop a run — the only project here with a battle-tested hard ceiling
The .traj format records the exact query messages sent to the model at each step, making runs genuinely auditable and reproducible
config.yaml emitted alongside every run so the exact configuration is recoverable
Docker-per-instance via SWE-ReX with startup jitter to avoid thundering-herd container init
mini-swe-agent is a strong empirical argument that a ~100-line harness reaches ~65% on SWE-bench — a real challenge to every heavyweight framework in this cluster, weft included
Academic credibility and a stable benchmark position
weaknesses: No crash resumability — an interrupted batch is repaired post-hoc with merge-preds, not resumed
No parallelism within a single task; one instance is a strictly sequential loop
Essentially no human-in-the-loop, no approval UX, no review flow
