YAML-only authoring means no real control flow: no conditionals, loops, or typed data passing between phases
Not a day-to-day developer tool — it is an evaluation harness, so iterating on your own repo is awkward
No multi-step review→fix→verify orchestration primitive

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Record the exact serialized model input (full message array) at every step in the journal, not just the prompt template and the result
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft journals step results for replay, but when a step's output is wrong the question is always 'what did the model actually see?'. Storing the resolved query makes weft's journal debuggable rather than merely resumable — and content-addressing it gives free dedup.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Emit the fully-resolved run configuration as an artifact next to every run (SWE-agent's config.yaml), capturing model IDs, provider routing, budget ceilings and determinism-gate settings as actually applied
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's edit-tolerant replay needs a baseline of what the config WAS. Without it, 'the workflow changed' and 'the config changed' are indistinguishable on resume.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Enforced per-unit cost limits as a first-class runner flag (per_instance_cost_limit) distinct from the global ceiling, so one pathological sub-workflow cannot consume the whole budget
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft shares a budget with sub-workflows; a per-step/per-sub-workflow sub-ceiling prevents one runaway fan-out branch from starving the other 39.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Startup jitter when launching many isolated environments at once (random_delay_multiplier) to avoid CPU thundering-herd and cascading timeouts
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft creates a git worktree (and potentially installs deps) per write step. A 20-way ctx.parallel fan-out on a laptop will hit exactly the container/CPU contention SWE-agent had to engineer around.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Take mini-swe-agent's minimalism seriously: publish a stripped 'weft-core' showing the smallest journal+schema+replay loop that still works, separate from the full engine
ideasWorthStealing.why: The strongest critique weft will face is 'why not 100 lines of Promise.all'. A minimal core that demonstrably provides durability the naive version lacks is the answer, and it doubles as the onboarding path.

projects.name: Aider
projects.popularity: 48,461 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24. BUT last push 2026-05-22 and last release v0.86.2 (Feb 2026) — roughly three months stale, with public discussion (HN, issue #4751 'future direction', issue #4584 'no new releases') questioning maintenance. Effectively maintenance mode; treat as declining.
projects.positioning: The original git-native terminal pair programmer. Its enduring contribution is that every AI change is a git commit with a sensible message, so review and undo are just git — a philosophy weft inherits and extends with worktree-scoped patches.

features.durability: Git IS the durability layer — that is the whole design. Every AI edit is auto-committed with a generated message, so /undo is a git revert and history is inspectable with ordinary git tooling. Chat history persists to .aider.chat.history.md and input history to .aider.input.history. There is no run journal, no step-level resume, no crash recovery of an in-flight multi-step task: interrupt Aider and you have commits, not resumable state.
features.schemaValidation: None in the weft sense. Edits are validated structurally by edit format (whole-file / unified diff / diff-fenced / SEARCH-REPLACE blocks) with retry on malformed edits — validation of the DIFF SHAPE, not of a typed step result.
features.humanInTheLoop: Turn-level and conversational: Aider proposes, commits, and you review with git diff; /undo reverts. --yes auto-confirms for scripting. Architect/editor mode is a two-model split (a reasoning model plans, a cheaper model applies) which is a form of structured multi-step but with no gate between the phases.
features.parallelism: None. Single sequential conversation, one repo, one working tree. Parallelism means running several Aider processes yourself — precisely the gap claude-squad, Crystal, Conductor and uzi exist to fill.
features.gitIsolation: Operates directly on the working tree with auto-commit; no worktree, no sandbox, no patch-return. Strongest git INTEGRATION in the cluster and the weakest git ISOLATION.
features.multiProvider: Excellent and provider-agnostic via LiteLLM — Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, local models. Architect/editor mode is real per-role routing: --model for the architect and --editor-model for the applier, with independent edit formats. The closest prior art to weft's per-step routing.
features.costControl: Reports token counts and USD per request and cumulative session cost in the terminal after each exchange, plus /tokens to inspect context composition. No enforced ceiling that halts a run.
features.observability: Terminal-only: cost/token line per exchange, /tokens breakdown, chat history markdown file, and the git log as the durable record. No dashboard, no structured event export.
features.testing: The repo-map (tree-sitter-derived symbol map of the whole codebase, relevance-ranked) is Aider's signature technical contribution. --lint-cmd and --test-cmd run linters/tests after every change and feed failures back to the model automatically — a genuine automated fix→verify loop, just fixed-shape rather than programmable. No harness for testing your own orchestration.
features.authoringModel: Chat commands in a terminal REPL (/add, /ask, /architect, /run, /test, /undo), plus scripting via --message / --message-file for one-shot batch use. A Python API exists (Coder.create(main_model=..., fnames=[...]); coder.run(...)) but the docs warn explicitly: 'The python scripting API is not officially supported or documented, and could change in future releases without providing backwards compatibility.'

strengths: Git-native by default: every change is a commit, so review/undo/blame are free and need no bespoke UI
The repo-map (tree-sitter symbol graph, relevance-ranked) is still best-in-class context selection for large repos and is widely copied
Automatic lint-and-test-and-fix loop (--lint-cmd/--test-cmd) is a real verify→repair cycle with zero configuration
Architect/editor split is genuine per-role model routing with independent edit formats and a demonstrable cost/quality win
Broadest practical model support via LiteLLM, including cheap local models
Per-exchange USD cost display trains good habits
weaknesses: Maintenance has clearly slowed: last push 2026-05-22, last release Feb 2026, public 'is this abandoned' threads
No parallelism at all — single tree, single conversation
No durable run journal or crash resume; interrupting a task leaves commits, not resumable state
Python API explicitly unsupported and unstable, so it is a poor embedding target
No approval gates, no isolation, no sandbox — it edits your working tree directly
No structured/typed outputs from steps

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A tree-sitter-derived, relevance-ranked repo map injected as context, rather than relying on the agent to grep its way to the right files
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's write steps run in fresh worktrees where the agent has no accumulated context. A cheap deterministic repo map is exactly the kind of computed, journalable, zero-model-call artifact weft can produce once and reuse across every parallel step.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Built-in lint/test commands wired as an automatic post-edit repair loop, so 'run the linter, feed failures back, retry' is configuration rather than orchestration code
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already has schema repair for step outputs; the same in-session repair machinery applied to lint/test failures would turn the most common review→fix→verify loop into one declaration instead of a hand-written ctx.pipeline.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Print resolved USD cost per step inline as the run proceeds, with a /tokens-style breakdown of what is actually occupying the context window
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has budgets and ceilings, but per-step visible cost is what makes a developer restructure a workflow. Ceilings tell you when you failed; per-step cost tells you where.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Architect/editor separation as a named, first-class pattern: an expensive reasoning model produces the plan, a cheap model applies the edits, each with its own output format
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has per-step routing but no opinionated pattern for it. Shipping a routing preset makes the cost win legible instead of leaving every user to rediscover it.

projects.name: Cline (+ Cline SDK multi-agent teams, Cline CLI)
projects.popularity: 66,780 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; very actively pushed (2026-08-24). Description now reads 'Autonomous coding agent as an SDK, IDE extension, or CLI assistant' — a deliberate broadening beyond the VS Code extension it started as
projects.positioning: The most direct open-source competitor to weft's orchestration layer that is ALSO a mainstream daily-driver agent. Cline now ships an SDK with multi-agent teams: a coordinator agent that spawns specialists, coordinating through a persisted task board and mailbox that survive restarts. That persistence-across-sessions is precisely weft's differentiator, implemented by an Apache-2.0 project with 66k stars.

features.durability: Two layers, and the team layer is the interesting one. (1) Checkpoints: Cline maintains a SHADOW git repository separate from your project's real git history, committing a file snapshot after every tool use; restore offers three granularities — Restore Files (code only), Restore Task Only (conversation only), Restore Files & Task. Because it's a shadow repo it captures untracked files and never pollutes your commit history. Documented cost: 'For very large repositories, checkpoints may use significant storage and slow down Cline as it commits file snapshots after each tool use.' (2) Teams: state persists to ~/.cline/data/teams/{team-name}/ as three JSON files — task-board.json (tasks + status), mailbox.json (inter-agent messages), mission-log.json (activity history) — and explicitly survives restarts, so `cline --team-name auth-sprint 'Continue -- pick up incomplete tasks'` resumes a team days later. Contrast with sub-agents, which are 'within session only'. This is a journal of coordination state, not of step results, and there is no replay.
features.schemaValidation: Tool-call schemas validated per the provider's function-calling contract, with retry/repair on malformed tool XML. No typed step-result contract across a workflow.
features.humanInTheLoop: The best per-action approval UX in the cluster. Plan mode explores the codebase and asks clarifying questions before Act mode touches anything; every file edit and terminal command surfaces a diff/command for approval, with per-tool auto-approve toggles and an auto-approve-all escape hatch. The diff view before an edit lands is the interaction developers actually trust. Inside a team run, a blocked specialist writes to mailbox.json and marks its task blocked; the coordinator reads the mailbox and resolves it — agent-to-agent unblocking, not human gating.
features.parallelism: Multi-agent teams: `team_spawn_teammate`, `team_delegate_task`, `team_check_status`, `team_get_result` as coordinator tools, described as 'peer-to-peer with task board' rather than hierarchical parent-child. Enabled with enableAgentTeams: true (vs enableSpawnAgent: true for lighter sub-agent delegation). The published SDK example spins up multiple specialist agents in parallel, streams each one's output to a web UI over SSE, and synthesizes the results.
features.gitIsolation: Shadow-git checkpoints are isolation of HISTORY, not of the working tree — specialists share cwd/workspaceRoot and the docs do not specify worktree isolation for team members. So parallel team agents can collide on the same files, exactly the failure mode weft's worktree-per-write-step design exists to prevent. This is Cline's clearest architectural gap versus weft.
features.multiProvider: Among the broadest: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter (200+ models), AWS Bedrock, Vertex, and local models via Ollama/LM Studio. Per-agent/per-mode model selection supported (different model for Plan vs Act, and per specialist).
features.costControl: Per-task token and USD accounting surfaced in the UI, with context-window usage shown live. No documented hard ceiling that halts a team run.
features.observability: Task view with per-step diffs and command output; context-window meter; per-task cost; the SDK example demonstrates SSE streaming of every agent's output to a custom web UI, and mission-log.json is a durable team activity record.
features.testing: No zero-model-call harness. The SDK makes programmatic driving possible, which is the raw material for one, but nothing published.
features.authoringModel: Three surfaces over one core: VS Code/JetBrains extension, CLI (`cline --team-name ...`), and a TypeScript SDK. Behaviour customization via .clinerules files (coding standards, architecture conventions, deployment procedures) and workflows; MCP for external tools. Teams are configured declaratively (enableAgentTeams) and then driven by the coordinator model, not by a script you write.

strengths: Team state (task board + mailbox + mission log) persists across restarts and is explicitly resumable — durable multi-agent coordination in an Apache-2.0 project with 66k stars
Shadow-git checkpointing gives file-level undo without touching the user's real git history, and captures untracked files
Three-way restore granularity (files / conversation / both) is more thoughtful than most rewind implementations
Per-action approval with an inline diff before every edit is the approval UX developers actually trust
Enormous provider breadth including 200+ models via OpenRouter and local models
Ships as extension + CLI + SDK over one core — the same shape as weft's three-surfaces-one-Engine architecture
Mailbox-based blocking/unblocking gives specialists a way to escalate instead of failing silently
weaknesses: No git-worktree isolation for team members — parallel specialists appear to share one working tree, so concurrent edits can collide
Coordination is model-driven (the coordinator LLM decides what to delegate next), so control flow is non-deterministic and unrepeatable; no script holds the plan
Persisted state is coordination metadata, not step results, so there is no replay and no content-addressed salvage
Shadow-git snapshot after EVERY tool use is acknowledged to degrade on large repos
No hard budget ceiling
Multi-agent teams are a newer ClineCore feature with correspondingly thin documentation

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Shadow git repository for step-level snapshots — a second .git that commits a full tree snapshot (including untracked files) after each tool use, entirely separate from the user's real history
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktrees isolate write steps, but read/inspect steps and any in-place mutation have no undo. A shadow repo gives weft file-level rewind for free, works for untracked files, and never pollutes the user's commits — complementary to, not competing with, worktree patches.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Three-way restore granularity: restore files only, restore conversation/journal only, or restore both, as distinct user-facing operations
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's journal replay is all-or-nothing. Separating 'rewind the code' from 'rewind the run state' is exactly what you want when a step produced a good analysis but bad edits.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A durable inter-agent mailbox where a blocked step writes a structured message and marks itself blocked, and a coordinator (or a human) drains the mailbox and unblocks it — persisted so it survives restarts
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has ctx.human.ask, but no channel for a sub-workflow to escalate a blocker to its parent or to a human asynchronously. A journaled mailbox makes 'this step is stuck and needs input' a first-class, resumable state rather than a failure.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Named, resumable long-running runs addressed by a human-chosen name (`cline --team-name auth-sprint 'pick up incomplete tasks'`) rather than by an opaque run id
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's journaled runs are its core asset but are only valuable if a developer can find and resume one three days later. Naming a run is a trivially cheap ergonomic win on machinery weft already has.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Ship an SSE-streaming reference example that renders every parallel agent's live output into a custom web UI
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has a daemon web UI, but a documented streaming API others build on turns the daemon from a bundled feature into an integration point.

projects.name: Roo Code (ARCHIVED) / Zoo Code (community successor)
projects.repo: https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code (archived 2026-05-15); successor: Zoo Code at zoocode.dev
projects.popularity: 24,328 stars at archival, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24 (archived: true, last push 2026-05-15). Roo Code announced sunset 2026-04-20 and shut down 2026-05-15; the team pivoted to Roomote, a Slack-first cloud agent producing PRs from a prompt. Zoo Code forked 2026-04-23 with an official handoff and published v3.54.0 to the VS Code Marketplace 2026-05-16. Zoo Code's own star count: unknown (not verified).
projects.positioning: Historically the most important prior art for weft's orchestration model: Roo Code's Orchestrator (formerly 'Boomerang') mode popularized decomposing a task into subtasks, dispatching each to a specialized mode with its OWN model and tool permissions, and returning a summary to the parent. Its death in May 2026 is itself a strategic signal — the maintainers concluded 'IDEs are not the future of coding' and moved to a cloud/Slack PR-producing agent.

features.durability: Checkpoints (shadow-git style, inherited from the Cline lineage it forked from) for file-level undo, plus task history persisted in extension storage. Subtask state was managed by the orchestrator within a task tree; no crash-durable journal and no replay.
features.schemaValidation: Tool-call XML parsing with retry on malformed output. Structured mode definitions (custom modes as JSON/YAML with roleDefinition, groups, fileRegex restrictions) validated at load. No typed step results.
features.humanInTheLoop: Per-action approval with diff preview and granular auto-approve toggles (read / write / execute / browser / MCP), inherited and extended from Cline. Ask mode and Architect mode gave read-only planning phases before implementation.
features.parallelism: Orchestrator mode decomposed work into subtasks, but dispatch was fundamentally SEQUENTIAL — each subtask ran to completion and returned a condensed summary to the parent before the next began. The 'boomerang' name describes the return trip, not concurrency. Later versions added experimental concurrent subtask execution.
features.gitIsolation: None. Operated on the working tree with checkpoint-based undo. No worktrees, no containers.
features.multiProvider: Very broad (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, Ollama, LM Studio) with the standout feature of PER-MODE model configuration: Architect on an expensive reasoning model, Code on a mid-tier, Ask on a cheap one, each with its own API profile. The most direct prior art for weft's per-step routing.
features.costControl: Per-task and per-subtask token/USD accounting displayed in the UI, with the orchestrator's context kept small by design (subtasks return summaries, not transcripts) — a cost architecture, not a cost limit. No hard ceiling.
features.observability: Task tree UI showing parent task and nested subtasks with per-node cost and token counts; per-message diffs; checkpoint timeline.
features.testing: None notable.
features.authoringModel: Custom modes defined declaratively (.roomodes / global) with name, roleDefinition, customInstructions, tool groups, and fileRegex write restrictions — a mode could be forbidden from touching anything but *.md. Orchestration was model-driven: the Orchestrator mode's system prompt told it to decompose and delegate; there was no script.

strengths: Per-mode model + API profile configuration was the cleanest per-step routing UX anyone shipped
fileRegex write restrictions per mode (a docs mode that can only write *.md) is a simple, powerful capability constraint
Subtask-returns-summary architecture kept the orchestrator's context small — a genuinely good cost/context design
Custom modes were declarative, shareable, and project-committable
Large adoption (24k stars, ~3M users cited) before shutdown
weaknesses: DEAD. Archived 2026-05-15; the repo is read-only and the extension is unmaintained. Continuity depends on the Zoo Code community fork, whose long-term viability is unproven
Orchestration was model-driven prose, not code — non-deterministic, unrepeatable, unresumable
Sequential subtask dispatch; no real fan-out
No isolation whatsoever — subtask modes shared the working tree
No durable journal or crash resume
The maintainers' own stated conclusion — that IDE-embedded agents are not the future — is a datapoint against the whole IDE-extension category

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-step capability restriction by file-path regex: a step declares it may only write files matching a pattern, enforced by the harness rather than requested in the prompt
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft validates step OUTPUTS with Zod but does not constrain what a write step may TOUCH. A docs step that can only produce *.md changes, enforced at patch-application time in ctx.integrate(), turns a prompt-level hope into a checkable invariant — and it composes naturally with weft's existing patch model.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Subtask returns a condensed summary to the parent rather than its transcript, as an explicit architectural rule, with per-node token accounting shown in a task tree
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's steps return schema-validated values, which is stricter — but the task-tree UI with per-node cost is the visualization that makes a deep ctx.pipeline comprehensible, and weft's journal already has the data to render it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Named modes bundling {system prompt, model, effort, tool groups, write restrictions} as one shareable, project-committable declaration referenced by name from a step
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has per-step routing but each step configures itself inline. A named role registry means 'reviewer' is defined once and referenced from twenty workflows, and changing the reviewer's model is a one-line edit rather than a codemod.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Treat Roo Code's death as strategic input: the team's stated reason was that IDE-embedded agents are the wrong form factor, and they moved to a Slack-first cloud agent producing PRs
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft is a library/engine, not an IDE extension, which is the right side of that bet — but it argues for prioritizing the daemon/MCP/webhook surfaces and PR-producing output over local interactive polish.

projects.name: opencode
projects.popularity: 200,999 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24 — the most-starred project in this cluster, ahead of Claude Code's issue tracker (142,871) and Codex (116,959). ~26,011 forks. Reported ~8M monthly active users as of May 2026 (unverified). Repo default branch is `dev`.
projects.positioning: The breakout open-source terminal agent of 2026 and the most credible model-agnostic alternative to Claude Code. Client/server by design: `opencode serve` is a headless HTTP server with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec and an SSE event bus, and the TUI is merely one client. That architecture — one engine, many surfaces — is exactly weft's CLI+MCP+daemon claim, already shipped and at massive scale.

features.durability: Sessions are server-side objects with full REST lifecycle: list, get, create, FORK, and child sessions. Forking a session to branch an exploration is a first-class operation. Undo/redo of agent changes is supported in the TUI. Share generates a public link to a conversation. But sessions are conversation state, not a step journal — there is no schema-validated step-result log and no deterministic replay after a crash.
features.schemaValidation: Tool schemas validated per provider; custom tools declare typed parameters. Structured output at the step level is not a documented primitive.
features.humanInTheLoop: Fine-grained declarative permissions rather than blanket approval: per-agent permission maps over read / edit / bash / glob / grep / task, each set to allow | ask | deny, plus a separate Policies layer. The built-in Plan agent sets edits and bash to `ask` by default, giving a read-only planning phase. The most configurable approval model in the cluster — approval is a matrix, not a mode.
features.parallelism: Subagents invoked automatically via the Task tool or manually by @mention (@general, @explore, @scout). The built-in General subagent is documented specifically for 'parallel multi-step work'; Explore is fast read-only codebase inspection; Scout researches dependencies without modifying the workspace. Max Steps per agent bounds agentic iterations to control cost. No worktree-per-subagent.
features.gitIsolation: None built in. Isolation is per-agent tool permissions (a read-only agent literally cannot write) rather than filesystem isolation. No worktrees, no containers, no patch-return flow — parallel subagents share the working tree.
features.multiProvider: The defining feature. Models.dev-backed provider catalogue covering effectively every provider plus local models, a curated 'Zen' option, OAuth flows for provider auth, and per-agent model override so each agent runs on a different model. Also supports ACP, so it can act as or host other protocol-compatible agents. Genuinely model-agnostic in a way Claude Code and Codex are not.
features.costControl: Max Steps per agent caps iterations. Token/cost reporting per session. No documented hard USD ceiling.
features.observability: SSE event stream (`server.connected` then bus events) exposes everything the server does to any client; OpenAPI 3.1 spec at /doc; LSP integration for symbol-level context; session sharing produces inspectable public transcripts. The most externally-consumable observability surface here.
features.testing: No zero-model-call harness documented. The SDK + OpenAPI spec make deterministic integration testing against a stubbed server plausible, but nothing published.
features.authoringModel: Agents declared either as JSON blocks in opencode.json or as markdown files in .opencode/agents/ (filename becomes the agent id: review.md → `review` agent), with fields for model, temperature, mode (primary|subagent), prompt (file reference), permissions map, and max steps. Plus Agent Skills, Rules, custom Tools, Plugins, MCP servers, and commands. Orchestration itself is model-driven — no script holds the plan.

strengths: Truly model-agnostic with a maintained provider catalogue (Models.dev), per-agent model override, and OAuth provider auth — the strongest multi-provider story in the cluster
Client/server split with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec and an SSE event bus means any surface (TUI, desktop, IDE ext, CI, your own web UI) is a first-class client — one engine, many surfaces, already proven
Permission MATRIX (read/edit/bash/glob/grep/task × allow/ask/deny) per agent is far more expressive than mode-based approval
Session fork as a REST operation makes branching an exploration trivial
Read-only-by-construction agents (Plan, Explore, Scout) prevent whole classes of accident without needing sandboxes
Enormous momentum: 201k stars, MIT, active daily development
ACP support and a plugin system
weaknesses: No filesystem isolation at all — parallel subagents share one working tree, so concurrent writes collide
No durable step journal, no crash-resume of an in-flight multi-step task, no replay
Orchestration is model-driven; no script, no determinism, no repeatability
No hard cost ceiling (only max-steps)
No patch/diff review-then-integrate flow
5,410 open issues (verified 2026-08-24) suggests the maintenance load of hypergrowth

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A permission MATRIX per step — {read, edit, bash, glob, grep, spawn} × {allow, ask, deny} — rather than a single permission mode, so a step's capabilities are declared as data alongside its schema
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's determinism gate constrains what workflow CODE may do; nothing constrains what a STEP's agent may do. Declaring capability per step makes 'this is a read-only analysis step' machine-checkable and journalable, and it's the natural place to hang weft's existing gate machinery.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Read-only agents as built-in primitives (Explore for fast codebase inspection, Scout for dependency research) that are incapable of mutation by construction, not by instruction
ideasWorthStealing.why: Most steps in a review→fix→verify loop are read-only. Making that structural means weft can skip worktree creation entirely for them — a large latency and disk win on wide fan-outs — and can safely parallelize them without isolation.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Publish the Engine as an OpenAPI-specified HTTP server with an SSE event bus, and make the CLI/MCP/web UI all be clients of that spec
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already claims CLI+MCP+daemon over one Engine class. Formalizing it as a published spec with a generated SDK turns that from an internal factoring into an ecosystem surface — and the SSE bus is exactly how a journaled engine should expose its append-only log to observers.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Agents as markdown files where the filename is the identity (review.md → `review`), with frontmatter for model/temperature/permissions/max-steps and the body as the prompt
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's steps are TypeScript, which is right for orchestration but heavy for prompt iteration. Letting a step reference a markdown role file separates 'the shape of the workflow' (typed, reviewed, versioned) from 'the wording of the prompt' (iterated hourly).

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Session fork as a first-class operation: branch a run at any point to explore an alternative without destroying the original
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's journal makes this nearly free — fork the event log at step N and diverge. It converts the journal from a recovery mechanism into an exploration mechanism, which is a much better story.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A maintained provider catalogue (Models.dev) with OAuth flows, rather than hand-maintained per-provider config
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's AgentProvider abstraction is a strength, but pricing/model-id drift is a maintenance tax that directly corrupts USD budget accuracy. Consuming an external catalogue keeps the cost ceiling honest.

projects.name: goose (Block → Agentic AI Foundation / Linux Foundation)
projects.popularity: 53,385 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24. Governance milestone: Block donated goose to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), a new Linux Foundation org announced Dec 2025 alongside MCP and AGENTS.md; the repo moved to aaif-goose/goose (announced 2026-04-07)
projects.positioning: The general-purpose on-machine agent, not code-specific — but its Recipes system is the most complete DECLARATIVE workflow spec in this cluster, and the only one besides weft with structured output schemas, retry-with-validation, sub-workflow composition and cron scheduling in one artifact. Vendor-neutral foundation governance is a real differentiator for enterprise adoption.

features.durability: Session resume (`goose session -r`) with sessions persisted locally; the scheduler creates automated sessions for recurring recipe runs and keeps run history. No append-only step journal, no deterministic replay, no content-addressed salvage. Durability is session-level, not step-level.
features.schemaValidation: The standout feature: a recipe's `response` field takes a `json_schema` that ENFORCES structured JSON output from the run — explicitly 'useful for automation workflows'. This is the closest analogue in the cluster to weft's schema-validated step returns. Combined with the `retry` block (requires max_retries and `checks`, where checks are shell commands validating success), goose has a real validate-and-repair loop — though repair is a whole-run retry rather than weft's in-session repair.
features.humanInTheLoop: Permission modes (approve / smart-approve / chat-only) gate tool execution; recipe parameters can be marked as user-prompted at launch, a genuine parameterized human input step. But there is no mid-run gate: once a recipe is running, a human cannot be a step in it.
features.parallelism: Subrecipes are the composition primitive: a recipe declares sub_recipes and goose can run 'multiple subrecipe instances concurrently' — a lead agent spawning worker agents. `sequential_when_repeated` forces linear execution when concurrency is unsafe, a nice explicit escape hatch. Documented tutorials cover scheduling a recipe that runs two subagents in parallel.
features.gitIsolation: None. goose runs on your machine against your working tree. No worktrees, no per-agent containers, no patch flow. Its weakest axis versus weft, and a direct consequence of being general-purpose rather than code-specific.
features.multiProvider: 15+ providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Azure, Bedrock, …). Lead/worker model routing assigns different models to different roles — one for planning, another for execution, a third for review — with active 2026 work (issue #4036) to consolidate multi-model/multi-provider config and auto-switching into one place. Recipe `settings` can override goose_provider/goose_model and temperature per recipe.
features.costControl: `max_turns` in recipe settings controls how many iterations an agent may perform before stopping — an enforced structural cap. Token/cost reporting per session. No USD ceiling.
features.observability: Session logs and transcripts; scheduler run history; MCP extension activity visible per call; desktop app UI. No per-step cost dashboard comparable to Claude Code's /workflows.
features.testing: The `retry` block's `checks` (shell commands that must pass for the run to be considered successful) is effectively a declarative acceptance test attached to the workflow — a genuinely good idea. No mock-provider harness for the orchestration itself.
features.authoringModel: YAML recipes: title + description (required), instructions and/or prompt, parameters with Jinja-style {{ }} substitution and typed inputs (string, number, boolean, date, file, select) that can be required/defaulted/user-prompted, extensions (declaring exactly which MCP servers are available — and notably, declaring an explicit extensions block EXCLUDES default platform extensions, a good least-privilege default), settings (provider/model/temperature/max_turns), response.json_schema, retry{max_retries, checks}, and sub_recipes. Supports template inheritance via {% extends %}, an indent() filter for multi-line values, and a recipe_dir variable. Recipes become slash commands; there is a Recipe Cookbook of templates.

strengths: Recipes are the most complete declarative workflow artifact in the cluster: parameters, typed inputs, JSON-schema-enforced output, retry-with-shell-check validation, sub-recipe composition, and per-recipe model/provider settings in one YAML file
response.json_schema enforcing structured output is direct validation of weft's schema-per-step thesis, arrived at independently
retry{max_retries, checks} where checks are shell commands is a declarative acceptance test bound to the workflow — 'this run succeeded iff pytest exits 0'
Explicit extensions block uses least-privilege semantics (declaring extensions EXCLUDES defaults)
sequential_when_repeated as an explicit opt-out of concurrency is a thoughtful safety valve
Built-in cron scheduler (6-field expressions) turning recipes into recurring automated sessions
Vendor-neutral Linux Foundation / AAIF governance — a real enterprise procurement advantage over any single-vendor tool
Rust: fast, single-binary, portable; desktop app + CLI + API
weaknesses: No filesystem/git isolation at all — no worktrees, no containers, agents work directly on your tree
No step-level journal, no crash resume mid-run, no replay

YAML recipes cannot express real control flow: no conditionals, no loops over computed data, no typed values passed between sub-recipes — the ceiling weft's plain-TypeScript model is designed to break through
Retry is whole-run, not in-session repair of a single bad step
Not code-specific: no diff review, no patch flow, no repo map, no test-fix loop primitives
No USD budget ceiling (only max_turns)

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Declarative acceptance checks attached to a workflow (retry: {max_retries: N, checks: [shell commands]}) so 'this run is successful iff these commands exit 0' is part of the workflow artifact, with automatic retry on failure
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has schema validation on step OUTPUTS but no notion of 'the run as a whole is only valid if the test suite passes'. A ctx.check() primitive that journals the command, its exit code and output — and can trigger bounded re-runs — turns review→fix→verify from hand-written orchestration into a declaration.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Least-privilege tool declaration: naming an explicit extensions/tools block EXCLUDES the platform defaults rather than adding to them
ideasWorthStealing.why: A quietly important default. weft's determinism gate replaces globals; applying the same allowlist-not-denylist posture to a step's MCP/tool surface means a step gets exactly what it declared and nothing else — and makes the journal's record of a step's capabilities complete.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Typed, user-promptable workflow parameters (string/number/boolean/date/file/select) with required/default/prompt-at-launch semantics, so a workflow is a parameterized artifact rather than a script you edit per run
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft workflows are TypeScript functions, so parameters are just arguments — but declaring them with types and prompt semantics is what lets the CLI, the MCP server and the web UI all render the same launch form. A concrete win for weft's three-surfaces-one-Engine architecture.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: sequential_when_repeated: an explicit per-sub-workflow flag forcing linear execution when concurrency is unsafe
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.parallel is opt-in concurrency, but a sub-workflow that is unsafe to run concurrently has no way to say so. Letting the callee declare its own concurrency constraint prevents a caller from unknowingly breaking it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A built-in cron scheduler that turns a saved workflow into a recurring automated run with retained run history
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon already runs; adding schedules makes journaled durability continuously valuable rather than only valuable when a human is watching.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Vendor-neutral foundation governance as a strategy (goose → Linux Foundation AAIF)
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft sits between Anthropic and OpenAI models. Neutral governance — or at least a clearly neutral license and trademark posture — is what makes an orchestration layer safe for enterprises to standardize on when it brokers competing vendors.

projects.name: OpenAI Codex CLI (+ Codex app, subagents)
projects.popularity: 116,959 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 17,833 forks; extremely active (pushed 2026-08-24). Second only to opencode and Claude Code in this cluster
projects.positioning: OpenAI's terminal coding agent, and — with weft — one half of the multi-provider story: weft's AgentProvider puts Codex and Claude behind one interface, so Codex is simultaneously a competitor and a dependency. Its 2026 additions of TOML-defined subagents, worktree isolation and a `multi_agent` feature flag move it directly onto weft's orchestration territory.

features.durability: Session rollout files persisted locally with `codex resume` to continue a prior session. Config precedence is layered and explicit: CLI flags > project .codex/config.toml > named profiles (~/.codex/profile-name.config.toml) > user ~/.codex/config.toml, with a managed-machine requirements.toml that administrators use to FORBID unsafe combinations. No step journal, no deterministic replay, no content-addressed salvage.
features.schemaValidation: Tool/function-call schemas per the Responses API. Subagent results return as SUMMARIES to the main thread; the docs do not describe a structured output contract for subagent results.
features.humanInTheLoop: approval_policy with three values — 'untrusted' (approve anything not on a trusted list), 'on-request' (agent asks when it needs escalation), 'never' (fully autonomous) — orthogonal to sandbox_mode. The orthogonality is the good design: 'what may it do without asking' and 'what may it do at all' are separate axes. The docs stress choosing the parent turn's permission mode BEFORE delegating, because subagents inherit it. No mid-run human step.
features.parallelism: Subagents spawn in parallel and the parent 'wait[s] for all of them, then summarize[s] the result'. Concurrency capped by agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session (reported default fan-out ~6 threads). Each subagent works in its own isolated environment, typically a git worktree created automatically by the subagent runtime. A `multi_agent` flag exists in the [features] table. As of v0.115.0 (2026-03-16) subagents reliably inherit sandbox and network rules from the parent session plus project-profile layering, making parallel subagent runs stable for CI.
features.gitIsolation: Two complementary layers, and Codex's strongest suit. (1) OS-level sandbox_mode: 'read-only', 'workspace-write' (writes confined to the workspace; .git and .codex remain protected EVEN IN writable modes; network access varies by level), 'danger-full-access'. On macOS this is Seatbelt, on Linux Landlock/seccomp, and there is a [windows] table with 'elevated'/'unelevated' native sandbox modes. (2) Git worktrees per subagent, created automatically by the subagent runtime, and worktree-isolated parallel agents in the Codex app. Protecting .git from the agent even in workspace-write is a detail nobody else got right.
features.multiProvider: OpenAI models primarily (gpt-5.6, gpt-5.6-terra for speed/efficiency, gpt-5.6-luna for fast narrow tasks), with model_providers config allowing other OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Per-subagent model AND reasoning effort (ultra/max/xhigh/high/medium/low), with [agents] defaults via default_subagent_model and default_subagent_reasoning_effort; unspecified subagents inherit the parent. Genuine per-step routing within the OpenAI family.
features.costControl: Reasoning-effort tiers and cheaper model variants (terra/luna) are the primary cost levers, plus max_concurrent_threads_per_session bounding fan-out. Usage visible against the ChatGPT plan. No documented hard USD ceiling in the CLI.
features.observability: Session rollout files; TUI progress; the Codex app surfaces parallel agent workspaces with per-agent diffs. Less instrumented than Claude Code's /workflows.
features.testing: `codex exec` non-interactive mode makes CI/scripted invocation straightforward, which is the substrate for testing but not a harness. No mock-provider replay.
features.authoringModel: TOML throughout. Subagents are standalone TOML files in ~/.codex/agents/ (personal) or .codex/agents/ (project), each with name (the source of truth for identity), description (guidance on when to use it), developer_instructions (behaviour), and optional model / reasoning_effort / sandbox_mode overrides. Config profiles switch whole named configurations. AGENTS.md for repo conventions (now a Linux Foundation AAIF project). MCP servers under [extend.mcp]. Feature flags under [features] (memories, multi_agent, web_search).

strengths: Real OS-level sandboxing (Seatbelt / Landlock / Windows native) with three named modes — the only project here with kernel-enforced isolation rather than convention
Protects .git and .codex from the agent even in workspace-write mode — prevents an agent rewriting history or its own config
approval_policy and sandbox_mode as ORTHOGONAL axes is the correct decomposition of 'may it ask' vs 'may it do'
Automatic git worktree per subagent so parallel agents never collide
Per-subagent model AND reasoning effort, with [agents] defaults and parent inheritance
Explicit config precedence chain (CLI > project > profile > user) plus requirements.toml letting admins forbid unsafe combinations on managed machines
Verified subagent inheritance of sandbox/network rules (v0.115.0) makes parallel runs CI-safe
116,959 stars, Apache-2.0, Rust, very active
weaknesses: OpenAI models only in practice — the counterpart to Claude Code's Anthropic lock-in, and precisely why weft's dual-provider abstraction has a market
No durable step journal, no crash resume of a multi-step orchestration, no replay
Subagents return prose summaries, not typed values, so composing them into a pipeline means re-parsing natural language
No human-in-the-loop mid-run; approval is per-action only
No hard USD ceiling
No script-held orchestration — delegation is model-decided, so runs are not repeatable
13,687 open issues (verified 2026-08-24)

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Separate the approval axis from the capability axis: approval_policy (untrusted / on-request / never) orthogonal to sandbox_mode (read-only / workspace-write / full-access), so a step can be fully autonomous yet incapable of harm, or heavily gated yet unrestricted
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft conflates these — ctx.gate is about human approval, worktrees are about blast radius, and there is no single place a step declares both. Making them two independent declarations per step is cleaner and maps directly onto weft's existing gate + worktree machinery.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Protect .git (and the engine's own state directory) from agent writes even in the most permissive writable mode
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's whole patch-then-integrate guarantee rests on git being trustworthy. An agent that runs `git reset --hard` or edits .git/config inside its worktree can corrupt the patch weft is about to integrate — and weft's own journal directory needs the same protection.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: OS-level sandboxing (Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock/seccomp on Linux) for write steps, layered underneath the git worktree rather than instead of it
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktrees isolate the filesystem by convention; a determined or confused agent can `cd` out. Kernel enforcement makes the isolation actually true, and weft already has the node:vm sandbox mindset for its determinism gate — this is the same idea applied to the agent's process.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: An explicit config precedence chain (CLI > project > named profile > user) plus a machine-level requirements.toml that ADMINS use to forbid unsafe combinations, which lower layers cannot override
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has budgets and a determinism gate but no notion of organizational policy a workflow author cannot relax. 'This repo may never run a step with full network access' is the kind of constraint that makes an engine adoptable at a company.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-subagent reasoning-effort tiers (ultra/max/xhigh/high/medium/low) alongside model choice, with sensible org-level defaults and parent inheritance
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft routes steps to models but treats effort as opaque. Effort is often a bigger cost lever than model choice, and it belongs in weft's per-step routing config next to the model id — and in the budget projection.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Named config profiles that swap a whole coherent configuration set at once (~/.codex/profile-name.config.toml)
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft users will want 'cheap local iteration' vs 'production CI run' as one switch across models, budgets, concurrency and gate behaviour, rather than a dozen independent flags.

projects.name: Gemini CLI
projects.popularity: 106,664 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 14,479 forks; very active (pushed 2026-08-24). Third-largest in the cluster
projects.positioning: Google's open-source terminal agent, notable for being the only major vendor CLI released under Apache-2.0 with the full source in the open (Claude Code's CLI is closed; Codex is open but OpenAI-model-bound). Relevant to weft mainly as a third AgentProvider candidate and as an ACP-compatible target that OpenHands, Vibe Kanban and Agent Canvas already route to.

features.durability: Local session/checkpoint state with resume; /chat save and /chat resume for named conversation branches. Checkpointing of file edits before tool application. No step journal, no deterministic replay.
features.schemaValidation: Gemini function-calling schemas for tools; MCP tool schemas. No typed step-result contract for orchestration.
features.humanInTheLoop: Per-tool-call approval with diff preview, YOLO/auto-accept mode, and configurable trusted-tool lists. Standard approve-per-action UX; no mid-run durable human step.
features.parallelism: Subagents and parallel tool execution supported; the CLI is also an ACP-compatible agent so external orchestrators (OpenHands Agent Canvas, Vibe Kanban, claude-squad) drive multiple instances. No native worktree-per-agent.
features.gitIsolation: Sandboxing available via Docker/Podman container or macOS Seatbelt, configured per project. Checkpointing gives file-level undo. No git-worktree primitive built in.
features.multiProvider: Gemini models (via Google AI / Vertex / Code Assist), with generous free-tier quota a major adoption driver. Not model-agnostic.
features.costControl: Token/quota reporting against the free tier and paid quotas; /stats for session usage. No hard USD ceiling.
features.observability: /stats, session transcripts, OpenTelemetry support, and MCP server activity display.
features.testing: Non-interactive mode for CI; no mock-provider replay harness.
features.authoringModel: GEMINI.md (and AGENTS.md) for repo conventions, TOML/JSON settings, custom slash commands, extensions, and MCP servers. Orchestration is model-driven.

strengths: Fully open source (Apache-2.0) including the agent core — unlike Claude Code
Sandboxing via Docker/Podman or macOS Seatbelt available out of the box
Very large free-tier quota lowers the cost of wide fan-out experimentation dramatically
ACP-compatible, so it plugs into OpenHands Agent Canvas, Vibe Kanban and other orchestrators as a drop-in agent
Massive adoption (106,664 stars) and rapid iteration
Huge context window models suit whole-repo analysis steps
weaknesses: Gemini models only — no provider abstraction
No durable step journal or crash-resumable multi-step orchestration
No git-worktree isolation built in
No script-held deterministic orchestration
No hard budget ceiling
Weaker agentic coding reputation than Claude Code/Codex on complex multi-file work (subjective; benchmark position unverified)

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Support Gemini as a third AgentProvider behind weft's existing interface, and exploit its free-tier quota specifically for wide, cheap fan-out steps (per-file audits, per-file summaries)
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's per-step routing is only as valuable as the spread of options behind it. A near-free provider for the 40-way read-only fan-out, with an expensive provider for the integrate step, is the strongest concrete demonstration of why per-step routing matters.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Ship container-based sandboxing (Docker/Podman) as a configurable per-project default alongside macOS Seatbelt, selectable per step
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft isolates writes in worktrees but does not contain the agent's process. Offering container isolation as a per-step option makes weft usable for untrusted repos and dependency-installing steps.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Adopt AGENTS.md (now an AAIF/Linux Foundation project) as the convention file weft passes into every step's worktree, rather than a weft-specific format
ideasWorthStealing.why: A fresh worktree strips an agent of context. Reusing the emerging cross-vendor standard means Claude, Codex and Gemini steps all receive repo conventions in a format they already understand, with zero weft-specific authoring burden.

projects.name: container-use (Dagger)
projects.popularity: 4,016 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 201 forks; actively maintained (pushed 2026-08-17)
projects.positioning: Not an agent — an isolation SUBSTRATE for agents, delivered as an MCP server so any MCP-capable agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, goose) gains containerized, branch-isolated environments without changing the agent. The purest expression of the idea weft implements as worktree-per-write-step, taken one layer further into containers, and the most directly stealable architecture in the cluster.

features.durability: Every environment is a git branch plus a container, so the durable artifact is git itself — an agent's entire history of work is recoverable via `git checkout <branch>` long after the agent exits. Complete command history and logs are retained per environment (`cu log`), so what the agent ACTUALLY did is recorded, not just what it claims. No step-result journal or replay (it isn't an orchestrator), but git-branch-as-durable-artifact is exactly weft's patch model with a longer half-life.
features.schemaValidation: MCP tool schemas define the environment operations the agent may call. No workflow-level schema.
features.humanInTheLoop: Review-centric rather than approval-centric, and this is its thesis: instead of interrupting the agent for permission, let it run fully isolated and review the result. `cu diff` shows changes, `cu log` shows the real command history, `cu checkout <branch>` puts the agent's work in your editor, `cu merge`/`cu apply` integrate it. Critically, you can 'drop into any agent's terminal to see their state and take control when they get stuck' — a takeover mechanism, not just an approval prompt.
features.parallelism: The core value proposition: 'Each agent gets a fresh container in its own git branch — run multiple agents without conflicts, experiment safely, discard failures instantly.' Unbounded parallel agents, each fully isolated at both container and branch level.
features.gitIsolation: The best in the cluster: DUAL isolation — a git worktree/branch for the code plus a dedicated Dagger container for the process. This closes the hole in every worktree-only approach (weft's included): a worktree isolates files but shares the process, network, installed dependencies and environment. Failures are discarded by deleting a branch and a container.
features.multiProvider: Agent-agnostic by construction. Because it's an MCP server, any MCP-capable agent gains the capability — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, goose and others — with no per-agent integration work.
features.costControl: None — it does not call models.
features.observability: Its differentiating feature: complete command history and logs per environment, explicitly framed as 'what agents actually did, not just what they claim'. Plus `cu list` to enumerate environments and terminal takeover into any live agent.
features.testing: Containers make reproducible per-environment test execution natural (an agent can install deps and run the suite without touching your machine), but there is no test harness for orchestration.
features.authoringModel: An MCP server plus a `cu` CLI (list / log / diff / checkout / merge / apply / terminal). Environments are configured per project. Built on Dagger, so environment definitions are containerized workflow definitions.

strengths: Dual isolation — git branch AND container per agent — is strictly stronger than worktree-only isolation, closing the process/network/dependency hole
Delivered as an MCP server, so it upgrades ANY MCP-capable agent with zero per-agent integration — the highest-leverage distribution model in this cluster
Complete per-environment command history and logs: verifiable ground truth about what the agent did, independent of the agent's own account
Terminal takeover into a live agent's environment when it gets stuck — human intervention without aborting the run
Review-after-isolation (diff / checkout / merge) instead of approve-before-each-action is a better ergonomic for long autonomous runs
Discard-a-failure is deleting a branch and a container — no cleanup, no contamination
Backed by Dagger, Apache-2.0
weaknesses: Not an orchestrator: no workflow, no steps, no schema, no journal, no resume, no cost tracking — solves exactly one layer
Requires Docker/Dagger, a real setup and resource cost, especially for wide fan-outs on a laptop
Container startup latency per environment makes very short steps uneconomic
Modest adoption (4,016 stars) relative to the agents it serves
No conflict resolution when merging several agents' branches — left to git and you

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Layer a container underneath weft's worktree so a write step is isolated in BOTH dimensions: git branch for the code, container for the process, network, installed dependencies and environment
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktree isolation is only half the guarantee. A step that runs `npm install`, mutates a global cache, opens a port, or reads an env var breaks isolation without ever writing outside its worktree — and weft's determinism gate covers the orchestration code, not the agent's process.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Journal the agent's COMPLETE command history and output per step as verifiable ground truth, presented alongside the agent's own summary — 'what it actually did, not what it claims'
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft journals schema-validated step RESULTS, which are the agent's self-report. When a step lies or is subtly wrong, the diagnostic artifact you need is the command log. weft's journal is the natural home for it and already has the append-only substrate.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Terminal takeover: let a human drop into a running step's isolated environment, inspect state, run commands and take control, then let the step resume — rather than only being able to abort
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.gate is a scheduled decision point. Unscheduled intervention — 'this step has been flailing for ten minutes, let me look' — is the operation that actually saves a long run, and weft's durable-step model can journal the human's intervention as part of the step.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Expose weft's isolation primitives as an MCP server so agents NOT running under weft can still request an isolated environment and return a patch
ideasWorthStealing.why: A distribution strategy, not just a feature. It lets weft's isolation+journaling reach Claude Code and Codex users who will never write a weft workflow, making weft the substrate rather than a competitor to the harness they already use.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Frame the default interaction as review-after-isolation (diff / checkout / merge) rather than approve-before-each-action, with `cu checkout`-style 'put this step's work in my editor' as a first-class command
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already returns patches that land only at ctx.integrate(). Adding 'check out step 7's worktree so I can poke at it in my IDE' converts weft's patch model from a safety mechanism into a review workflow developers will actively want.

projects.name: Sculptor (Imbue)
projects.license: MIT (verified by fetching LICENSE.md: 'MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 Imbue, Inc.')
projects.popularity: 218 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 15 forks. Small but from a serious AI research lab; self-described 'experimental research preview'
projects.positioning: A desktop workspace for parallel, container-isolated coding agents from research lab Imbue. Its distinctive contributions are containers-not-just-worktrees per agent, and 'Pairing Mode' — syncing an agent's isolated container work back to your local checkout so you can run and edit it live, a genuinely novel answer to the biggest practical objection to isolation (you can't easily try the result).

features.durability: Each workspace is a persistent isolated worktree of the repo with its own branch and setup, so work survives as a branch. Agent sessions persist per workspace. No step journal or replay.
features.schemaValidation: None documented at the orchestration level.
features.humanInTheLoop: Review-and-commit UI built in, plus GitHub PR integration with status tracking. The standout is 'suggestions' (on by default in recent releases) — the system proactively surfaces observations about the agent's work rather than waiting to be asked. Bundled skills include /sculptor-workflow:fix-bug which 'conducts a short reproduction interview, writes failing tests, then makes them pass' — a scripted human-interview → test → fix loop, one of the few concrete review/fix/verify workflows shipped as a product primitive in this cluster.
features.parallelism: 'Run 5+ agents on 5+ tickets at the same time', each in its own workspace with its own branch, terminal and diff view. Parallel-first by design.
features.gitIsolation: Isolated worktree + branch per workspace, with an experimental Docker/remote container backend and devcontainer port forwarding. Merge back to main through the built-in review/commit UI or a GitHub PR. Pairing Mode syncs container work to the local machine so you can run and edit the agent's code live without merging first.
features.multiProvider: Claude Code and Imbue's own Pi agentic harness are integrated; 'any terminal-based agent' can be run and managed. Recent releases added Opus 4.5 support and support for any Anthropic-compatible API key.
features.costControl: None documented.
features.observability: Per-workspace terminal, diff view and PR status. Suggestions surface issues proactively.
features.testing: The bundled fix-bug workflow is explicitly test-first (write a failing test, then make it pass), which is a testing DISCIPLINE encoded as a workflow rather than a harness for testing workflows.
features.authoringModel: Desktop GUI (Mac) plus bundled skills/workflows (spec generation, mock creation, bug fixing) invoked as slash commands. Not programmable orchestration.

strengths: Container backend per agent in addition to worktrees — stronger isolation than worktree-only managers
Pairing Mode (sync isolated container work back to the local checkout to run and edit live) directly solves the 'isolation makes it hard to actually try the change' problem
Ships opinionated multi-step workflows as product primitives, notably a reproduction-interview → failing-test → fix loop
Proactive suggestions rather than purely reactive review
MIT licensed, from a credible research lab, with devcontainer port forwarding for running services inside isolated environments
Supports arbitrary terminal agents, not just one vendor
weaknesses: Tiny adoption (218 stars) and self-described experimental research preview — adoption risk
Mac desktop app: not a library, not scriptable, not CI-usable
Container backend still marked experimental
No journal, no resume, no cost tracking, no schema validation
No programmable orchestration — workflows are bundled skills, not composable code
Last significant public activity around May 2026 (v0.30 docs) suggests slow cadence

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Pairing Mode: sync a step's isolated worktree/container back to the developer's local checkout so they can RUN and EDIT the agent's work live without merging first — then let the agent continue from the human's edits
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the missing half of weft's patch model. weft's write steps return patches that land only at ctx.integrate(), which is safe but means a human cannot easily try the change before deciding. A ctx.pair() that materializes a step's worktree locally, lets the human edit, and folds those edits back into the step's patch would make weft's isolation genuinely reviewable — and the human's edits become a journaled part of the step.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Devcontainer port forwarding from an isolated agent environment, so a step that starts a dev server is actually reachable from the developer's browser
ideasWorthStealing.why: Any web-app workflow needs the agent's isolated environment to be runnable. Without port forwarding, worktree/container isolation makes verification steps impossible for exactly the projects that most need parallel agents.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Ship a reproduction-interview → failing-test → make-it-pass workflow as a bundled, named weft workflow
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's pitch is that workflows are plain TypeScript, which is powerful but abstract. A bundled bug-fix workflow using ctx.human.ask for the reproduction interview, a schema-validated failing-test step, and a verify loop is the single best demonstration of why weft's primitives exist together.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Proactive suggestions: surface observations about a running step's work unprompted, rather than waiting for the human to open a review
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's gates are pull-based (the human is asked when the workflow decides). Push-based observations during long runs are what keep a human usefully in the loop across a 40-step workflow without turning every step into a gate.

projects.name: claude-squad
projects.popularity: 8,361 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 611 forks; actively maintained (pushed 2026-08-20). The most-adopted open-source terminal-based parallel agent manager
projects.positioning: A terminal multiplexer for parallel coding agents: tmux session + git worktree per agent, agent-agnostic (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, Amp, Aider). It solves the same isolation problem as weft's worktree-per-write-step but with zero orchestration — a human is the scheduler. Useful to weft as proof that worktree-per-agent is the accepted primitive, and as a source of interaction design.

features.durability: Git worktrees and branches persist across restarts; the `c` (checkout) key PAUSES a session while preserving changes, and `r` resumes it later — an explicit pause/resume model over persistent worktrees. No journal, no run state, no replay: durability is entirely what git holds.
features.schemaValidation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Human-as-scheduler by design: a TUI listing every agent session with status, a diff tab to review changes before applying, separate preview and diff views, `s` to commit and push a branch to GitHub, `c` to checkout/pause, `r` to resume. `--autoyes` (experimental) auto-accepts prompts for Claude Code and Aider so tasks finish unattended. Review is per-session diff inspection before push, not per-action approval.
features.parallelism: The whole point: N agents, each in its own tmux session and its own git worktree/branch, running simultaneously with a unified TUI over them. Supports mixing different agent programs across sessions via `-p` or configured profiles.
features.gitIsolation: Git worktree + branch per session — 'each session works on its own branch'. No containers; agents share the host process space, network and dependencies.
features.multiProvider: Agent-agnostic rather than model-agnostic: manages Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, Amp, and local agents like Aider, with multiple named profiles configurable so different sessions run different agents. Effectively a per-session provider router driven by a human.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: TUI with per-session status, preview pane, diff tab, and direct attach into any agent's tmux session for full terminal interaction.
features.testing: None.
features.authoringModel: Interactive TUI with keyboard commands; a config file for agent profiles. No programmatic orchestration whatsoever.

strengths: Dead simple and it works: tmux + git worktree is the minimum viable parallel-agent architecture, with no daemon, no containers, no database
Agent-agnostic with configurable profiles — mix Claude Code, Codex and Aider sessions in one board
Explicit pause (checkout) / resume model over persistent worktrees preserves work across restarts
Diff review before push, with attach-into-session for full terminal control
Terminal-native, so it works over SSH and anywhere a GUI orchestrator cannot
Most-adopted open-source tool in its niche (8,361 stars)
weaknesses: AGPL-3.0 — a genuine adoption barrier for commercial embedding, and notably the only copyleft license in this cluster
No orchestration at all: no dependencies between agents, no fan-in, no review→fix→verify loop, no scheduling — the human is the control flow
No journal, no cost tracking, no schema, no resume of a run (only of a session)
No container isolation; agents share host process space and network
--autoyes is experimental and only covers two agents
Requires tmux, limiting platforms and embedding contexts

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Explicit pause/resume of an isolated agent session that preserves the worktree (checkout to pause, resume to continue), presented as two keystrokes
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft resumes RUNS from the journal, but has no notion of parking a single in-flight step and coming back to it. For long-running write steps this is the operation a developer actually wants, and weft's journal + worktree pair already contains everything needed to implement it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A unified status board over heterogeneous agents where each row can be a different provider, selected from named profiles — so one workflow's steps can visibly run on Claude, Codex and Aider side by side
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already routes steps to providers. Rendering that heterogeneity in the daemon UI (which provider served which step, and what each cost) is what makes multi-provider routing a visible feature rather than a config detail.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Attach directly into a running step's live terminal session from the orchestrator UI, then detach and let it continue
ideasWorthStealing.why: Complements container-use's takeover idea and is much cheaper to build: if weft's write steps run under a multiplexer, the daemon UI can offer 'attach' as a link. Debugging a stuck step currently requires abandoning weft's abstraction entirely.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Reconsider licensing posture deliberately — claude-squad is AGPL-3.0 and it is repeatedly the reason teams pick alternatives
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft is an ENGINE meant to be embedded in other people's build systems and products. The license choice is a distribution decision as much as a legal one, and this cluster's evidence (Apache-2.0/MIT everywhere that grew large) is unambiguous.

projects.name: Crystal (now Nimbalyst)
projects.repo: https://github.com/stravu/crystal — the description now reads '(Crystal is now Nimbalyst)' and points to nimbalyst.com
projects.popularity: 3,109 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 196 forks. LAST PUSH 2026-02-26 — roughly six months stale; the project has been rebranded/relaunched as Nimbalyst and the open-source repo appears effectively frozen. Nimbalyst's own license and openness: unknown
projects.positioning: A desktop app for running multiple Codex and Claude Code sessions in parallel git worktrees, with an explicit emphasis on COMPARING approaches — run the same task several ways and diff the outcomes. That comparison framing is its distinctive contribution and is directly applicable to weft's fan-out.

features.durability: Sessions and their worktrees persist in the app's local store; work survives as branches. No journal, no replay.
features.schemaValidation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Per-session diff view, commit/squash, and rebase-from-main controls in the GUI; run scripts per session to verify a change before merging. Review is diff-centric and comparison-centric.
features.parallelism: Multiple concurrent sessions each in its own worktree, explicitly designed so you can run several attempts at the same task and compare approaches side by side.
features.gitIsolation: Git worktree per session with branch management, squash/rebase helpers, and per-session run scripts. No containers.
features.multiProvider: Claude Code and Codex sessions manageable from one app.
features.costControl: None documented.
features.observability: GUI with per-session output, diff view, and git status.
features.testing: Per-session run scripts let you execute a build/test command in a session's worktree before merging — a lightweight verify step.
features.authoringModel: Desktop GUI. No programmatic orchestration.

strengths: Explicitly designed for comparing multiple approaches to the same task, not just parallelizing different tasks
Worktree lifecycle helpers (squash, rebase from main, per-session run scripts) address the real friction of merging parallel work
MIT licensed and cross-platform desktop
Supports both Claude Code and Codex in one UI
weaknesses: Effectively stale as open source: last push 2026-02-26, rebranded to Nimbalyst with unknown licensing — high continuity risk
No orchestration, journal, schema, cost tracking, or resume
GUI-only; not scriptable or CI-usable
No container isolation
Small adoption (3,109 stars) and now split across two identities

ideasWorthStealing.idea: N-way comparison as a first-class orchestration primitive: run the SAME step k times (varying model, temperature, or prompt), collect all k patches, and present them side by side for a human or a judge step to choose from
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has ctx.parallel for different work, but not for the same work done differently. Best-of-k on a hard step is one of the highest-value uses of parallel isolated worktrees, and weft is the only project here with the patch model and schema validation to make automated selection rigorous rather than vibes-based.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-step run scripts: a declared build/test command executed inside a step's worktree before its patch is offered for integration, with the result attached to the patch
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.integrate() decides whether a patch lands, but has no evidence about whether the patch is any good. Attaching a verification result to each patch turns integration from a trust decision into an evidence-based one — and makes best-of-k selection automatic.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Built-in worktree lifecycle helpers — squash, rebase-from-main, conflict surfacing — rather than leaving merge mechanics to the user
ideasWorthStealing.why: When k parallel steps each produce a patch against a base that has since moved, integration conflicts are the normal case, not the exception. weft's ctx.integrate() needs a real rebase/conflict story or the parallel model breaks down exactly when it's most useful.

projects.name: Vibe Kanban
projects.popularity: 27,903 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24 — but LAST PUSH 2026-04-24 (four months stale) and the README states plainly: 'Vibe Kanban is sunsetting.' A cautionary datapoint: 27.9k stars did not make it sustainable
projects.positioning: A kanban board over coding agents: plan work as issues, create isolated workspaces where any of 10+ agents execute, review diffs inline, and ship via PR. It was the most-adopted attempt at a task-management-shaped orchestration layer, and its sunsetting is a meaningful signal about that shape of product.

features.durability: Tasks and task attempts persisted in a local database; each attempt maps to a branch/workspace so work survives. Worktree cleanup is configurable (DISABLE_WORKTREE_CLEANUP). No step journal or replay.
features.schemaValidation: None at the orchestration level.
features.humanInTheLoop: Its strongest axis. Inline commenting on diffs without leaving the UI; a built-in preview browser with devtools, inspect mode and device emulation for verifying UI changes; AI-generated PR descriptions with GitHub integration. Review is the product's center of gravity — the closest thing in the cluster to a real code-review UX over agent output.
features.parallelism: Many tasks in flight simultaneously, each in its own workspace with an isolated branch, terminal and dev server. Multiple attempts per task are supported so you can retry with a different agent.
features.gitIsolation: Isolated branch + workspace per task attempt, with its own terminal and dev server. Worktree-based.
features.multiProvider: Widest agent support in the cluster: Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Amp, OpenCode, Droid, CCR, Qwen Code — 10+ agents interchangeable per task, so you can retry a failed task with a different agent.
features.costControl: None documented.
features.observability: Kanban board as the status surface; per-attempt logs, terminal and diff; preview browser for visual verification.
features.testing: Per-workspace dev server and preview browser with device emulation constitute a real manual verification loop for UI work.
features.authoringModel: Web/desktop kanban UI (`npx vibe-kanban`), plus MCP integration. Orchestration is human-driven card movement, not code.

strengths: Best human review UX in the cluster: inline diff comments, plus a preview browser with devtools, inspect mode and device emulation for visually verifying UI changes
10+ interchangeable agents per task — retry a failed task with a different agent is a first-class operation
Per-task-attempt isolated workspace with its own terminal and dev server
AI-generated PR descriptions closing the loop to normal team review
Single-command install (npx vibe-kanban); Rust backend
weaknesses: SUNSETTING — the README announces discontinuation; last push 2026-04-24. Do not build on it
No orchestration logic: the board is the control flow and a human moves the cards
No journal, schema, cost tracking, resume, or programmatic API for workflows
Its failure despite 27.9k stars suggests a kanban-shaped wrapper is not a defensible product on its own

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Inline diff commenting on a step's patch inside the orchestrator UI, where each comment becomes structured feedback fed back into a retry of that step
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.human.review returns a value, but the natural UX for reviewing a patch is line-anchored comments. Turning those comments into a typed, journaled input to a repair step is exactly weft's durable-human-step model applied to the interaction developers already know.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Multiple ATTEMPTS per task as a modelled entity, where a failed attempt can be retried with a DIFFERENT agent/provider while keeping the task's identity and history
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's journal records what happened once. Modelling attempt-as-a-first-class-entity means 'this step failed on Codex, retry it on Claude' is a recorded, comparable operation rather than a new run — and it makes weft's multi-provider routing valuable at failure time, not just at planning time.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A preview surface per isolated workspace: dev server plus a browser with devtools and device emulation, so a UI change made in an isolated worktree can actually be looked at
ideasWorthStealing.why: Complements Sculptor's port-forwarding idea. For any front-end workflow a patch you cannot render is a patch you cannot review, and weft's isolation currently makes rendering harder rather than easier.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Heed the negative signal: a 27.9k-star kanban wrapper around agents was not sustainable and is shutting down
ideasWorthStealing.why: Direct strategic input for weft.
