The defensible layer is not the board or the UI over agents — it is the durable, schema-validated, replayable execution substrate. weft should resist the pull toward becoming a nicer dashboard and keep investing in the journal, determinism and patch semantics a wrapper cannot replicate.

projects.name: uzi
projects.popularity: 582 stars, verified via GitHub API 2026-08-24; 27 forks. LAST PUSH 2025-06-04 — over fourteen months stale. Effectively abandoned; included for completeness and because its one idea is worth taking
projects.positioning: 'CLI for running large numbers of coding agents in parallel with git worktrees.' Its distinguishing bet was SCALE: not 3-5 agents but many, launched from one command with a single prompt broadcast across them, then compared.

features.durability: Git worktrees/branches only; no state beyond git.
features.schemaValidation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: `uzi ls` to see all agents, `uzi prompt` to broadcast an instruction to every running agent at once, `uzi checkpoint` to take a named agent's work and merge it. Review is comparison across many concurrent attempts.
features.parallelism: The entire premise: launch N agents (potentially dozens) on the same task from one command, each in its own worktree, then pick a winner.
features.gitIsolation: Git worktree + branch per agent; also handles per-agent dev server ports so many agents can each run the app simultaneously.
features.multiProvider: Configurable agent command, so any CLI agent can be launched.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: `uzi ls` status listing across all running agents.
features.testing: None.
features.authoringModel: CLI commands driven by a config file. No orchestration logic.

strengths: Committed to genuinely large-scale fan-out (dozens of agents) rather than a handful
Broadcast-prompt-to-all-agents is a uniquely useful primitive for steering a fleet mid-run
Automatic per-agent dev server port assignment so many agents can run the app concurrently
Tiny, MIT, single Go binary
weaknesses: Abandoned — no commits since June 2025
No orchestration, journal, schema, cost tracking, or resume
Best-of-N with no automated evaluation means the human must review dozens of attempts by hand, which does not scale
Negligible adoption (582 stars)

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Broadcast a mid-run instruction to every currently-running parallel step at once ('all of you: also update the tests'), journaled as a single event that fans out to each in-flight step
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.parallel launches steps and waits. When a human notices a shared mistake across a 20-way fan-out, the only current option is to kill the run. A journaled broadcast is a durable, replayable steering primitive no orchestrator in this cluster has.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Automatic per-step resource allocation — dev server ports, container names, temp dirs — so N isolated steps can each run the application concurrently without collision
ideasWorthStealing.why: Port collision is the first thing that breaks a wide fan-out in any real web project, and it breaks it silently. weft creates the worktrees already; allocating and injecting a unique port per step is a small addition that makes verification steps possible at width.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Pair large-scale best-of-N with an automated judge step rather than human comparison — uzi's failure mode was N attempts and no way to evaluate them
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has schema-validated steps and patches with (per Crystal's idea) attached verification results. That is precisely the machinery needed to make best-of-N automatic instead of a human reviewing 20 diffs — the thing uzi could not do and the reason it died.

projects.name: Conductor (Melty Labs)
projects.repo: https://conductor.build — PROPRIETARY, no public source repository
projects.license: Proprietary, closed source. Free to use (bring your own Claude or Codex subscription). Included because the brief names it; it is NOT open source, unlike the rest of this cluster
projects.popularity: Star count: not applicable (no public repo). Adoption: widely discussed in 2026 as the leading Mac GUI for parallel Claude Code/Codex agents; exact numbers unknown/unverified. From a YC S24 team that previously built Melty, an open-source AI code editor
projects.positioning: The polished commercial answer to claude-squad: a free Mac app that runs multiple Claude Code and Codex agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree on its own branch, with a workspace-centric UI. Relevant to weft as the benchmark for what parallel-agent UX looks like when someone invests in design rather than a TUI.

features.durability: Workspaces map to git worktrees and branches, so work persists as branches. No agent-run journal or replay documented.
features.schemaValidation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: Workspace-centric review: per-workspace diff, commit, and PR creation. 'New Workspace' runs git worktree add on a fresh branch behind a single button. Approval follows the underlying agent's own permission model (Claude Code / Codex).
features.parallelism: Many workspaces open simultaneously, each fully isolated, with a UI designed for switching between them quickly.
features.gitIsolation: Git worktree + branch per workspace, created automatically. No containers.
features.multiProvider: Orchestrates Claude Code and Codex agents; you bring your own subscription for either.
features.costControl: None (costs accrue to your underlying Claude/Codex subscription).
features.observability: Per-workspace agent output, diff, and git status in a native Mac UI.
features.testing: None documented.
features.authoringModel: GUI only. No programmatic orchestration.

strengths: The best-polished UX for parallel worktree-isolated agents; one-click workspace creation hides git worktree mechanics entirely
Free, with BYO subscription — no incremental cost over the agent you already pay for
Supports both Claude Code and Codex in one surface
Native Mac app performance and integration
weaknesses: Proprietary and closed source — not extensible, not auditable, not self-hostable, not CI-usable
Mac only
No orchestration, journal, schema, cost tracking, resume, or API
Entirely dependent on the underlying agents' capabilities; adds isolation and UI, nothing else
Single-vendor continuity risk with no fork option

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Hide git worktree mechanics completely behind a single 'new workspace' action — no branch naming, no worktree paths, no cleanup decisions surfaced to the user
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktree-per-write-step is architecturally right but leaks git concepts into the developer's mental model. Conductor's adoption relative to the equally-capable claude-squad suggests hiding the mechanics, not exposing them, is what drives usage.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A workspace-centric rather than run-centric UI: the primary object a developer switches between is an isolated piece of work with its own diff and agent, not a log of an execution
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon UI is naturally run-and-step shaped, which matches the engine but not how developers think. Offering a workspace view over weft's worktrees — one card per in-flight write step, with its diff and its agent's output — would make weft's parallelism legible without changing the engine.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Free tool, bring-your-own-subscription as a distribution model
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft brokers Claude and Codex, both of which users already pay for. Removing any incremental cost to trying weft is the cheapest possible adoption lever for an orchestration engine whose value only becomes apparent after a few real runs.

cluster: Human-in-the-loop infrastructure, agent sandboxing/isolation, adjacent standards, and CI-native agent runners

projects.name: HumanLayer / CodeLayer
projects.language: Python + TypeScript SDKs; CodeLayer desktop app in Go/TypeScript
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (SDK and CodeLayer sources, per project statements)
projects.popularity: 11.3k stars shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24. Caveat: the repo header now says "the code here is pretty much all deprecated" and redirects to humanlayer.com, so the star count reflects the historical approval-SDK, not the current product.
projects.positioning: Started as the canonical 'human-in-the-loop as an API' layer: wrap any high-stakes tool call in require_approval() and route the approval to Slack/email with escalation and timeouts. Has since pivoted to CodeLayer, an opinionated agentic IDE/orchestrator for Claude Code sessions built around a research→plan→implement pipeline with human review gates. The old SDK is the direct conceptual ancestor of weft's ctx.gate/ctx.human.approve.

features.durability: Approvals are server-side state, not process state: each request gets a durable run_id/call_id, the SDK blocks or polls against the HumanLayer backend, and webhooks fire on agent/response events. Durability is scoped to the approval object only — there is no journal of the surrounding agent run, so a crashed agent does not resume mid-workflow, it only re-reads a still-pending approval. Fundamentally a hosted-service durability model, not an append-only local event log.
features.schemaValidation: Approval requests carry a function name + kwargs payload and typed response options (approve/deny/custom response options with names, descriptions, and prompt-fill text). There is no schema-validated return value contract for arbitrary steps and no repair loop; validation is of the human's choice, not the model's output.
features.humanInTheLoop: The core product, and considerably richer than weft's gates: require_approval() decorator plus human_as_tool() (the agent can call a human as a tool). Contact channels are first-class objects — Slack (channelOrUserId + contextAboutChannelOrUser), email (address + contextAboutUser) — so routing is per-call and context-aware. Documented production controls include escalation paths, timeouts, granular routing to a team vs an individual, and learned auto-approval from prior decisions. CodeLayer adds staged review gates between pipeline phases.
features.parallelism: CodeLayer runs multiple Claude Code sessions in parallel, keyboard-driven, worktree-friendly. The SDK itself has no fan-out primitive — parallelism is whatever the host framework provides.
features.gitIsolation: CodeLayer is worktree-friendly for parallel sessions; the SDK has none. No patch-capture / deferred-integrate model equivalent to weft's ctx.integrate().
features.multiProvider: Deliberately provider-agnostic ("bring your LLM and framework of choice") — integrations shipped for LangChain, CrewAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, ControlFlow etc. CodeLayer is Claude Code-centric.
features.costControl: None visible. No token or USD budgets, no ceilings.
features.observability: Hosted dashboard of approval requests and their outcomes, webhooks for agent/response events, run/call IDs for correlating an approval to the agent run that raised it. CodeLayer adds session logs/context inspection.
features.testing: No documented deterministic replay or zero-model-call harness.
features.authoringModel: Decorator-over-functions (@hl.require_approval()) in Python, wrapper functions in TS. Not a workflow DSL — the workflow is whatever your agent framework does; HumanLayer only intercepts the calls you mark.

strengths: The most mature approval-routing UX in open source: per-call channel selection with human-readable context about who is being asked, custom response options, escalation, and timeouts — weft's gate is a single blocking prompt by comparison.
human_as_tool() inverts the model: instead of the workflow author pre-declaring gates, the agent decides at runtime when to consult a human, which covers cases the author didn't anticipate.
Learned auto-approval from prior decisions — a policy layer that reduces gate fatigue over time.
Run IDs / call IDs give a stable correlation key between an approval and the agent run, which is exactly the join key an audit trail needs.
Framework-neutral by design, so it composes with anything rather than demanding you adopt an engine.
weaknesses: The open-source repo is self-declared deprecated; the live product is a hosted service plus a private-beta IDE, so 'open source' is now partly historical. Verify before depending on it.
Approval state lives in a vendor backend — self-hosting story unclear, which is a hard blocker for teams that cannot send function names/args to a third party.
No durability for the workflow itself: it makes the approval durable, not the run. A crash between approval and the next step loses everything after it.
No cost control, no schema validation of step outputs, no determinism story.
CodeLayer's pivot to an IDE means the library-shaped, embeddable version of the idea is the deprecated half.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Contact-channel objects with human-readable context strings ('the compliance team', 'the on-call SRE') attached per approval call, rather than one global reviewer.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.human.ask/approve is addressed to whoever is watching. Making the addressee a first-class, per-step, routable value lets the same workflow escalate a schema-repair failure to the author and a production deploy to a different team.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Timeouts and escalation ladders on gates: if nobody answers in N minutes, escalate to a second channel, then apply a default policy.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's gates are durable steps, which means a crashed-and-resumed run can sit blocked forever on an unattended gate. A timeout+escalation+default-decision policy on ctx.gate turns an indefinite block into a bounded one, and the decision (including 'auto-approved by timeout policy') is exactly the kind of fact the journal should record.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Learned/policy-based auto-approval — remember prior decisions on structurally similar calls and skip the gate.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Gate fatigue is what kills HITL adoption. Since weft already journals every step, it has the substrate to hash a gate's inputs and auto-satisfy gates matching a previously-approved shape, with the auto-approval recorded as its own journal event.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: human_as_tool(): expose 'ask a human' to the agent inside a step, not just as an author-declared edge.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's gates are static in the workflow graph. Letting a write step call out to a human mid-execution (and journaling that call) covers ambiguity the author didn't predict without forcing a workflow redesign.

projects.name: Dagger Container Use
projects.popularity: 4k stars shown on the GitHub README page when fetched 2026-08-24. Self-described as experimental / early development.
projects.positioning: The closest thing in this cluster to weft's git-worktree write-step model, but delivered as an MCP server rather than an engine. Every coding agent gets its own container plus its own git branch; you review and merge agent work with ordinary git commands. Competes with weft precisely on 'isolate the agent's writes and land them deliberately'.

features.durability: Environment state is persisted as git branches plus recorded command history/logs, so an environment survives the agent process dying and can be re-entered. There is no workflow journal and no replay — durability is 'the branch and its container still exist', not 'the run can resume from step 7'.
features.schemaValidation: None. It exposes MCP tools (create environment, run command, file ops); tool arguments are JSON-schema'd by MCP itself, but there is no validation of step return values and no repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: Human control is exercised out-of-band rather than as a workflow primitive: `cu terminal` drops you into a running agent's container to take over, `cu log` shows what it actually ran, and `git checkout <branch>` lets you review before merging. There is no blocking approval gate, no notification channel, no escalation. The human is a reviewer at the end, not a durable step in the middle.
features.parallelism: Explicitly the headline feature — multiple agents run concurrently, each in its own container + branch, with no interference. Discarding a failed agent is deleting a branch.
features.gitIsolation: The strongest git-isolation story here and a direct competitor to weft's worktrees: branch-per-environment, container-per-environment, full command history attached, merge/apply via normal git. Because the isolation is a container and not just a worktree, the agent's *environment* (installed deps, services) is isolated too, which weft's worktrees do not do.
features.multiProvider: Agent-agnostic via MCP: works with Claude Code, Cursor, VSCode, Codex, Goose — anything that speaks MCP. It does not route between providers; the host agent chooses the model.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: Complete command history and logs per environment, viewable with `cu log`; `cu watch` for live following; drop-in terminal access to inspect live state. Good forensic observability, no metrics/spans/cost.
features.testing: No deterministic replay harness. Containers make runs reproducible-ish in environment terms, not in model-output terms.
features.authoringModel: Not authored at all — there is no workflow. You point an MCP-capable agent at the server and the agent decides what to do. Configuration is container/image setup.

strengths: Container-per-agent is a real environment boundary, not just a filesystem boundary: an agent that `npm install`s garbage or starts a rogue server cannot pollute the host or its siblings.
Branch-per-agent makes the review surface something every developer already knows how to use — no bespoke patch UI.
Full command-history capture means you can audit what the agent actually executed, not just what it said it did.
MCP-native, so it plugs into whatever agent the team already uses instead of asking them to adopt a new engine.
'Discard failures instantly' — the cheap-abandonment property is a genuine workflow ergonomic, not just a safety feature.
weaknesses: No workflow layer at all: no steps, no ordering, no fan-out primitive you control, no resumption. It isolates agents; it does not orchestrate them.
No human-in-the-loop primitive — approval is 'look at the branch afterwards', which cannot gate an action mid-run.
Experimental stability; API and CLI churn.
Requires Docker/Dagger locally, which is a heavier dependency than weft's worktrees.
No cost or token accounting, so parallel agents can burn budget invisibly.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Isolate the *environment*, not just the working tree — give each write step a container so installs, daemons, and env mutations are discarded with the step.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktree isolates files but shares the host's node_modules, ports, env, and package manager caches. A write step that corrupts a global cache leaks across steps, and weft's node:vm fence explicitly is not a security boundary. Optional container-backed worktrees would close that gap without changing the ctx.integrate() contract.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: `cu terminal` — a first-class 'take over this step's environment interactively' escape hatch.
ideasWorthStealing.why: When a weft write step goes wrong, the human's only options are approve, reject, or edit-and-replay. Being able to attach a shell to the step's worktree at the point of failure, fix it by hand, and let the step complete would make gates far more useful than binary approve/reject.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Recording the complete command history of a step as a reviewable artifact attached to its branch.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft journals step inputs/outputs, but a write step's *actions* (every shell command the agent ran) are the thing a reviewer actually needs at ctx.integrate(). Journaling the command trace alongside the patch makes the gate reviewable rather than a diff-with-no-context.

projects.name: E2B
projects.language: TypeScript and Python SDKs; infrastructure in Go
projects.popularity: 13.5k stars shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24.
projects.positioning: The default 'secure sandbox as a service, with a real self-host path' for running AI-generated code. Firecracker microVMs give a hardware-enforced boundary — precisely the guarantee weft's node:vm fence explicitly disclaims. Not a workflow engine; it's the substrate a workflow engine would run untrusted steps on.

features.durability: Genuine VM-level durability: pause() snapshots both filesystem and memory (running processes, in-memory variables) and resume() restores the exact state — ~4s per GB of RAM to pause, ~1s to resume. Paused sandboxes persist indefinitely with no automatic expiry until .kill(). Timeout behavior is configurable to auto-pause instead of terminate, and that auto-pause is sticky across resumes. This is durability by memory snapshot rather than by journal — it does not give you an event log or edit-tolerant replay, but it survives a crash of everything outside the VM.
features.schemaValidation: None at the sandbox layer. Code Interpreter SDK returns structured execution results (stdout/stderr/results/errors) but nothing schema-driven.
features.humanInTheLoop: None. E2B has no approval concept; a human can attach to a sandbox but there is no gate primitive.
features.parallelism: Sandboxes are cheap and independent — Firecracker boots in roughly ≤125ms with a few MiB of per-VM overhead, so thousands of concurrent sandboxes are the intended usage. Parallelism is 'spawn N sandboxes', not a structured fan-out.
features.gitIsolation: None built in. You clone a repo into a sandbox; there is no branch/patch/integrate model.
features.multiProvider: Model-agnostic by construction — E2B runs code, it doesn't call models. Used by every major provider's agents.
features.costControl: Billing is by sandbox runtime/resources. Continuous-runtime limits (24h Pro, 1h Hobby) act as an implicit ceiling and reset after a pause/resume cycle. No token or USD budget concept.
features.observability: Sandbox metrics, logs, and lifecycle states (Running / Paused / Snapshotting / Killed); process and filesystem APIs for inspection. No agent-level tracing.
features.testing: No replay harness. Custom templates make environments reproducible, which helps test setup determinism.
features.authoringModel: Imperative SDK: Sandbox.create(), commands.run(), files.write(), pause/resume. Environments are declared as templates (Dockerfile-like).

strengths: A real security boundary: Firecracker/KVM hardware virtualization with its own guest kernel, which is the correct answer for running model-generated code you have not reviewed.
Pause/resume with full memory snapshot is a durability primitive nothing else in this cluster matches — a long-lived agent session can be frozen mid-process and revived a week later.

The infra is actually open source (Apache-2.0, Terraform-deployed, Nomad+Consul) with a documented self-host path on AWS/GCP/Azure/bare Linux — the open-source claim survives the vendor-disappears test.
Sub-second resume and ~125ms cold boot make per-step sandboxing economically viable, not just a special case.
Mature TS SDK, which matters for a TypeScript engine wanting to shell out to it.
weaknesses: Zero workflow semantics: no steps, no journal, no gates, no fan-out, no cost accounting. It is one layer below weft, not a competitor to it.
Self-hosting means operating a Nomad + Consul scheduling cluster — real ops burden, not a docker-compose.
Paused sandboxes never expire, so cost leaks are easy: you must explicitly kill them.
Timeout semantics are subtle (connecting extends rather than resets lifetime), an easy source of surprise bills.
No git-aware model; repo isolation is DIY.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Pause/resume of a live step with memory snapshot, and 'auto-pause on timeout' rather than 'kill on timeout'.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's durability resumes by replaying journaled steps. A long-running write step that is 40 minutes in has nothing to resume from. Backing write steps with a snapshottable sandbox would let weft suspend a step at a gate and resume the *same process*, rather than replaying it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Offer a hardware-isolated execution backend as a first-class alternative to the node:vm fence, with the fence downgraded to 'determinism gate only'.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft is already explicit that node:vm is not a security boundary. Wiring an E2B (or microsandbox) backend behind the same step API gives users a supported answer to 'can I run this untrusted step safely?' instead of a documentation caveat.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Explicit sandbox lifecycle states surfaced to the user (Running / Paused / Snapshotting / Killed) with a documented cost/latency figure for each transition.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's steps are either running or done. A visible suspended state with known resume cost is what makes long human gates operationally sane, and gives the daemon web UI something honest to render.

projects.name: Daytona
projects.language: Python, TypeScript/JavaScript (SDKs in Python, TypeScript, Ruby, Go, Java)
projects.license: Open-source license file present on the repo (AGPL-3.0 historically; verify current — not directly confirmed in this pass)
projects.popularity: The GitHub repo page reported 71.9k stars when fetched 2026-08-24 — treat the precise figure as unverified since it was read from a rendered page and is unusually high for this category. More important: the repo header states that as of June 2026 Daytona's core development has moved to a private codebase and the repo is no longer maintained, though it remains public and forkable.
projects.positioning: An 'elastic infrastructure runtime for AI-generated code execution and agent workflows' — sandboxes advertised as full isolated computers (own kernel, filesystem, network stack, vCPU/RAM/disk) booting in under 90ms, with stateful snapshots for multi-turn agent sessions. Positioned as the fast-cold-start alternative to E2B; now effectively a source-available artifact of a company that went closed.

features.durability: Stateful environment snapshots persist a sandbox across sessions so multi-turn agent workflows resume where they left off. Declarative image builder makes environment construction reproducible. Same shape as E2B: infrastructure-level state persistence, not an application-level journal or replay.
features.schemaValidation: None.
features.humanInTheLoop: None as a primitive.
features.parallelism: Elastic — sandboxes spin up in under 90ms, so per-task and per-agent sandboxes are cheap; concurrency is a scheduling property, not a workflow construct.
features.gitIsolation: Git operations are exposed as a first-class SDK surface (clone, branch, commit, push inside the sandbox), which is more than E2B offers, but there is no patch-capture/deferred-integration model.
features.multiProvider: Model-agnostic; SDKs across five languages so any agent stack can drive it.
features.costControl: Resource-based billing on the hosted service; no token/USD budget primitives.
features.observability: Sandbox-level logs, process and filesystem APIs, session management for long-running commands.
features.testing: None specific.
features.authoringModel: Imperative multi-language SDK plus a declarative image/snapshot builder.

strengths: Sub-90ms sandbox creation makes truly per-step isolation affordable — fast enough that isolating each write step costs nothing perceptible.
Git operations as an SDK primitive rather than 'shell out to git', which is closer to what a coding-workflow engine actually needs.
Widest SDK language coverage in the cluster (Python, TS, Ruby, Go, Java).
Declarative image + snapshot pairing gives reproducible environments with fast warm starts.
weaknesses: No longer maintained in the open: core development moved private in June 2026. Adopting it now means adopting a fork.
No workflow, approval, budget, or replay semantics at all.
Isolation strength claims ('own kernel') need independent verification against the actual runtime for any untrusted-code use.
License specifics should be checked before commercial dependence — historically copyleft.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Treat git operations as typed SDK calls against an isolated environment rather than shelling out.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktree steps ultimately drive git through the shell. A typed git surface makes the patch-capture path testable and lets the zero-model-call harness assert on git state without spawning processes.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Declarative image/snapshot definition paired with warm-start restore.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's edit-tolerant replay salvages step *results*; it has no story for the environment a step ran in. A content-addressed environment snapshot would let a replayed step start from the same dependency state, not just the same inputs.

projects.name: Modal Sandboxes
projects.repo: https://modal.com/docs/guide/sandbox (client library: https://github.com/modal-labs/modal-client, Apache-2.0; the platform itself is proprietary)
projects.language: Python SDK (client open source); platform closed
projects.popularity: Widely adopted commercial platform; Modal states its sandboxes support 50,000+ concurrent sessions. Star counts not applicable to the platform — unverified for the client library in this pass.
projects.positioning: Serverless-compute-first sandboxing: Sandboxes are 'secure containers for executing untrusted user or agent code', built on gVisor with additional custom syscall filtering. The pitch is that you get sandboxing on top of a real autoscaling compute platform (GPUs, volumes, secrets) rather than a sandbox-only service.

features.durability: Modal Volumes provide persistent filesystem storage across sandboxes; sandbox lifecycle is Created → Scheduled → Started → Ready → Finished with readiness probes (TCP and exec) to know when a service inside is actually up. Named sandboxes are unique per app, so re-requesting a name attaches to the existing sandbox instead of duplicating it — a lightweight idempotency key. No memory snapshot/resume equivalent to E2B pause. Durability is 'the volume survives', not 'the process resumes'.
features.schemaValidation: None at the sandbox layer.
features.humanInTheLoop: None.
features.parallelism: The platform's core competence — autoscaling fan-out of containers is what Modal is. Sandboxes inherit that: spawn thousands, they schedule.
features.gitIsolation: None built-in; documented use case is 'clone a repo and run its test suite' inside a sandbox, but branch/patch semantics are yours to build.
features.multiProvider: Model-agnostic; runs whatever you put in the image, including GPU workloads, which is unusual in this cluster.
features.costControl: Per-second resource billing; default 5-minute sandbox lifetime, configurable up to 24 hours, plus idle-termination. The short default timeout is an effective runaway-cost guard. No token/USD budget concept.
features.observability: Platform logs, metrics, and dashboards; readiness probes; tunnels/port mapping for reaching services inside a sandbox.
features.testing: No agent-replay harness; standard Modal local-development ergonomics.
features.authoringModel: Python-first imperative API — sandboxes inherit Function configuration (images, volumes, secrets), so the same declarative image definitions serve both.

strengths: gVisor plus custom syscall filtering is a serious, battle-tested boundary for untrusted code — weaker than a microVM against kernel exploits, stronger than a plain container, and far stronger than node:vm.
Sandboxes inherit the whole platform: GPUs, secrets management, volumes, autoscaling. Nothing else here gives you a GPU sandbox for free.
Readiness probes (TCP + exec) are a genuinely useful primitive that most sandbox APIs lack — knowing a dev server is actually listening before the agent hits it.
Named sandboxes give idempotent attach-or-create semantics.
Conservative 5-minute default lifetime is the right default for cost safety.
weaknesses: The platform is proprietary — no self-host, so this is a vendor dependency, unlike E2B or microsandbox.
Python-centric; a TypeScript engine drives it awkwardly.
gVisor is a weaker boundary than hardware virtualization for genuinely hostile code, a distinction that matters if a workflow runs attacker-influenced input.
No workflow, approval, git, or budget semantics.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Readiness probes (TCP connect / exec command) as a declarative part of a step's environment setup.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft workflows that start a dev server and then test against it currently need ad-hoc sleep/poll loops inside a step, which is exactly the nondeterminism the determinism gate is trying to ban. A declared readiness probe makes waiting a structured, journalable part of the step.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Named/idempotent resource creation — asking for a resource by name attaches to the existing one instead of creating a duplicate.
ideasWorthStealing.why: On edit-tolerant replay, weft re-executes steps whose content hash changed. If those steps provision external resources, replay duplicates them. A name-keyed attach-or-create convention makes replay safe for side-effecting setup steps.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A short, conservative default lifetime on any spawned execution context, with explicit opt-in to extend.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has token/USD ceilings but wall-clock runaway is a separate failure mode — a hung write step burns nothing in tokens and everything in time. A per-step default deadline complements the budget ceilings.

projects.name: microsandbox
projects.language: Rust (SDKs for TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, Ruby)
projects.popularity: 7.9k stars shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24; 416 forks. Self-described beta with expected breaking changes.
projects.positioning: 'Easy, fast, local microVMs for untrusted workloads' — libkrun-based microVMs launched as ordinary child processes, no cluster, no cloud account. This is the self-hosted, local-first answer to E2B: hardware isolation with roughly the operational weight of running a subprocess, which makes it the most realistic security backend for a local-first TypeScript engine like weft.

features.durability: Sandboxes are child processes with their own filesystem; persistence across runs is via mounted volumes rather than memory snapshots. No pause/resume-with-memory equivalent documented. No journal or replay.
features.schemaValidation: None; exposes code/command execution APIs.
features.humanInTheLoop: None.
features.parallelism: Each sandbox is an independent child-process microVM booting in under ~100ms on Apple Silicon, so many concurrent sandboxes are practical on a single dev machine — the key difference from cloud sandboxes, which need a control plane.
features.gitIsolation: None built in; you mount or clone.
features.multiProvider: Model-agnostic. Ships an MCP server so Claude Code and other MCP agents can drive sandboxes directly, plus Agent Skills support.
features.costControl: None — but because it runs locally on your own hardware, there is no metered cost to control.
features.observability: Process-level logs and exec results; nothing agent-aware.
features.testing: None specific.
features.authoringModel: SDK calls per language plus a CLI; MCP server for agent-driven use. Sandbox definition is image-based.

strengths: Hardware-level isolation (KVM on Linux, Hypervisor.framework on Apple Silicon, WHP on Windows) with no infrastructure to stand up — the single best fit for weft's local-first posture.
Sub-100ms boot means per-step microVMs are viable, not a special case.
First-class TypeScript SDK, so it is directly callable from a TS engine.
Apache-2.0 and genuinely self-contained: no vendor, no control plane, no account.
Cross-platform including macOS Apple Silicon and Windows, which cloud-only sandboxes make irrelevant but local engines need.
weaknesses: Beta, with the maintainers explicitly warning about breaking changes and missing features.
Requires virtualization support (KVM / Apple Silicon / WHP) — CI runners and nested-virt environments may not have it, which is exactly where a coding-workflow engine often runs.
No persistence/snapshot story comparable to E2B pause/resume.
Smaller ecosystem and less production mileage than gVisor or Firecracker-on-a-platform.
No networking policy story documented in the depth E2B/Modal offer.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Local microVMs as child processes — hardware isolation with subprocess ergonomics and no control plane.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the missing piece under weft's honest caveat that node:vm is not a security boundary. A microsandbox-backed step executor would let weft say 'untrusted steps get a real boundary' while staying a local-first npm-installable engine, no cloud account required.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Shipping an MCP server that exposes the isolation primitive itself, so external agents can request sandboxes.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already ships an MCP server over its Engine. Exposing 'run this in an isolated worktree and give me the patch' as an MCP tool would let Claude Code and Cursor users get weft's integrate-gated write model without writing a weft workflow.

projects.name: gVisor
projects.popularity: 19.1k stars shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24. Production-deployed at Google (GKE Sandbox) and underneath Modal Sandboxes.
projects.positioning: Not an agent tool — the isolation primitive several agent sandboxes are built on. A userspace application kernel (Sentry) written in memory-safe Go that implements most of the Linux syscall surface so workload syscalls never reach the host kernel; ships runsc, an OCI runtime that drops into Docker/Kubernetes. Relevant to weft as the reference point for what a real security boundary means versus a node:vm fence.

features.durability: Container-level checkpoint/restore exists in gVisor (save/restore of sandbox state) but is not an agent-workflow durability story. Not comparable to a journal.
features.schemaValidation: N/A.
features.humanInTheLoop: N/A.
features.parallelism: Runs as a standard OCI runtime, so parallelism is whatever Docker/Kubernetes gives you. Startup is faster than a VM, slower than a bare container.
features.gitIsolation: N/A.
features.multiProvider: N/A — it isolates processes, not models.
features.costControl: N/A.
features.observability: Syscall-level visibility is inherent: because Sentry implements the syscall surface, it can log and filter every syscall the workload attempts — a far richer audit surface than any container runtime.
features.testing: Extensive syscall conformance test suite; useful as a model for how to test a compatibility layer.
features.authoringModel: OCI runtime configuration (`--runtime=runsc`), plus platform selection (systrap/KVM) for the syscall interception mechanism.

strengths: A genuine, deployed-at-scale security boundary: the workload's syscalls terminate in a memory-safe userspace kernel rather than the host kernel, so kernel-exploit surface collapses.
Drops into existing container tooling — `--runtime=runsc` and you are done; no new orchestration.
Meaningfully faster startup and lower memory overhead than full VMs, which is why platforms pick it for interactive agent workloads.
Explicitly documents what it is *not* (not a seccomp filter, not a wrapper around namespaces, not a VM) — an intellectual honesty weft's node:vm docs already emulate.
Syscall-level introspection makes it possible to actually see what an agent's code tried to do.
weaknesses: Not hardware-enforced: a Sentry bug is a host-escape path, so it is a weaker boundary than Firecracker/KVM for genuinely hostile input.
Syscall compatibility gaps break some workloads (exotic filesystem, networking, or ioctl use).
Performance overhead on syscall-heavy workloads (I/O-bound builds, large test suites) is real.
Linux-only and needs host support; irrelevant for a macOS developer machine.
Nothing agent-shaped — it is infrastructure, and adopting it means adopting containers.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Publish an explicit, itemized threat model that says what the sandbox is not, alongside what it is.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already states node:vm is not a security boundary. gVisor's 'What it isn't' framing is the gold standard: name the specific attacks in scope and out of scope, so users can reason rather than guess. This is a docs change with outsized trust value.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Syscall/operation-level interception as an audit log, not only as enforcement.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's determinism gate bans Date.now/Math.random/network via AST rules and replaced globals. Recording every *attempted* banned call into the journal — instead of only failing — turns the gate into a diagnostic surface that tells the author exactly which line of a generated step is nondeterministic.

projects.name: Anthropic sandbox-runtime (srt)
projects.popularity: 5.1k stars shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24. Experimental (under anthropic-experimental).
projects.positioning: OS-level sandboxing for agents without containers: bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt (sandbox-exec) on macOS, a dedicated sandbox account with WFP egress filtering on Windows — plus a host-side proxy that enforces a network domain allowlist. This is the closest existing implementation of the boundary weft actually needs: process-tree-scoped, no daemon, no VM, works on a laptop.

features.durability: None — it is a process wrapper, not a runtime with state.
features.schemaValidation: None; configuration is a policy file (allowed read paths, allowed write paths, allowed domains).
features.humanInTheLoop: None directly, though it is the enforcement layer that makes 'auto-approve this tool call' safe in Claude Code — i.e. it converts approval prompts into policy.
features.parallelism: Wraps individual process trees; N sandboxed processes run concurrently with no coordination layer.
features.gitIsolation: None, but write-path allowlisting composes naturally with a worktree: allow writes only under the worktree path and the step physically cannot touch the rest of the repo.
features.multiProvider: Provider-agnostic; built for Claude Code but wraps any process.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: Proxy logs of allowed/denied network requests; OS-level denial reporting.
features.testing: None specific.
features.authoringModel: Declarative policy: filesystem reads use deny-then-allow (permissive default), filesystem writes use allow-only (restrictive default), network is deny-all with an explicit domain allowlist routed through host HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies.

strengths: No container, no VM, no daemon — it wraps a process tree using OS primitives, so it is installable and usable in exactly the environments weft already runs in.
The asymmetric default (reads permissive, writes restrictive, network deny-all) is the correct policy shape for coding agents and worth copying verbatim.
Domain-allowlist egress via a host proxy is the practical answer to exfiltration and prompt-injection-driven data leaks — far more useful than all-or-nothing network toggles.
Cross-platform including Windows, which most sandboxing projects ignore.
Small enough to read and audit, unlike a container runtime.
weaknesses: Explicitly experimental; not a hardened boundary against a determined kernel-level attacker (bubblewrap/Seatbelt are namespace/profile mechanisms, not virtualization).
macOS Seatbelt is deprecated-ish Apple surface with thin documentation; long-term maintenance risk.
Policy authoring is fiddly — over-tight write allowlists break builds in confusing ways.
No workflow integration; it is a wrapper you must invoke correctly around every step.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-step OS-level filesystem policy: writes allow-only (scoped to the worktree), reads deny-then-allow.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's worktree isolation is conventional, not enforced — a write step can `fs.writeFile` outside its worktree and weft finds out at integrate time, or never. Wrapping write steps in bwrap/Seatbelt with writes scoped to the worktree path makes the isolation actually true, using the same primitive Claude Code ships.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Network egress domain allowlist enforced by a host proxy, configured per step.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's determinism gate bans network access in the vm sandbox, but real write steps must reach npm and the model API. A per-step domain allowlist is the middle ground: the step gets network, but only to declared hosts, and every denied request is journaled — which is both a determinism signal and an exfiltration control.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Sandboxing as the mechanism that lets you *drop* an approval prompt, not just as defense in depth.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This reframes weft's gates economically: any action whose blast radius is provably contained by policy does not need a human. Pairing weft's ctx.gate with a declared policy means gates fire only for actions that escape the fence, which is the sustainable version of human-in-the-loop.

projects.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
projects.language: Spec in TypeScript schema; SDKs in TS, Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust, Swift
projects.popularity: The dominant agent-tooling standard; adopted by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, GitHub (VS Code ships an MCP registry with one-click server install). Specific star counts not verified in this pass. Current spec revision is 2026-07-28 (confirmed on the spec page).
projects.positioning: The interop substrate for tools/context, and — as of the Tasks extension — increasingly a substrate for *durable, long-running, human-gated* operations. weft already ships an MCP server; the strategic question is whether weft's gates, journal, and budgets should be expressed in MCP's vocabulary rather than a bespoke one.

features.durability: The Tasks extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks) is the relevant mechanism: instead of blocking, a server returns a CreateTaskResult with a taskId, initial status, ttlMs, and pollIntervalMs; the task must be durably created before the response is sent. The client polls tasks/get and can resume polling with the same ID after a client crash or restart. Status lifecycle is working / input_required / completed / failed / cancelled, with completed/failed/cancelled terminal. Optional notifications/tasks push updates via subscriptions/listen instead of polling. tasks/cancel is cooperative — the server acknowledges intent but need not stop.
features.schemaValidation: Tools declare JSON Schema input schemas and (since mid-2025 revisions) output schemas with structured content, so tool results are schema-checked at the protocol boundary. This is the closest thing in the cluster to weft's Zod-validated step returns, but there is no in-session repair loop — validation failure is an error, not a retry-with-feedback.
features.humanInTheLoop: Two mechanisms. Elicitation is a client capability: the server requests additional information from the user mid-operation, with a declared schema for the response. Combined with Tasks, a task transitions to input_required, the tasks/get response carries an inputRequests map of pending elicitations, and the client answers via tasks/update — an explicitly documented approval-gate pattern that survives disconnects. The spec's security principles also require explicit user consent before invoking any tool and warn that tool descriptions/annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted.
features.parallelism: No fan-out primitive. Concurrency is per-request; a client may have many outstanding tasks.
features.gitIsolation: N/A.
features.multiProvider: The entire point — one server serves any MCP-capable host (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Cursor, Zed, …).
features.costControl: None in the protocol. Progress notifications and TTLs bound duration, not spend.
features.observability: Progress tracking, cancellation, structured error reporting, task status messages, logging utility. Per-request capability negotiation makes the wire self-describing.
features.testing: Reference SDKs plus an inspector tool; no replay harness in the spec.
features.authoringModel: Declare tools/resources/prompts on a server; JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or streamable HTTP. Extensions (Tasks, Skills over MCP, MCP Apps) are opt-in and negotiated at initialization.

strengths: MCP Tasks is, in effect, a standardized wire format for exactly weft's core proposition: a durable handle to long-running work that can pause for human input and be resumed after a crash. Adopting it means weft's durability becomes interoperable rather than proprietary.
Elicitation gives human-in-the-loop a schema — the server declares what shape of answer it needs, so the client can render a real form instead of a free-text prompt.
Output schemas on tools normalize the 'validated step result' idea across the ecosystem.
Universal adoption: implementing the standard is now cheaper than not implementing it.
Extensions are negotiated and opt-in, so the protocol grows without breaking clients — a governance design worth imitating.
weaknesses: Tasks is an extension with per-client support variance — you cannot assume a host implements it, so servers must handle both result shapes.
Cancellation is cooperative and explicitly not guaranteed, which is weak for budget-ceiling enforcement.
Polling-by-default is chatty; notifications require additional opt-in machinery.
No cost/budget vocabulary at all, so weft's token/USD ceilings have nowhere standard to live.
The spec cannot enforce its own security principles — consent and sandboxing are entirely the host's problem, which is how prompt-injection-to-tool-call keeps happening.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Expose weft runs as MCP Tasks: return a durable taskId with ttlMs and pollIntervalMs instead of blocking, and map ctx.gate to the input_required status with an inputRequests payload.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already has an MCP server and a journal. Speaking Tasks would let any MCP host — Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code — start a weft workflow, disconnect, reconnect, see it paused on a human gate, answer the gate, and collect the result. That is weft's differentiator delivered through the ecosystem's own vocabulary rather than only through weft's CLI and web UI.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Schema-typed elicitation for gates: ctx.human.ask should declare the Zod schema of the answer it expects, and the UI should render from that schema.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft already validates every step return with Zod. Applying the same discipline to human answers means gate responses are validated and repairable the same way model outputs are, and the daemon web UI can generate the form automatically instead of hand-rolling one per gate.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-request capability negotiation with opt-in extensions.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's CLI, MCP server, and daemon UI all sit on one Engine. Negotiated capabilities would let each front-end declare which features it can render (gates, live budgets, patch review) so the Engine degrades gracefully instead of assuming the richest client.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Documenting that tool descriptions and annotations are untrusted input.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft workflows call agents that call MCP tools. The spec's stance — treat server-supplied text as untrusted unless the server is trusted — should be encoded in weft's provider layer, not left to the workflow author.

projects.name: Agent2Agent (A2A)
projects.language: Spec (JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S)); SDKs in Python, Go, JavaScript, Java, .NET, Rust
projects.popularity: Reported to have surpassed 22,000 GitHub stars as of April 2026 and 150+ supporting organizations including AWS, Cisco, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow — figures from Linux Foundation/PRNewswire announcements, not directly read off the repo page, so treat as reported-not-verified. Donated by Google to the Linux Foundation (project launched June 2025).
projects.positioning: The complement to MCP: MCP connects an agent to tools, A2A connects an agent to another *opaque* agent that will not expose its internal state, memory, or tools. Relevant to weft as the standard shape for sub-workflow delegation across a trust boundary — weft's sub-workflows with shared budget ceilings are the in-process version of the same idea.

features.durability: Task-centric: a task is a durable, addressable unit with a lifecycle and artifacts, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous patterns. Push notifications deliver completion/state changes to a webhook so a client need not hold a connection — the durability model is 'the task ID outlives the connection', same family as MCP Tasks.
features.schemaValidation: Agent Cards declare capabilities, skills, and input/output modalities; messages and artifacts are typed parts (text, file, structured data). Interaction-format negotiation is explicit. No repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: First-class via the input-required task state: a task can suspend awaiting human or client input and resume when supplied — the same pause-for-a-human pattern as MCP Tasks, standardized across agent boundaries rather than client-server. Roadmap work includes mid-task UX negotiation.
features.parallelism: A client can drive many tasks against many agents concurrently; no structured fan-out/join primitive in the protocol.
features.gitIsolation: N/A.
features.multiProvider: The purpose: any A2A agent talks to any other regardless of vendor or framework, without exposing internals.
features.costControl: None in the protocol.
features.observability: SSE streaming of incremental task updates, push notifications for async state changes, artifacts as inspectable outputs, and the task state machine itself.
features.testing: SDK-provided test servers; no replay harness in the spec.
features.authoringModel: Publish an Agent Card describing your agent, implement the task endpoints. Not a workflow-authoring format — it is an inter-agent RPC.

strengths: Opacity as a design principle: agents collaborate without exposing memory or tools, which is the right boundary for delegating work to a system you do not control.
Agent Cards give machine-readable capability discovery — you can find a suitable delegate at runtime rather than hardcoding.
Real neutral governance (Linux Foundation) and unusually broad enterprise backing, which makes it a safe bet as a stable interface.
Streaming (SSE) plus push notifications covers both interactive and fire-and-forget, so long-running delegation does not need a held connection.
input-required is the same pause-for-human primitive as MCP Tasks, so a single gate implementation can serve both.
weaknesses: Enterprise-integration flavored: heavier than a coding-workflow engine needs for local sub-workflows, and no coding-specific vocabulary (no patches, diffs, repos).
No budget, cost, or resource-limit concepts, so weft's shared-ceiling-with-sub-workflows semantics have no standard expression.
Overlaps confusingly with MCP for many users; the two-standard story remains a real adoption tax.
No structured parallelism, so fan-out patterns are reinvented per client.
Authorization schemes were still being formalized per the project's own roadmap — verify current state before relying on them.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Agent Cards — a machine-readable declaration of what a workflow/agent can do, its input/output modalities, and its skills.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's per-step AgentProvider routing is configured by the author. A card-style capability manifest for each provider (and for each weft workflow) would let routing be selected by declared capability rather than hardcoded name, and would let one weft workflow discover and call another.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Push notifications on task state change to a caller-supplied webhook.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon UI and CLI poll or watch locally. A webhook on 'run reached a gate' / 'run completed' / 'budget ceiling hit' is what makes a durable, hours-long workflow usable by a human who has walked away — and it is the transport that would make weft's gates reachable from Slack or Linear.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Opaque delegation: a sub-workflow that exposes only tasks, artifacts, and status — never its internal steps.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's sub-workflows share a budget ceiling with the parent, implying tight coupling. An opaque delegation mode would let a weft workflow call an external agent under the same budget and gate discipline without importing its internals into the journal.

projects.name: AGENTS.md
projects.license: Open/permissive (spec site and repo; MIT reported — verify)
projects.popularity: Over 60,000 open-source projects reported using it on agents.md as of the fetch on 2026-08-24, including OpenAI Codex, Apache Airflow, and Temporal's Java SDK; supported by 20+ agent tools including Claude, Cursor, Aider, VS Code, GitHub Copilot. Adoption figure is site-reported, not independently verified.
projects.positioning: The de facto configuration format for the whole 'run an agent on my repo' category — a README for agents, holding build commands, test commands, conventions, and security notes. It is the one interchange format every competitor in this cluster already reads, which makes it free distribution for weft.

features.durability: N/A — a static file, versioned with the repo, which is its own kind of durability: agent guidance is reviewable in PRs and travels with the code.
features.schemaValidation: Deliberately none. Plain Markdown, no required fields. Common sections (overview, build/test commands, code style, security) are conventions, not schema.
features.humanInTheLoop: Indirect but real: because the file is in-repo, changes to agent behavior go through normal code review. Guidance about what agents must not do without asking lives here.
features.parallelism: N/A.
features.gitIsolation: N/A, but nested AGENTS.md files scope guidance per directory — the closest file to the edited file wins, so a monorepo can give different subtrees different rules.
features.multiProvider: Its defining strength: one file read by Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Aider, Jules, VS Code, and others. No per-vendor duplication.
features.costControl: N/A.
features.observability: N/A.
features.testing: N/A.
features.authoringModel: Markdown. Precedence is by file proximity (nearest wins), and an explicit user prompt overrides the file.

strengths: Genuinely universal — solved the 'five vendor-specific dotfiles' problem by being boring and unopinionated.
Nested files with nearest-wins precedence is a simple, correct scoping rule for monorepos.
Being in-repo means agent guidance is versioned, diffable, and reviewed like code.
Zero adoption cost; a project supports it by reading one file.
weaknesses: No schema means no validation, no tooling, and no way to express machine-actionable policy (allowed commands, network policy, budget) — it is prose for a model, not configuration for an engine.
Precedence rules are convention; agents implement them inconsistently.
Nothing prevents drift between what AGENTS.md claims and what the build actually does.
Prose instructions are a prompt-injection surface if the repo accepts outside contributions.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Read AGENTS.md (with nearest-wins nested precedence) as a first-class input to weft steps, and journal which files were in scope for each step.
ideasWorthStealing.why: Every competing runner already honors it. weft honoring it costs almost nothing and immediately makes weft workflows behave consistently with the Claude Code/Codex sessions the same team already runs — and journaling which guidance applied makes replay faithful when the file changes.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Nearest-wins directory-scoped configuration as a general pattern for step config, not just prose.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft routes providers per step by author declaration. Directory-scoped defaults ('everything under packages/api uses the stricter reviewer') would scale better in monorepos than per-step configuration, and matches a convention users already understand.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Ship the machine-actionable half AGENTS.md deliberately omits — a schema-validated sidecar (allowed commands, network allowlist, budget ceiling, required gates) that weft enforces.
ideasWorthStealing.why: AGENTS.md is prose the model may ignore. weft's differentiator is enforcement: a typed policy file the determinism gate and budget ceilings actually honor turns 'please don't' into 'cannot', and is a natural complement rather than a competitor to the existing standard.

projects.name: Agent Client Protocol (ACP)
projects.language: Rust (official libraries in Rust, TypeScript, Python, Java, Kotlin)
projects.popularity: 4.1k stars shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24. Driven by Zed Industries; positioned as the LSP-for-agents.
projects.positioning: Standardizes the editor↔agent boundary the way LSP standardized editor↔language-server: JSON-RPC over stdio for local agents (agent runs as an editor subprocess), HTTP/WebSocket for remote (WIP). Reuses MCP's JSON representations where possible and adds coding-specific types — notably diff display and permission requests. Directly relevant to weft's front-end story: this is the protocol an IDE would use to drive a weft run.

features.durability: Session-based: a session holds conversation state across prompt turns. Remote transport is explicitly work-in-progress, so cross-disconnect resumption is not the mature path today.
features.schemaValidation: Typed JSON-RPC methods with schema-defined content blocks, largely borrowed from MCP; user-readable content is Markdown. Coding-specific types for diffs are the notable extension over MCP.
features.humanInTheLoop: A core primitive: the agent issues a permission request for a tool call and the client (editor) renders the prompt and returns the decision — this is the mechanism behind every 'allow / allow always / deny' dialog in an ACP-speaking editor. Tool calls stream with status and locations so the human sees what is happening as it happens, and diffs are a first-class content type so the human reviews changes inline rather than in a terminal.
features.parallelism: Prompt turns within a session are sequential; multiple sessions can run concurrently. No fan-out primitive.
features.gitIsolation: None — but the diff content type is the review surface a patch-based model needs, and is the standard way to render one.
features.multiProvider: The entire point: any editor to any agent. Official libraries across five languages; agent and client implementation lists maintained on agentclientprotocol.com.
features.costControl: None in the protocol.
features.observability: Streaming tool-call updates with status and file locations, plan/thought streaming, and Markdown-rendered agent output — designed for a human watching live.
features.testing: Reference libraries; no replay harness in the spec.
features.authoringModel: Implement the protocol on either side; not a workflow-authoring format.

strengths: Permission requests are in the protocol, not the app — so approval UX is consistent across every editor that speaks it, and an agent gets human-gating for free.
Diffs as a first-class content type is the right primitive for reviewing agent code changes, and it is exactly what a patch-returning write step needs to display.
Streaming tool-call status with file locations gives the human a live, legible picture rather than a wall of logs.
Deliberately reuses MCP representations instead of inventing a parallel type system.
Multi-language official libraries including TypeScript, so a TS engine can implement it directly.
weaknesses: Editor-centric: assumes a human is present at an IDE, which is the opposite of weft's crash-and-resume-hours-later posture.
Remote transport is work-in-progress, so the cloud/daemon story is immature.
Narrower adoption than MCP; ecosystem is real but concentrated around Zed and a handful of agents.
No durability, budget, or task-handle concepts — a dropped connection is a lost session.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Implement ACP on weft's Engine so any ACP-speaking editor can drive a weft workflow, with ctx.gate surfacing as a native permission request.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has CLI + MCP + daemon web UI over one Engine. ACP adds the fourth front-end — the editor — for free, and it is the one where a developer is most likely to actually answer a gate quickly. weft's gates map onto ACP permission requests almost exactly.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Diff as a typed, streamed content block rather than text output.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's write steps return patches that land at ctx.integrate(). Emitting those patches as ACP diff blocks means the review happens inline in the editor, with syntax highlighting and per-hunk accept, instead of in a terminal — turning ctx.integrate() from a yes/no prompt into a real review surface.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Streaming tool-call updates carrying status plus the file locations touched.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft journals steps on completion. Streaming in-progress locations would let the daemon UI show which files a long-running write step is currently modifying, which is the difference between a progress spinner and actual supervision.

projects.name: GitHub Agentic Workflows (gh-aw)
projects.popularity: 5,000 stars and 504 forks shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24. A GitHub Next project; the repo carries an explicit 'use with caution, at your own risk' warning.
projects.positioning: The most direct competitor to weft on the 'declare a repeatable agent workflow over my repo' job, and the strongest security architecture in the CI-native group. Workflows are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, compiled by `gh aw compile` into ordinary GitHub Actions `.lock.yml` files. The key insight — agent job runs read-only, writes are buffered as validated 'safe outputs' and applied by a separate job with scoped permissions — is a structurally different answer to the same problem weft solves with worktrees and ctx.integrate().

features.durability: Durability is GitHub Actions' durability: each run is a logged, re-runnable job with retained artifacts and logs. There is no step-level journal, no resume-from-step-N, and no edit-tolerant replay — a failed run is re-run from the top. Compilation to a checked-in .lock.yml means the executed workflow is pinned and diffable, which is a different and quite strong form of reproducibility.
features.schemaValidation: The frontmatter is schema-validated at compile time by `gh aw compile`, so misconfiguration fails before it ever runs — a compile-time analogue of weft's determinism gate. Safe outputs are validated against per-type schemas and sanitized before being applied. There is no validation of intermediate step results, because there are no typed steps.
features.humanInTheLoop: Structural rather than interactive. The agent cannot write; it can only *request* writes, which are then applied by a separate permission-scoped job — so the blast radius is bounded by construction rather than by a human answering a prompt. A staged mode lets outputs be previewed instead of applied. Beyond that, review is the GitHub PR itself, plus the platform's requirement that a human approve workflow runs on PRs from agents. There is no mid-run blocking gate, no notification routing, no escalation, no timeout policy.
features.parallelism: GitHub Actions job/matrix parallelism; multiple workflows fire on different events concurrently. No in-workflow fan-out/join primitive of its own.
features.gitIsolation: Each run gets a fresh ephemeral runner checkout. Writes reach the repo only through safe outputs (create-pull-request, push-to-pull-request-branch, create-issue, add-comment, add-labels, update-project, create-code-scanning-alert, …) with per-type max limits, required-label and title-prefix filters, and explicit target-repo/allowed-repos configuration for cross-repo work.
features.multiProvider: Genuinely multi-engine: GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, and Pi, selected in frontmatter. Per-workflow engine selection, comparable in spirit to weft's per-step AgentProvider routing but coarser (per workflow, not per step).
features.costControl: Actions minutes plus whatever the model provider bills; the compile step enforces configured limits and the platform enforces job timeouts. No token/USD budget with a hard ceiling.
features.observability: Full Actions run logs, artifacts, and the compiled .lock.yml as the ground truth of what ran; companion MCP Gateway centralizes and logs MCP access; the Agent Workflow Firewall logs and controls network egress.
features.testing: `gh aw compile` validates workflows statically before they run. No zero-model-call execution harness or deterministic replay.
features.authoringModel: Markdown body (the agent's instructions) plus YAML frontmatter (triggers, permissions, engine, tools, network, safe-outputs). This is the interchange format of the category: prose for the model, declarative config for the machine, compiled to a standard runtime.

strengths: Read-only agent + validated safe outputs applied by a separate scoped job is the best structural answer to prompt injection in this cluster — the agent literally lacks the credentials to do damage, so a compromised prompt produces a rejected output rather than a force-push.
Compiling to plain GitHub Actions YAML means zero new runtime to operate and the executed artifact is checked in and diffable — a supply-chain property weft's TypeScript workflows do not have.
Per-safe-output max limits, required-label filters, and title prefixes are fine-grained blast-radius controls, not just an on/off switch.
Companion Agent Workflow Firewall (network egress control) and MCP Gateway (centralized MCP access) address the two attack surfaces most agent runners ignore.
Multi-engine by frontmatter, so switching from Claude to Codex is a one-line change.
Compile-time schema validation catches configuration errors before burning a run.
weaknesses: No durable resume: a run that dies at minute 50 restarts from zero. No journal, no step salvage, no replay.
Markdown+YAML is not a programming language — no typed values flowing between steps, no loops or conditionals beyond what the model does in prose, no composition of workflows as functions.
No blocking human gate mid-run; approval is structural (outputs are constrained) or after-the-fact (review the PR), never 'stop and ask me now'.
Locked to GitHub Actions — no local execution, and running it means paying Actions minutes and living with runner cold starts.
No token/USD budget ceilings; cost control is indirect.
Self-described experimental with an explicit at-your-own-risk warning.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Read-only agent execution plus 'safe outputs': the agent emits a validated *request* to mutate, and a separate, differently-privileged process applies it.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is weft's ctx.integrate() generalized beyond git. weft isolates file writes in worktrees but a write step still holds whatever credentials the process has — it can post to Slack, call an API, push a branch. Making every side effect a schema-validated output object that only a privileged integrate phase can execute would extend weft's best idea to the whole surface, and would make prompt injection structurally non-fatal.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-output-type limits and filters: max counts, required labels, title prefixes, explicit allowed target repos.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's integrate step is all-or-nothing on a patch. Declaring 'this workflow may create at most 1 PR, only against these repos, only with this label' gives the author a static, auditable bound that holds even when the model misbehaves — enforced without a human present.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Compile the workflow to a pinned, checked-in artifact that is the actual thing executed.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft workflows are TypeScript that can change under you between runs; edit-tolerant replay exists precisely because of that. A compiled lock artifact per run — capturing resolved config, provider routing, model versions, and the determinism-gate verdict — would make 'what exactly ran' answerable from the repo rather than only from the journal.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A network egress firewall with a declared allowlist as a companion to execution, with denials logged.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft bans network in the determinism sandbox but real write steps need npm and provider APIs. A declared per-workflow egress allowlist, enforced and logged, is the missing control between 'no network' and 'all network'.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Compile-time validation of the whole workflow config before any model call.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has a determinism gate over step code. Extending static validation to routing, budgets, gate configuration, and integrate targets — failing fast before spending a token — is a cheap extension of machinery weft already has.

projects.name: Claude Code Action
projects.popularity: 8.7k stars, 2.1k forks shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24.
projects.positioning: The reference way to put Claude Code into GitHub Actions: @claude mentions in issues/PRs, issue assignment, or explicit prompts in a workflow file. Competes with weft for 'run an agent workflow on my repo' but at a much lower level of structure — it is one agent, one turn, on a runner, with no multi-step orchestration or durability.

features.durability: None beyond Actions: a run is a job, it succeeds or fails, re-running starts over. Progress is surfaced as a live-updating comment with checkboxes as tasks complete, which is presentation, not persistence.
features.schemaValidation: Can emit structured JSON outputs for downstream workflow steps to consume, but there is no per-step schema contract or repair loop.
features.humanInTheLoop: Trigger-level and review-level rather than mid-run. A human invokes it by @mention or assignment, and reviews the resulting commits/PR. The docs reference human approval workflows and commit signing; GitHub's own rule that a maintainer must approve Actions runs on PRs is the real gate. There is no in-run blocking prompt — the run is unattended once started.
features.parallelism: One agent per triggered job; parallelism is multiple triggered jobs. No fan-out primitive.
features.gitIsolation: Works on an ephemeral runner checkout, commits to a branch and opens/updates a PR. Isolation is 'it's a throwaway runner', not a patch-capture model — the agent commits directly rather than returning a patch for deferred integration.
features.multiProvider: Claude only, but across four backends: direct Anthropic API, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry, plus workload identity federation for credential-free auth. That is provider portability of a different axis than weft's Claude/Codex routing.
features.costControl: None built in — Anthropic API spend plus Actions minutes, bounded only by job timeout.
features.observability: Actions logs, plus the progress comment with checkboxes as a human-facing live view. Runs on your own runners so code stays in your infrastructure.
features.testing: None specific to workflow replay.
features.authoringModel: YAML workflow step with `prompt` and `claude_args` (aligned with the Claude Code SDK), plus documented solution templates for PR review, issue triage, and doc sync.

strengths: Lowest-friction path from zero to an agent working on your repo: one workflow file and an @mention.
Four model backends including Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry with workload identity federation — the best enterprise-auth story in this group.
Runs on your runners, so source never leaves your infrastructure.
The live-updating progress comment with checkboxes is genuinely good HITL *presentation* — the human sees the plan and its progress in the place they already are.
Commit signing support, which matters for repos with verified-commit requirements.
weaknesses: Single-agent, single-turn: no multi-step workflow, no fan-out, no sub-workflows, no typed values between steps.
No durability or resume; a timeout loses everything.
No budget ceilings — an unattended run can burn arbitrary tokens.
The agent commits directly rather than returning a reviewable patch, so there is no deferred-integration gate.
Claude-only, so no cross-provider step routing.
GitHub-only.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A live-updating checklist comment in the place the human already is — the issue or PR thread — showing the plan and ticking items as steps complete.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon web UI requires the human to go somewhere new. Rendering a run's step list as a progress comment (GitHub, Slack, Linear) meets people where they work, and it is the natural surface for a gate to appear on when weft needs an answer.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Multiple credential backends for one provider (direct API, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) with workload identity federation.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's AgentProvider abstraction routes between Claude and Codex. Abstracting the *credential/endpoint* axis separately from the model axis is what makes an engine adoptable inside enterprises that cannot call vendor APIs directly.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Curated solution templates (PR review, issue triage, doc sync) as first-class documentation.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's authoring model is plain TypeScript, which is maximally flexible and therefore maximally blank-page. A library of runnable canonical workflows is the cheapest adoption lever available.

projects.name: GitHub Copilot coding agent / Agent HQ
projects.positioning: The platform-incumbent answer to 'run an agent workflow on my repo', and the biggest structural threat to every project in this cluster. Agent HQ (announced late 2025, expanded through 2026) is mission control: assign tasks to Copilot, Claude, or Codex across repos from GitHub, VS Code, or mobile; watch real-time session logs; steer mid-run (pause, refine, restart); land in the resulting PRs. Custom agents are defined by in-repo AGENTS.md.
projects.popularity: Bundled with GitHub Copilot subscriptions, which is the largest installed base in the category. Exact adoption numbers unknown.

features.durability: Sessions run in an ephemeral GitHub Actions-powered development environment with a hard 59-minute maximum execution time per session. Work persists as branch commits and the PR, so the durable artifact is the branch, not a resumable run. No journal, no resume-from-step.
features.schemaValidation: None exposed to users. Repository custom instructions, AGENTS.md, hooks for validation/security scanning, and skills shape behavior, but there is no typed step contract.
features.humanInTheLoop: The strongest *steering* story in the cluster and the weakest *gating* one. Mission control gives real-time session logs and mid-run steer — pause, refine the instructions, restart — which is interactive supervision rather than a blocking approval. Structural gates: the agent works only on a branch, a human controls when the PR is created and merged, the agent cannot modify repos other than the one the task started in, and workflows on agent-authored PRs require human approval to run. Hooks allow custom validation and security scanning to run at defined points.
