features.parallelism: Assign many tasks across many repos concurrently from one mission control view; each runs its own isolated session.
features.gitIsolation: Branch-per-task in an ephemeral environment; changes surface as a PR. Network access from the environment is firewall-restricted by default with a configurable allowlist.
features.multiProvider: The headline of Agent HQ: Copilot, Claude, and Codex agents run on the same platform under one control surface — closer to weft's per-step provider routing than anything else at this scale, though selection is per task rather than per step.
features.costControl: Premium request quotas per subscription tier, plus Actions minutes. Quota-based rather than a per-run token/USD ceiling.
features.observability: Real-time session logs viewable mid-run, the PR diff as the output artifact, session history in mission control, and hooks for injecting checks.
features.testing: The agent runs your tests and linters in its environment; no replay harness for the agent run itself.
features.authoringModel: Assign an issue or write a prompt; behavior configured via AGENTS.md, repository custom instructions, custom agents, skills, and hooks. Not a programmable workflow — there is no way to express 'these three steps, then fan out, then integrate'.

strengths: Distribution: it is already in the tool every user has open, with no installation, and it is where the AGENTS.md convention gets enforced by default.
Multi-vendor agents under one control plane with a single review surface — the thing every point solution in this cluster is trying to become.
Mid-run steering (pause, refine, restart) is a genuinely different HITL modality from approve/reject, and closer to how humans actually supervise.
Network firewall on by default with an allowlist, and a hard 59-minute session cap — safe defaults that most self-hosted setups never configure.
Cross-repo task assignment from one view; mobile access means a gate can be answered from a phone.
weaknesses: No programmable workflow layer: you cannot express multi-step pipelines, typed data flow, fan-out/join, or deferred integration. Every task is one agent, one session.
59-minute hard cap with no resume kills genuinely long refactors.
Fully proprietary and GitHub-locked; no self-host, no local execution, no portability.
Quota-based cost control rather than hard per-run budget ceilings.
No durability guarantees beyond the branch — a failed session is redone, not resumed.
Opaque: you cannot inspect or test the orchestration logic, only its output.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Mission control: one view across many concurrent runs and many repos, with per-run live logs and the ability to steer mid-run.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon web UI shows runs; a cross-run control surface with mid-run steering — pause a running step, amend the prompt, resume from the journal rather than restart — would use weft's journal for something Agent HQ cannot do, since weft can actually resume from a step boundary instead of starting over.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Mid-run steering as a distinct primitive from approval: pause / refine instructions / resume.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's gates are yes/no/edit decisions at declared points. 'Pause this run wherever it is, let me amend the instruction, resume' is the interaction developers actually want when they see an agent going wrong, and weft's journaled step boundaries are precisely the safe points to offer it.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Network firewall enabled by default with a configurable allowlist, plus a hard session time cap.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's write steps run with the host's full network. Defaulting to deny-with-allowlist and a wall-clock cap per step matches what the incumbent does by default, and closes the gap between weft's strong determinism story and its weak egress story.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Hooks at defined points in the agent's lifecycle for custom validation and security scanning.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft validates step outputs with Zod schemas but has no place to run org-mandated checks (secret scanning, license checks, policy lint) between a step and its integration. A hook surface around ctx.integrate() is a small addition that makes weft deployable under a security team's rules.

projects.name: OpenAI Codex Cloud
projects.repo: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud (proprietary service; the Codex CLI at https://github.com/openai/codex is Apache-2.0)
projects.license: Proprietary service; Codex CLI open source (Apache-2.0)
projects.popularity: Bundled with ChatGPT paid plans; the Codex CLI is one of the most-starred agent CLIs (exact count unverified in this pass). Codex is also the origin of the AGENTS.md convention.
projects.positioning: Cloud-hosted, task-parallel coding agent: each task runs in its own isolated sandboxed container preloaded with your repo, configured by AGENTS.md and setup scripts. Tasks start from the web, GitHub PRs, GitLab MRs, Linear issues, or Slack — the broadest set of human entry points in the cluster, which is the interesting part for weft's gate-routing ambitions.

features.durability: Task-scoped containers; results are diffs and PRs. A task is a unit that completes or fails; there is no journal or mid-task resume. Environment reproducibility comes from configured setup scripts and container definitions rather than from replay.
features.schemaValidation: None user-facing.
features.humanInTheLoop: Entry-point HITL rather than mid-run gating: tasks are initiated by a human from the web UI, a GitHub PR, a GitLab MR, a Linear issue, or a Slack channel, and results are reviewed as a diff before a PR is created. Reviewing the diff before PR creation is the closest analogue to weft's ctx.integrate(). No blocking mid-task gate, no escalation, no timeout policy.
features.parallelism: Explicitly designed for it — 'start work in parallel and return as each task reaches a reviewable result'. Multiple long-running tasks run simultaneously off your machine, each in its own container.
features.gitIsolation: Container per task with the repo cloned in; output is a reviewable diff that becomes a PR on approval. The diff-before-PR step is real deferred integration.
features.multiProvider: OpenAI models only.
features.costControl: Plan-based usage limits; no per-run token/USD ceiling exposed.
features.observability: Task logs, the produced diff, and integration surfaces (PR/MR comments, Linear, Slack) as the notification channels.
features.testing: Setup scripts make environments reproducible; no replay harness.
features.authoringModel: Natural-language task plus AGENTS.md and environment setup steps. Not a workflow language. Internet access is configurable per environment, off or restricted by default.

strengths: Multi-surface task initiation — web, GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Slack — meaning the human never has to context-switch to a new tool to start or receive work.
Per-environment internet access policy, off/restricted by default, which is the strictest network posture among the cloud runners.
Diff review before PR creation is a real integration gate, not just after-the-fact review.
Parallel task execution with no local resource cost.
Originated AGENTS.md, so its configuration convention is the ecosystem's.
weaknesses: Proprietary and OpenAI-only; no self-host, no provider choice.
No workflow structure: one task, one agent, no typed steps, no fan-out you control, no sub-workflows.
No durability or resume semantics exposed.
No hard budget ceilings.
Strict network isolation, while safest, breaks dependency installation unless setup scripts pre-provision everything — an ergonomics tax.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Task initiation and result delivery through the surfaces people already live in — GitHub PRs, GitLab MRs, Linear issues, Slack threads.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has CLI + MCP + web UI, all of which require the human to come to weft. Adding Linear/Slack/GitHub as both triggers and gate-answer channels is the difference between gates that get answered in minutes and gates that block a run overnight.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Per-environment internet access policy that defaults to off, paired with a setup phase that runs *with* network before the agent phase runs *without* it.
ideasWorthStealing.why: This is the clean resolution of weft's determinism-versus-reality tension: let a declared, journaled setup step fetch dependencies, then execute the agent step with network denied. Determinism is preserved for the part that matters, and dependency installation still works.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: 'Return as each task reaches a reviewable result' as the interaction model for parallel work.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.parallel fans out and joins. A streaming variant that surfaces each branch's patch for review the moment it is ready — rather than waiting for the join — would make parallel write steps reviewable incrementally instead of as one large batch at integrate time.

projects.name: Google Jules
projects.language: N/A (hosted); Action wrapper published by Google Labs
projects.license: Proprietary service; the jules-action wrapper is published on GitHub (license unverified in this pass)
projects.popularity: Launched as a Google Labs experiment December 2024, beta at I/O May 2025, exited beta August 2025. Adoption numbers unknown.
projects.positioning: Asynchronous coding agent: clones your repo into an ephemeral Google Cloud VM, writes a plan, executes multi-file changes, runs tests, and opens a PR — then destroys the VM. Notable contrast with Codex Cloud: Jules keeps network access on so it can install dependencies and run builds, trading strict isolation for practicality.

features.durability: Ephemeral VM per task; code does not persist after completion and Google states it is not used for training. The durable artifact is the PR. No resume, no journal.
features.schemaValidation: None user-facing. Jules produces a plan before executing, which the user can review — a structured intermediate, but prose rather than schema.
features.humanInTheLoop: Plan-review-then-execute: Jules writes a plan first, which the human can inspect and adjust before changes are made. Output is a PR with summary, diff, and test output, reviewed on GitHub like any contribution. That plan-approval step is the strongest pre-execution gate among the hosted runners, but there is no mid-execution interruption.
features.parallelism: Cloud VMs allow many concurrent tasks — the documented pattern is running a large migration across many services simultaneously.
features.gitIsolation: Full VM per task, branch + PR as output, VM destroyed afterward. Isolation is maximal (fresh VM) and integration is conventional (PR review).
features.multiProvider: Gemini only.
features.costControl: Plan-based task limits; no token/USD ceiling.
features.observability: The plan, the diff, and test output attached to the PR. Less live-log visibility than Agent HQ or Codex.
features.testing: Runs your test suite inside the VM and includes the output in the PR — test evidence as a deliverable. No replay harness.
features.authoringModel: Natural-language task; AGENTS.md honored. A GitHub Action wrapper exists to trigger Jules from repository events, which is the CI-native surface.

strengths: Plan-first with human review before execution is a well-placed gate: cheap to review, and it catches misunderstanding before tokens are spent on the wrong change.
Full VM per task with destruction afterward is a clean isolation and data-retention story.
Network stays on, so dependency installation and real builds work without pre-provisioning gymnastics — the pragmatic opposite of Codex Cloud's stance, and worth understanding as a deliberate trade.
Test output shipped as part of the PR makes the agent's claim verifiable at review time.
GitHub Action wrapper gives an event-driven trigger path.
weaknesses: Gemini-only, proprietary, no self-host.
No workflow structure, durability, or resume.
Network-on means a compromised prompt has an exfiltration path — the explicit cost of its ergonomics.
Less mid-run visibility than competitors.
No budget ceilings.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Plan-as-a-reviewable-artifact: emit a structured plan, gate on it, then execute — with the approved plan journaled as the contract the execution is checked against.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's gates sit between steps that already ran. A plan gate before any write step is the cheapest possible human intervention point, and because weft validates every step with Zod, the plan can be a schema-validated object rather than prose — making 'did the execution match the approved plan?' a checkable assertion rather than a vibe.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Ship test output as a first-class part of the integration artifact, alongside the patch.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's ctx.integrate() reviews a patch. A patch plus the test run that validated it is a materially better review surface, and weft's journal already has the substrate to attach the verifying step's output to the patch it justifies.

projects.name: AgentOps
projects.popularity: 5.8k stars, 615 forks shown on the GitHub repo page when fetched 2026-08-24.
projects.positioning: Observability and cost tracking for agents: two lines of code to instrument, then session replay with step-by-step execution graphs, per-provider spend tracking, and a dashboard. The closest thing in this cluster to what weft's journal could expose if it had a rendering and analytics layer — and it is where weft's token/USD budget data belongs.

features.durability: Sessions are recorded to a backend (hosted or self-hosted) as traces — durable for analysis, not for resumption. It observes runs; it does not run them. Built on OpenTelemetry semantics, so traces are portable to other backends.
features.schemaValidation: None; it captures whatever the instrumented framework emits.
features.humanInTheLoop: None as a primitive. The dashboard is where a human inspects after the fact.
features.parallelism: Traces concurrent agent activity across multi-agent frameworks; parallelism is the instrumented framework's.
features.gitIsolation: N/A.
features.multiProvider: Very broad: OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Cohere, plus framework integrations for CrewAI, AG2/AutoGen, LangGraph, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Agno, and the OpenAI Agents SDK. Cost is normalized across providers, which is the hard part.
features.costControl: The distinguishing feature: token and dollar spend tracked per session and per foundation-model provider, with cost normalization across models. It measures rather than enforces — no hard ceiling that aborts a run.
features.observability: Session replay with step-by-step execution graphs, LLM call inspection, latency and error tracking, dashboards. OpenTelemetry-based, so it interoperates with existing tracing infrastructure.
features.testing: No deterministic replay-as-test — 'session replay' here means visual reconstruction for debugging, not re-execution.
features.authoringModel: Instrumentation: agentops.init() at the start, framework auto-instrumentation in between. Not a workflow format.

strengths: Cost normalization across many providers and models is genuinely hard and genuinely done — the exact capability weft's budget ceilings depend on being accurate.
Two-line instrumentation with automatic framework coverage; adoption cost is near zero.
OpenTelemetry foundation means traces are not locked into the vendor and slot into existing observability stacks.
Self-hostable on private infrastructure, which matters when traces contain source code and prompts.
Step-by-step execution graphs are the right visualization for multi-step agent runs, and are what weft's journal should render as.
weaknesses: Observation only — no enforcement, no gates, no budget ceiling that actually stops a run.
Python-only SDK, so a TypeScript engine cannot use it directly.
Provides no isolation, durability, or workflow semantics.
'Replay' is visual reconstruction, not re-execution, so it cannot serve as a test harness.
Cost accuracy depends on a maintained model-pricing table, which drifts.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Emit the journal as OpenTelemetry spans, with each step a span and each agent call a child span carrying token counts and normalized cost as attributes.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft has the richest execution record in this cluster and no standard way to export it. OTel export means weft runs appear in Datadog/Honeycomb/Grafana next to the rest of the system's traces, for free — and makes weft's journal legible to platform teams who will never open its web UI.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Normalized cross-provider cost accounting with a maintained pricing table.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's budget ceilings are only as trustworthy as its cost model. A versioned pricing table, journaled with each run so historical costs stay reproducible under replay, is the difference between a ceiling and an estimate.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Step-by-step execution graph as the primary debugging view.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's daemon web UI has the data — journaled steps, parallel branches, sub-workflows — to render a real DAG with per-node cost, duration, schema-repair attempts, and gate decisions. That view is the most compelling artifact weft could show, and no competitor here can produce it because none of them have the journal.

projects.name: Linear Agent Sessions (Agent Interaction Protocol)
projects.popularity: Linear is widely used for issue tracking; the agents API was in Developer Preview when fetched 2026-08-24, with GitHub Copilot's cloud-agent Linear integration reported GA on 2026-07-23 and Linear's own coding sessions (backed by Claude Code or Codex) shipped in June 2026. Adoption numbers unknown.
projects.positioning: Not a workflow engine — the best-designed *host surface* for agent work in a tool humans already use. The Agent Session model makes an agent a delegate on an issue, with its lifecycle rendered inline in the issue thread. This is the answer to 'where does weft's gate actually appear so a human sees it?'

features.durability: An AgentSession is a durable server-side object tracking the lifecycle of an agent task, created automatically on mention or delegation and updated by activity events. It survives the agent process; state lives in Linear, not in the agent. Webhooks (AgentSessionEvent) drive the integration.
features.schemaValidation: Typed activity kinds and a typed session object over GraphQL; webhook payloads are structured. No validation of the agent's work product.
features.humanInTheLoop: The most thoughtfully designed HITL model in the cluster, and it is a UX design rather than infrastructure. Agents are set as *delegates*, not assignees — 'humans maintain ownership while agents act on their behalf' — so accountability never transfers. Activity types render the agent's state inline: thought (an acknowledgement is expected within 10 seconds so the human sees the agent is alive), action, elicitation (the agent asks the human a question in-thread), response, and error. The human answers by replying in the issue thread. Linear's own coding sessions add a diff attached to the issue and structural/AI-guided review beside the discussion that caused the change, then merge from Linear.
features.parallelism: Many sessions across many issues concurrently; no in-session fan-out.
features.gitIsolation: Linear's coding sessions run through Claude Code or Codex in a secure session and produce a PR with a diff attached to the issue; the isolation belongs to the underlying agent, not to Linear.
features.multiProvider: Any third-party agent can implement the protocol; Linear's own coding sessions run on Claude Code or Codex, and Copilot's cloud agent integrates too.
features.costControl: None.
features.observability: The issue thread itself is the observability surface — every thought, action, elicitation, and error appears in context next to the discussion that motivated the work. Workspace admins manage agent permissions by scope (mention, assignment, customer data, initiatives), with webhooks fired on permission change so an app can react to revocation.
features.testing: None.
features.authoringModel: Implement webhook handlers for AgentSessionEvent and post activities back. Not a workflow format — a host protocol.

strengths: The delegate-not-assignee distinction is a small modeling choice with large consequences: accountability stays with a human, which is what makes teams comfortable letting agents act.

Elicitation as a rendered activity type in the issue thread means an agent's question reaches the human in the tool they already have open, with full surrounding context — the single best answer to 'why do gates go unanswered?'.
The 10-second acknowledgement expectation is a real UX contract: the human learns immediately that the agent is working, which is what makes async delegation tolerable.
Scoped permissions with revocation webhooks is a genuinely well-designed authorization model for third-party agents.
Placing the diff and review beside the discussion that caused the change preserves the thread from report to implementation — context weft's web UI cannot reconstruct.
weaknesses: Proprietary, single-vendor, and in developer preview with functionality subject to change — not a standard despite being protocol-shaped.
Locked to Linear; no value if the team uses Jira or GitHub Issues.
No durability, isolation, budget, or workflow semantics of its own — it hosts agents, it does not run them.
Overlaps with A2A and MCP without interoperating with either, which is a fragmentation cost the ecosystem pays.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Render weft's gates and human questions into Linear/Slack/GitHub threads as typed activities (thought / action / elicitation / response / error) rather than only in weft's own UI.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's gates are durable steps, which means a run can block for hours. Durability solves the technical problem of waiting; it does nothing about the human problem of *noticing*. Surfacing gate requests as activities in the issue thread that motivated the work is what converts a durable block into a fast answer.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: The delegate-not-assignee ownership model, recorded in the journal: every run has a human owner who remains accountable, and every gate decision records who made it.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft journals steps but the human is anonymous. Recording the accountable owner per run and the decider per gate turns the journal into an audit trail, which is the artifact a security or compliance team actually asks for.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: A liveness contract — the agent must emit an acknowledgement within a bounded time, and the UI shows the difference between 'thinking' and 'hung'.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft's long-running steps are opaque until they return a validated value. A required heartbeat activity per step, journaled, lets the CLI and web UI distinguish a slow step from a dead one, and gives the resume logic a signal about which steps were actually in flight when the process died.

ideasWorthStealing.idea: Scoped agent permissions with change webhooks, so revoking access is an event the running system reacts to.
ideasWorthStealing.why: weft routes steps to Claude or Codex with whatever credentials the process holds. Per-provider, per-capability scopes that can be revoked mid-run — with the revocation landing as a journal event that halts affected steps — is the enforcement counterpart to weft's budget ceilings.
